title: NTT Data Puts Ultralight Touch On Edge AI
text:
Technology narrows. As a rule of thumb, the more effective any given application, data service or platform becomes, it starts to experience a narrowing specificity as we custom-tune IT tools to make them more precision-engineered for whatever task they are supposed to perform.
A few decades ago, if an IT project manager wanted to deploy a point of sale and stock inventory tracking system for a golf club pro shop, it would need to buy a retail software solution and then attempt to graft its IT functionalities to fit its own operations. In this mostly bygone age, we used to work according to how the software wanted us to work. These days, with more considerately created software available to us, a golfclub pro shop retail operation can buy dedicated golf shop software. In the modern era, life is easier because can enjoy the use of Happy_HoleInOne™ (it doesn’t exist, but something like it does) that works with Zebra Technologies handhelds and is simpler all round.
Data - Where It’s At
Looking at how we can create smaller, task-specific AI models that make advanced AI capabilities more accessible in edge computing environments across the Internet of Things, NTT Data is narrowing and therefore (arguably) also widening and sharpening its approach in this zone. The IT infrastructure and services company has explained how its new Edge AI platform is designed to increase “operational technology” convergence (IT systems responsible for anything from physical manufacturing to call center operations, all of which with the potential for edge sensors or some form of digital enablement) to IT itself. NTT Data says its fully managed solution will do this by processing data when and where it is generated and unifying diverse IoT devices, systems and data.
“Our Edge AI platform represents a significant leap forward in driving AI at the edge securely and cost-effectively,” said Shahid Ahmed, group executive vice president of edge services at NTT Data. “By harmonizing data from disparate sensors and devices with lightweight AI models, powering all kinds of automation use-cases, NTT Data Edge AI is pioneering industrial AI adoption as the first fully managed offering, helping organizations modernize with tailored, industry-specific solutions.”
Potent Distillation
Ahmed used a couple of important words there: lightweight & tailored.
Both terms represent a narrowing or (for want of a kinder term) an amplification for specificity that results in a more potently distilled end technology product. Reminding us just how much focus there has been on generative artificial intelligence and the use of large language models, Ahmed and team remind us that these technologies are less practical for industries requiring real-time localized decision-making. NTT Data’s Edge AI solution therefore has been engineered to process massive data sets on compact computing platforms, using smaller, more efficient machine learning models for real-time AI.
“Computing and AI must happen where they create the most value for the enterprise; for many industrial enterprises, this is where the data is generated. By ingesting operational technology and IT data and [using] AI models to drive use case-specific results, the NTT Data solution takes another step towards realizing the industry 4.0 vision. Additionally, using task-specific small AI models will help drive AI democratization by making it easier for the enterprise to introduce AI where and when is needed, without the need for an extensive overhaul of an entire infrastructure,” said Pablo Tomasi, principal analyst at Omdia.
The technology on offer here from NTT Data is presented as an all-inclusive managed service platform; that’s technology-speak for a software system that comes with all the systems, tools and capabilities required for AI at the edge. The “managed services” aspect here includes the usual functions associated with any managed technology (everything from user and device authentication onward to maintenance, data storage, monitoring, backup and so on), but with additionally specific functions narrowed in on edge use cases (data discovery, collection, integration, computation power, seamless connectivity and so on) so that the whole deployment works with NTT Data looking after the AI model management in the back-end.
Shining Light On Shadow IT
According to IDC, worldwide spending on edge computing is expected to reach US$232 billion in 2024, an increase of 15% over 2023. This growth is being perpetuated by the growing number of connected IoT devices worldwide, expected to exceed 41 billion by 2025.
Whether it’s 41 billion or 42 billion, this surge does have side effects in terms of its ability to create so-called shadow IT (applications, data functions or physical devices and machines that have not been sanctioned for deployment by the IT management), so NTT Data is making much of its consulting data scientists’ abilities which are aligned to address shadow IoT challenges and AI infrastructure requirements. The total platform on offer here does this by auto-discovering, unifying and processing data from IoT devices and IT assets across the organization, simplifying AI deployment and management.
“Designed to support industry-specific requirements, the Edge AI platform leverages lighter, cost-effective AI models, enabling it to run within a small compute box. Edge AI will perform specific tasks, such as supporting safety or operational efficiency, by collecting data from disparate devices across a network environment, enabling instantaneous and secure data processing and analytics,” details NTT Data, in a technical product descriptor.
Edgeing Towards Edge Experts
The company says that manufacturing operations could benefit from improved predictive maintenance by accessing data from sensors, machinery, cameras and applications to plan and address failures. In addition, NTT Data’s Edge AI can monitor and optimize energy consumption in real-time, predicting energy spikes and optimizing machine usage, reducing costs and CO2 emissions with renewable energy. As well as 1,000 industry experts, NTT Data can evidence hundreds of use cases from predictive maintenance, fleet management, connected factories, energy consumption monitoring and sustainability. It has already trained over 500 sales experts globally to accelerate its Edge AI go-to-market efforts.
The move to narrow in technology functions for more specifically engineered use cases is being widely popularized across the IT landscape; after all, we now work with containers and microservices in serverless computing environments that have the ability to coalesce and function when needed, but also break apart into compartmentalized technologies ready for reassembly later. To take that leaner lightweight approach and apply it to edge AI services designed to make intelligent devices not just smarter, but also more manageable and sustainable sums up a lot of what NTT Data has done here.
Your connected refrigerator just got its service update and will now direct additional cool air over your yoghurt and poultry. You also just got an alert from the fridge image scanner: never keep bread in the fridge. Smart things are narrowing in and getting smarter.

title: AI Boom And Soaring Temperatures Trigger Global Electricity Surge, IEA Report Says
text:
Topline
Global electricity demand is set to grow at its fastest pace in nearly two decades this year, the International Energy Agency said Friday, with green sources continuing an upwards trend as rising temperatures, growing economies and artificial intelligence drive up energy consumption worldwide.
Key Facts
Global electricity demand is set to grow by around 4% in 2024, up from 2.5% in 2023, according to the IEA’s Electricity Mid-Year Update report.
If realized, the figure would represent the highest annual growth rate since 2007, the IEA said, barring exceptional years where demand rebounded in the wake of the global financial crisis and COVID-19 pandemic, and the agency said worldwide electricity consumption is expected to grow again by another 4% in 2025.
Increasing use of air conditioning will be a key driver of growing power demand as climate change pushes global temperatures higher, the report said, with numerous “intense heatwaves in the first half of 2024” already that boosted demand and strained electricity systems.
The rapid deployment and expanding uses of artificial intelligence are expected to push electricity demand up for years to come, the IEA said, though the agency said there remains a great deal of uncertainty on how much electricity data centers use.
Demand is expected to be particularly strong in India, surging 8% this year, as well as in China, growing more than 6%, with demand in the U.S. rebounding 3% amid steady economic growth, an expanding data center sector and rising demand for cooling.
Renewable sources of energy are set to expand sharply this year and are forecast to make up 35% of global electricity in 2025, the IEA said, a five percentage point increase from last year.
How Much Electricity Is Ai Consuming And Is It Contributing To Climate Change?
It is difficult to calculate precisely how much energy AI consumes but it is well known the technology uses a lot of power. The IEA said it is difficult to forecast AI-related electricity demand for the future as there is little reliable data on how much electricity data centers consume and many uncertainties over how quickly and widely the technology will be deployed. Many top companies leading the AI vanguard today like Microsoft, Meta, Google and OpenAI are not totally transparent about the energy and climate impacts of their AI research and products but reports suggest they are becoming bigger carbon emitters and, in turn, bigger contributors to climate change. While AI requires a lot of power to run, it is possible the technology could serve to reduce overall emissions if used to identify better ways of meeting climate goals. Billionaire philanthropist and Microsoft cofounder Bill Gates, who we estimate is worth $134.7 billion, is of this opinion. In June, he told journalists AI could help countries use less energy by making electricity grids and other technology more efficient in spite of the power needed to run more data centers. “Let’s not go overboard on this,” Gates said, crunching the numbers on how much energy AI is likely to use and save. “The question is, will AI accelerate a” reduction more than what it uses? “And the answer is: certainly.”
Surprising Fact
The amount of electricity generated from renewables globally is forecast to surpass electricity generated from coal for the first time in 2025, according to the IEA report. Solar power from solar cells alone is expected to meet roughly half the global growth in electricity demand in 2024 and 2025, the IEA said. Solar and wind combined meet as much as 75% of growth. Electricity generation from coal is unlikely to fall on account of strong demand in countries like India and China, which still rely on the heavily polluting fuel for much of their energy.
Crucial Quote
“It’s encouraging to see clean energy’s share of the electricity mix continuing to rise, but this needs to happen at a much faster rate to meet international energy and climate goals,” said Keisuke Sadamori, the IEA’s Director of Energy Markets and Security. “At the same time, it’s crucial to expand and reinforce grids to provide citizens with secure and reliable electricity supply – and to implement higher energy efficiency standards to reduce the impacts of increased cooling demand on power systems.”

title: Open AI & Thrive’s AI Health Coach Is A Bold Step Towards Hyper-personalized Healthcare
text:
Open AI and Arianna Huffington’s Thrive Global entered a landmark partnership earlier this month, announcing the creation of a new venture: Thrive AI Health. Sam Altman, CEO of Open AI, and Huffington, Founder of Thrive Global, co-wrote a piece in Time announcing the launch, explaining that using AI to harness the power of hyper-personalization can truly make a difference in improving daily behaviors and ultimately, improve health outcomes: “These are the ideas behind Thrive AI Health, the company the OpenAI Startup Fund and Thrive Global are jointly funding to build a customized, hyper-personalized AI health coach.”
Although digital health coaches are becoming more popular, this new venture aims to enable a hyper-personalized approach by learning daily routines to better accommodate healthy lifestyle changes. For example, the authors explain that perhaps the AI coach may recommend healthy changes that are congruent to a user’s existing tasks for the day: “go on a 10-minute walk with your child after you pick them up from school at 3:15 p.m.” or “start your wind-down routine at 10 p.m. since you have to get up at 6 a.m. the next morning to make your flight.”
This hyper-personalization is what will ultimately retain users and actually provide impact. While most AI driven coaches can harness health data to provide generic recommendations, few actually seamlessly embed themselves into the daily schedules of users, which makes it challenging to actually complete the daily health tasks. As the ecosystem of AI driven tools and digital health platforms grows, users are finding the variety of services increasingly siloed from one another; that is, while there is significant growth in the numerous services and platforms that can truly improve health outcomes, they often do not connect with each other, forcing users to approach their health in a disjointed manner.
For Thrive AI Health, the data, learning and platform pieces are already relatively mature, as both founding companies are kingpins in their own industries, respectively. Open AI’s revolutionary work with artificial intelligence has made it one of the industry’s dominant forces in using data and information to create insight driven systems. Congruently, Thrive Global’s platform has already seen incredible success with insight driven coaching and user outcomes.
Nevertheless, despite the success of its parent companies, the new venture will have its work cut out in an effort to prove just how seamless it can truly become, so that it does not become just another application and distract away from the key essence of the mission.
This is where Huffington explains that Thrive Global’s behavior change methodology will be deeply integrated and woven into the Thrive AI Health Coach platform. In addition to the latest science, the new platform will also be trained based on Thrive’s expansive IP content library, including Microsteps – “tiny daily acts that cumulatively lead to healthier habits,” and Resets, the platform’s stress reduction methodology. Hyper-personalization will truly distinguish this new service from the rest; Huffington emphasizes that “with an advanced long-term memory, the Thrive AI Health Coach will remember and utilize cumulative user histories and preferences, and be able to serve up Microsteps, nudges, and content from Thrive’s platform across the five behaviors in real time. As Thrive’s platform continues to grow, so will the capabilities of the Thrive AI Health Coach.” This will ultimately enable a curated and tailored service, specific to each user’s needs and desires.
Indeed, though this work is just getting started, this venture has broken-ground in an otherwise relatively nascent space.

title: Dispatch From InstructureCon: All Eyes On AI, Lifelong Learning
text:
Instructure may not be a name you know.
But if you’re in education, you are nearly certain to know their core product, Canvas. The learning management system is nearly ubiquitous. As of last year, the company said that about half of all college students and approximately one in three K-12 school districts use Canvas.
This means that what Instructure does impacts millions of students, teachers, and education providers. It also means that what company leaders say, or promise, or are working on – that matters too. Fortunately, Instructure hosts a well-attended and anticipated annual conference with educators, administrators, and innovators, called InstructureCon.
I was fortunate enough to attend last year. Although my schedule did not permit my in-person participation this year, as the conference opened, I was able to sit down with Shiren Vijiasingam, Instructure's Chief Product Officer, for a remote conversation about what Instructure was planning and thinking about for its services and, consequently, for its customers and partners.
Vijiasingam described InstructureCon as “edtech’s burning man.” Having been last year, that feels exuberant. But that’s excusable. Vijiasingam is exuberant about what he and his team are doing. It’s impossible to miss.
“We are continuing to iterate our core LMS,” Vijiasingam said. “We’re strengthening our tools and continuing to build on what is clearly a lifelong learning journey for most people. Teaching and learning don’t stop at a degree or graduation anymore, and we’re really embracing that as part of our approach,” he said.
But, Vijiasingam said, the two little letters that were on everyone’s mind were also forefront for his team, and for his presentations at the conference. Those letters, of course, are “A” and “I.”
“We are talking about and thinking about AI along this progression, akin to a hierarchy of needs,” Vijiasingam said. “That progression follows along how it’s being used, from basic awareness and readiness, to internalizing and owning your own artificial intelligence tools and systems that we can build on to or connect with,” he said.
It’s the tiered thinking about AI adoption and use in education that will drive Instructure’s product lines in the near term and may also work as a make-shift template for education providers to assess their own individual and institutional positioning.
As described by Vijiasingam, the first tier of education AI is awareness and willingness to try it out. “The next tier,” he said, “is the people who are already doing basic things with LLM.” An LLM is a large language model that powers generative AI tools such ChatGTP.
“Those folks in tier two, are doing things like generation of content, using AI to generate questions and ideas," Vijiasingam said. “And it’s in this second-tier area where we’ve seen the biggest proliferation of solutions out there, coming into the market from a host of new startups and even some older companies,” he said.
Next, in Instructure’s way of thinking about it, is the group of people for whom AI has changed the way they work or teach. Using AI to navigate a large, remote course, for example.
“Imagine trying to read and wade through a conversation thread that’s four, five conversations deep across a thousand students,” said Vijiasingam. “Good AI tools can summarize those conversations, allow you to ask questions of the summaries. It can even have tools that help drive equity,” he said. As an example, he said AI can help students search for things in their native language, get results in English, and add to a discussion. Or allow students to compose a text in their native language and easily convert it back to English.
Finally, tier four, Vijiasingam says, is where institutions are building and bringing their own LLM to the party. Those making big investments and big bets on AI are coming to Canvas with their eyes on integration and interoperability.
“Working with customers and partners to build out tools and services in tier three and tier four is the sweet spot for us,” Vijiasingam said.
We are close, he says, to the point where teachers and other teaching leaders can ask simple language questions of their data and unearth actionable information. “Show me all my students who missed two assignments and are scoring below 70 percent,” Vijiasingam offers as an example. “Using these tools in these ways will make data accessible, give meaning to the people looking for real insights in haystacks of data,” he said.
Looking ever further ahead, Vijiasingam talks about Instructure’s work on developing a standard for badging and a standard for comprehensive learning records. Goals, he says, that relate back to some of Instructure’s acquisitions and the company’s ongoing focus on learning anywhere, all the time, both formally and informally.
“It’s not new for us,” Vijiasingam said. “But post-pandemic we are seeing a deeper appreciation of lifelong learning and non-degree programs at traditional institutions, as well as those that exist outside those traditional institutions.”
Instructure is so influential and their shadow so large that, if you follow education at all, it’s worth looking at whatever they’re looking at. For now, Vijiasingam has his gaze firmly fixed on AI and the far horizon of continuous teaching and learning.

title: Widespread Technology Outages And The Imperative For AI Guardrails
text:
Friday’s global technology outage should serve as a stark reminder of the potential dangers of overreliance on artificial intelligence and cloud-based services for critical operations. These disruptions underscore the need for robust guardrails to ensure that our increasing dependence on AI does not compromise essential services and human safety in the future.
A Wake-Up Call: The Global IT Outage
The world woke up Friday to a massive IT outage, driven by a patch update from security company CrowdStrike, which in turn led to a widespread blue-screen issue on Windows-operated computers. This disruption affected multiple industries worldwide, highlighting the risks of relying on a single technology for mission-critical operations. The outage, one of the largest in recent history, has grounded planes in the U.S., halted trains in the U.K., and left TV stations unable to broadcast. The full magnitude of the issue will probably not be known for days. This should prompt businesses, government institutions, and especially tech companies to reconsider their dependence on single providers and explore strategies to enhance their operational resilience.
The incident serves as a crucial lesson in the interconnected nature of modern business technology. Major cloud and software-as-a-service providers, while offering significant benefits, also introduce risks of single points of failure. We have seen this in the past with cybersecurity outages caused by SolarWinds and Kaseya. When multiple companies depend on the same critical infrastructure, a disruption can cascade across various sectors, halting operations and causing widespread chaos, as we saw today.
The Risks Of Overreliance On AI
As AI technology continues to advance, the potential for overreliance becomes a pressing concern. Overreliance on AI occurs when users start accepting AI outputs without sufficient scrutiny, leading to errors and a loss of trust in AI systems. This can be particularly dangerous in fields requiring precise and critical decision making, such as healthcare, air transport, military use, judicial oversight, and more.
Consider the scenario of an emergency heart or brain surgery scheduled based on AI-driven systems. If the underlying technology fails due to a patch update from CrowdStrike or another company in the software supply chain, such as a machine not rebooting correctly, the consequences could be fatal. In military use, AI systems could make decisions to launch attacks or be slow to counterstrike without human intervention, leading to catastrophic outcomes in either scenario. Similarly, a judge overrelying on AI to interpret the law and issue a ruling without proper oversight could result in grave injustices. These are only a few examples of what overreliance on AI could mean.
Ensuring appropriate guardrails and safeguards to avoid overrelying on AI use is essential to prevent such catastrophic outcomes.
Human Oversight: The Last Line Of Defense
One of the primary goals of AI system design should be to empower users to develop appropriate reliance on AI, with robust human oversight. This is critical, as a few wise policymakers and practitioners call for greater human involvement to act as the final safeguard against AI failures. These calls need to be joined by industry luminaries to show they are responsible citizens, and not just driven by greed and technological wizardry. Sam Altman, Elon Musk, Sundar Pichai, Satya Nadella, and other leading CEOs should join in a pact to ensure AI development is not inadvertently stunting human growth.
While AI offers numerous benefits, such as enhanced information processing and improved decision making, it cannot replace human emotional nuance, critical thinking, and ethical considerations. AI overreliance leads to multiple biases, including confirmation bias and the overestimation of AI explanations. Our biggest fear should be when people stop learning how to think and overrely on AI outputs. What happens when there is an outage? Will the surgeon not know how to operate to save a life? Will the air traffic controller forget how to help flights land safely without AI-driven technology? Overreliance on AI can lead to vulnerabilities, ethical dilemmas, and a decline in personal growth, thinking skills, and learning opportunities.
Balance And Diversification
The recent global outage and growing AI integration into daily operations highlight the urgent need for balanced technology strategies guided by proven and solid principles that have withstood the tests of time. Businesses must diversify their technology dependencies, implement robust contingency plans, and ensure strong human oversight of AI and technology systems.
AI and technology in general should be viewed as tools to augment human capabilities, not replace them. By striking the right balance, we can harness the power of AI while safeguarding against its potential risks, ensuring that technology serves humanity without compromising safety and reliability.

title: Council Post: Addressing AI Risks: Protecting Your Organization In The Age Of Generative Tools
text:
John Bruggeman, CISSP, consulting (CISO) for CBTS and OnX, both are MSPs and MSSPs.
When I'm asked, "What risk does AI present to an organization?" I respond, “What kind of AI are you concerned about?” Often, leaders aren't aware that there are various flavors of artificial intelligence (AI), so I want to make sure we're talking about the same thing.
There's a good Forbes article by Naveen Joshi that discusses seven ways to define or classify AI. He describes four main types of AI processing: reactive, limited memory, theory of mind and self-aware. Then, he presents three broad categories of AI: artificial narrow intelligence (ANI), artificial general intelligence (AGI) and artificial super intelligence (ASI).
Only the first two types of AI exist at this point. IBM’s Deep Blue is an example of reactive (it has no memory and must be programmed to do everything), and Alexa and Siri are examples of limited-memory AI. Most people think of limited-memory AI when they say AI.
When you think of limited-memory AI, you're probably not considering it in those terms though. You think of a tool that uses machine learning (ML), predictive analytics (PA) or a large language model (LLM) with a generative pre-trained (GPT) interface, such as ChatGPT.
Now that we've defined the terms, you're probably thinking about the risks that GPT—in tools like ChatGPT, Microsoft’s Copilot or Google’s Gemini—present to your business or organization. Although this topic has been widely discussed, I'll highlight the principal risks and then discuss how I've seen threat actors use them and ways you can protect your organization.
Top Four GPT Risks
First, here are the four major risks of GPT tools.
1. Social Engineering: Tools like ChatGPT can write extremely convincing phishing emails from simple prompts, and other GPT tools can create phishing phone calls that sound like a real person or fake videos (paywall) that can be used to trick someone in a video call. We can no longer rely on our old techniques to spot phishing emails, phone scams or video deepfakes.
2. Accuracy: GPT tools can give results that are correct, incorrect or somewhere in between. The issue is that AI will present incorrect answers with extreme confidence. The generated answer to a prompt can be 100% wrong but sound 100% right. As the user of the tool, you must already know if the answer is right, wrong or mostly right or wrong. And if you think that repetitiveness is a sign of accuracy, think again: You won't get the same answer to the same prompt (or question) every time. GPT tools aren't deterministic, which means you really need to know the right answer before you ask it a question.
3. Data Privacy: There are countless examples of employees uploading sensitive or confidential corporate data into open GPT tools. That data is then incorporated into that tool's training data. An article from Forbes contributor Gene Marks details the risks of using GPT tools to help with business processes like analyzing spreadsheets, taking meeting notes and summarizing documents. You need to know where your data is and make sure it doesn’t end up in AI.
4. Data Poisoning: Because generative tools require large datasets, developers often train tools like ChatGPT and Gemini on billions of websites. Google recently partnered with Reddit to include content more easily from Reddit in Google search results. This can be a good thing and potentially a bad thing. It's good that all the human-generated content can now be quickly searched and bad in that the goofy, satirical and misinformative posts on Reddit are also elevated. An example of this is Google’s own AI search, which returned results from Reddit that suggested you add non-toxic glue to your pizza when asked how to make cheese stick better to pizza.
Mitigating The Risks
Now that we've identified the four risks, how can we mitigate them? Thankfully, cybersecurity teams that are prepared and knowledgeable in AI are addressing the risks that organizations are facing. Here are some tools you can use.
1. Social Engineering: Cybersecurity companies have been integrating ML and PA for over a decade to prevent phishing emails. Don’t rely on security tools alone to prevent social engineering attacks, but start there. There are many free AI-detection tools out there that can help determine if an email was written by generative AI. In fact, you can even paste an email into ChatGPT and ask if it wrote it.
2. Accuracy: Tools are being developed to monitor generative content, but the best tool is human oversight. Companies risk financial losses if they remove human oversight from the generative AI cycle. You will need to move carefully while you evaluate the accuracy of your AI model.
3. Data Privacy: The solution to minimizing the risk of staff uploading organization data into GPT systems is a combination of policy and governance with data loss prevention tools. Employees need to know what they can and can't upload to ChatGPT and other generative AI tools, so communicate your AI policy to all staff.
4. Data Poisoning: To help prevent data poisoning, implement data sanitization, regular monitoring and secure data handling. These controls are what you do anytime you expose an application to the internet.
If your organization is looking to adopt generative AI, start with these simple steps. From there, you'll be in a better position to control and benefit from AI instead of creating risk.

title: The Transformative Power Of Generative AI And Knowledge Management
text:
In today’s fast-paced business landscape, the need for speed has become a driving force. Organizations that fail to adapt quickly to changing market demands often fall behind their competitors. This realization has led to a shift in operating models, where traditional policies and processes have given way to a culture of fail-fast experimentation and agile working methods.
Collaboration And Knowledge-Sharing
At the heart of this transformation lies the importance of collaboration. Organizations must break down silos and enable seamless information sharing across departments, allowing insights and issues to flow freely and trigger the development of new ideas or solutions. Knowledge management and generative AI (genAI) are two powerful enablers of this new way of working.
Combining knowledge management and genAI can unlock a new level of knowledge-sharing and collaboration. Users can now seamlessly ask questions and receive personalized responses. This conversational approach to knowledge access and utilization can foster a more engaging and efficient knowledge-sharing environment, ultimately driving innovation and business success.
For example, IT operations professionals can improve decision-making by using AI to process vast amounts of data quickly, providing insights that humans might miss. Humans, on the other hand, can add critical judgment and ethical considerations to AI-generated recommendations.
Embracing Agility
Traditional knowledge management practices often followed a waterfall methodology, where knowledge articles were meticulously crafted and published, only to become outdated when they reached the end users. This approach no longer aligns with the need for speed. Instead, organizations are embracing a more agile approach, capturing knowledge snippets in the workflow and making them immediately available to everyone, even if the information is not perfectly polished.
The introduction of genAI can accelerate this agility even further. By applying genAI to knowledge management, many time-consuming tasks, such as creating summaries, generating metadata, and formatting content, can be automated. This frees up knowledge workers to focus on more value-added activities while ensuring that knowledge is accessible and easily consumable by all users, regardless of their technical expertise.
Knowledge-Capacity Building
The success of this integration between knowledge management and genAI hinges on the organization’s knowledge capacity. Outdated or neglected knowledge repositories can propagate inaccurate or irrelevant information, resulting in the dreaded “hallucinations” that can plague generative AI systems. To combat this, organizations must prioritize the active curation and maintenance of their knowledge assets, ensuring that the information fed into the genAI models is accurate, up to date, and valuable.
Beyond managing the knowledge, organizations must also focus on empowering their knowledge community. This means breaking down the traditional silos and barriers that have often stifled the free flow of information and ideas. By fostering a culture of trust, where knowledge-sharing is encouraged and valued, organizations can unlock the true potential of their employees, allowing them to contribute their insights and spark innovative solutions.
The Transformative Power Of Generative AI And Knowledge Management
While the potential of this convergence is undeniable, organizations must also be mindful of the challenges that come with it. Issues such as bias, data quality, and continuous training and refinement must be addressed to ensure the reliable and ethical deployment of genAI within the knowledge-management ecosystem.
By embracing the synergy between knowledge management and genAI, organizations can position themselves as champions in the knowledge economy. This transformation requires a shift in mindset, from simply capturing knowledge to actively cocreating it, as well as shifting from finding information to discovering new possibilities. Organizations can unlock unprecedented levels of innovation, collaboration, and business success by empowering their knowledge community, fostering a culture of trust, and leveraging the capabilities of genAI.
The Future Looks Bright
The future of knowledge work is undoubtedly bright, with the convergence of knowledge management and genAI poised to revolutionize how organizations operate. By embracing this powerful combination, leaders can empower their teams, drive innovation, and position their organizations for long-term success in the ever-evolving knowledge economy.
