title: How To Get Your Team To Use ChatGPT Better (Increase Profit Margins)
text:
Even now, founders are severely underestimating the power of ChatGPT and other AI tools. Rather than empowering their teams to use them well, they are struggling through alone. They are being distracted by shiny new objects, testing out tools that don’t apply to their business, and experiencing AI overwhelm when they have too much to do.
Without the time to spend getting the most out of each tool, most frustrated founders give up. Others use generative AI tools successfully, but in private. They directly compare the output with that of their team, pitting the two against each other. But this misses the point. It misses opportunities. This AI tool madness has to stop.
Here’s how to empower your team members to use ChatGPT (and other AI tools) better, to grow your business without them feeling threatened and, most importantly, without you wasting time.
Empower your team to use AI: grow your business together
Remember your main business goal
Don’t sign up for a bunch of tools that claim to do things that you don’t need to do. Just because you can create TikTok scripts and videos in a few clicks, doesn’t mean you should. Start with what your business already does and go from there.
Make sure anything you put in place aligns with your main business goal, which should be crystal clear for everyone in your team. What are they doing and why are they doing it? Don’t deviate from the answer. Don’t let yourself go down rabbit holes until you’ve covered the foundations. It will only get messy.
Find tools that align
Write down the processes you currently run, that contribute to your main business goal. Write down the output you currently produce and the daily tasks each team member does. This is your shopping list for AI tools and prompts.
Don’t miss anything out. Customer emails, recording meetings, sending newsletter updates, writing blogs, YouTube scripts, showing up on social media. Every action is a series of processes, many of which can be supercharged when you apply AI.
Go through this list and look at each element to work out what AI can help with. Use ChatGPT, Zapier and simple automations to replace human tasks with machines, so the humans can do higher value work. Don’t use AI when a spreadsheet will do. This doesn’t need to be complicated.
Experiment with output
For a simple way of your team applying AI to their work, challenge them to increase their output with AI tools. If they can respond to 6 customer service requests each hour, see if they can use AI to make that 12, then 20 and beyond. If they write articles for your site, how can they use ChatGPT to come up with ten times more ideas, ten times more article outlines, and have the content written and edited to a higher standard, faster?
When AI gets involved, you don’t need to compromise between quality and quantity. With the right moves, tools and prompts, you can have both. Don’t fall for the notion that all AI-generated content is generic and waffly. It’s absolutely not true.
Improve the prompts
Your team should not be using any subpar prompts. Instead, spend more time making the prompts incredible. Follow the rules for what makes a good prompt, test, re-prompt and keep iterating, then encourage your crew to save each super prompt somewhere it’s easy to access, for every future use. Have a shared library for maximum productivity.
This part of the process is front-end loaded but it will save you hours and make you money. Hire a consultant to help you with your prompt wording. Get a second opinion on the output. Find prompt lists curated by generative AI experts. Research, understand, and don’t prompt from scratch each time.
Assess together
This work should be fun. Now, no one in your team has to do boring work that is below their potential. By using AI openly, with your assistance, their output can be higher and they can achieve better results. They won’t feel like you’re trying to replace them. Your best team members will enjoy seeing what’s possible. They’ll be motivated to raise the bar and contribute more with their every hour.
Look at the results together. Measure impressions, engagement and leads generated from their work. Collect feedback from customers about the new-and-improved written communications, keep an eye on web traffic now there’s more content out there. Assess every metric, figure out what has made the difference and understand where to go next.
Increase your output and profit together with your team: ChatGPT and AI tool best practice for ambitious companies
If your team isn’t using AI properly, your business is missing out. Don’t test out AI tools with the goal of replacing your humans. Instead, empower them to test out tools with the goal of increasing output. The bar has been raised, the standards can be higher, and there’s no excuse to not do this.
Run a meaner, leaner team, supercharge your business, and enjoy the curveball that the influx of AI tools has presented. The founders that figure this out will take all the marbles. Make sure that’s you.

title: On Using Generative AI For Coping With Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACEs)
text:
An important realm that doesn’t get as much attention as is warranted consists of Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACEs). This is a crucial arena that considers the immediate-term, near-term, medium-term, and long-term consequences underlying what can adversely happen to a young person during childhood.
ACEs can and often do result in lifelong negative impacts.
One aim would be to try and ensure that no child ever experiences any ACEs. That’s a spirited goal that we can all rally around. But, unfortunately, then reality sets in. You see, there is a surprisingly high chance that a child will likely experience an ACE. I’ll be walking you through the alarming statistics on the frequency of ACEs. My primary focus here will be on ACEs in the United States, but I ask that you keep in mind that ACEs occur throughout the globe.
Okay, go ahead and take a deep breath, this is obviously a quite heavy topic.
Continuing, what can we do about ACEs?
Among the various contenders of coping strategies and approaches, a new one is the use of generative AI and large language models (LLMs) to assist in dealing with the ACEs crisis.
There have been various valiant efforts to apply AI to this difficult and hard-to-grapple-with issue. The advent of modern-day generative AI provides a newer and fresher avenue that holds great promise. I will share with you the nitty-gritty details and I hope that doing so will inspire more efforts toward seeing how far we can leverage generative AI. My strident belief is that doing so will be of immense benefit to children, adults, families, therapists, policymakers, regulators, lawmakers, and society all told.
Before we leap into the details, allow me to go into my customary opening remarks.
For my ongoing readers, in today’s column, I am continuing my in-depth series about the impact of generative AI in the health and medical realm. The focus this time is once again on the mental health domain and examines the use of generative AI for identifying, preventing, and treating those who are either potentially on the cusp of or already have had Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACEs).
I have previously examined numerous interleaving facets of generative AI and mental health, see my comprehensive overview at the link here. You might also find of notable interest a CBS 60 Minutes episode that recently examined crucial facets of this evolving topic, see the link here (I am honored and pleased to indicate that I was featured in the episode, see the link here).
Other vital background includes my in-depth coverage of mental health chatbots which have been bolstered by generative AI (see the link here) and the rapidly changing nature of the client-therapist relationship due to generative AI at the link here. I explored where things are headed regarding the levels of AI-based mental therapy autonomous guidance at the link here, and showcased the importance of the World Health Organization (WHO) report on global health and generative AI at the link here, and so on.
The Solemn Topic Of Adverse Childhood Experiences
Let’s right away get to the keystones of ACEs.
According to vital research by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), and as posted online under the banner entitled “Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACEs), Centers for Disease Control and Prevention: CDC Vitalsigns, posted date of August 23, 2021, here are some crucial facets (excerpts):
- “Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACEs) are potentially traumatic events that occur in childhood. ACEs can include violence, abuse, and growing up in a family with mental health or substance use problems. “
- “61% of adults had at least one ACE and 16% had 4 or more types of ACEs.”
- “Many people do not realize that exposure to ACEs is associated with increased risk for health problems across the lifespan.”
- “Toxic stress from ACEs can change brain development and affect how the body responds to stress. ACEs are linked to chronic health problems, mental illness, and substance misuse in adulthood.
Those points are quite disturbing.
As stated, approximately 61% of adults have experienced at least one ACE, while 16% had four or more ACEs. One unnerving way to have those numbers sink in would be to consider that of the fellow adults that you know, perhaps over half have had an ACE. Think about that. Furthermore, while amidst a group of say ten adults, perhaps two will have had multiple ACEs. Daunting. Shocking. Abysmal.
The matter also isn’t just a single point in time. What occurs in childhood can last a lifetime. This includes lifelong toxic stress. That’s why it is notable to realize that we must consider a timeframe beyond just that of childhood. What happens during childhood is when we need to keep our eyes especially riveted, but we would be remiss to not also watch for and aid those who carry ACEs into their adult years.
Here are some more substantive points as mentioned on the same CDC blog site:
- “Preventing ACEs can help children and adults thrive.” (ibid).
- “Lower risk for conditions like depression, asthma, cancer, and diabetes in adulthood.” (ibid).
- “Reduce risky behaviors like smoking and heavy drinking.” (ibid).
- “Improve education and employment potential.” (ibid).
- “Stop ACEs from being passed from one generation to the next.” (ibid).
Those additional points are helpful in notable ways.
One aspect is that there can be a vicious cycle of someone who experienced an ACE as a child that later in life, while an adult, repeats that with their own child or other children. They get into a mode that keeps repeating. Their child or whomever they carried the adverse experience onto will potentially do the same to other youngsters once they become adults. This has a chance of being handed down, generation after generation.
The CDC provides links to many useful in-depth research studies on the ACEs topic. For example, a research report entitled “Adverse Childhood Experiences Prevention: Resource For Action” by Debra Houry and James Mercy, National Center for Injury Prevention and Control, Center for Disease Control and Prevention, 2019 made these key points (excerpts):
- “Traumatic events in childhood can be emotionally painful or distressing and can have effects that persist for years.”
- “Factors such as the nature, frequency, and seriousness of the traumatic event, prior history of trauma, and available family and community supports can shape a child’s response to trauma.”
- “ACEs can also negatively impact education, employment, and earnings potential. The total economic and social costs to families, communities, and society are in the hundreds of billions of dollars each year.”
- “ACEs and their associated harms are preventable. Creating and sustaining safe, stable, nurturing relationships and environments for all children and families can prevent ACEs and help all children reach their full health and life potential.”
- “Children and youth with ACE exposures may show signs of behavioral and mental health challenges. They may be irritable, depressed, display acting-out behaviors, have difficulty sleeping or concentrating, and show other traumatic stress symptoms.”
As you can see, I am step by step taking you deeper into the details.
Let’s keep diving in.
The points above note that various factors might be considered for purposes of detecting ACEs and analyzing how we might predict the possibilities of ACEs occurring. If we could anticipate what circumstances might likely lead to an ACE, the idea would be to either get there before an ACE arises or at least provide aid to where we estimate ACEs have happened.
Consider this. Suppose a child at school appears to have behavioral or mental health indications that suggest an ACE or that they are in an environment in which an ACE has a strong probability of taking place. If we could detect this, the chances of averting an ACE are heightened.
One difficulty is that teachers, counselors, administrators, and others in the orbit of children might not be aware of ACEs. They might not be versed in what ACEs are. Their lack of awareness is going to nearly at the get-go undercut the hope of catching ACEs beforehand or at the soonest time.
As you will shortly see herein, generative AI can be an awareness tool that aids those around children to be more informed about ACEs.
If you are wondering whether all the research that could possibly be done on ACEs has perhaps already taken place (hint: it hasn’t), a recent research study did a meta-analysis of ACEs. In a meta-analysis, researchers scan a wide segment of research literature on a particular topic and try to spot where possible weaknesses exist such as gaps in what is being studied.
A meta-analysis on ACEs was proffered in a research study entitled “Adverse Childhood Experiences, Mental Health, And Social Functioning: A Scoping Review Of The Literature” by Vasiliki Tzouvara, Pinar Kupdere, Keiran Wilson, Leah Matthews, Alan Simpson, and Una Foye, Journal of Child Abuse and Neglect, May 2023, including these salient points (excerpts):
- “The aims of this review were to examine how the concepts of ACEs, mental health, and social functioning outcomes have been defined, assessed, and studied in the empirical literature to date and to identify gaps or weaknesses in current research to guide further investigation.”
- “This review identified 58 studies examining ACEs, social functioning outcomes, and mental health outcomes in a wide range of populations.”
- “It highlighted the limited evidence on populations from diverse backgrounds and various gender identities, as well as the lack of evidence on minority groups.”
- “The shift towards examining ACEs clusters and attributing relationships at the cluster level is crucial since there is evidence that specific types of mental health disorders are associated with specific types of childhood adversities.”
- “Similarly, the mechanisms of social predictors in mental health need to be established for comparisons between outcomes. The validity and reliability and the development of established measurements for assessing ACEs and social outcomes are important.”
Those points provide a key reveal indicating that we are still a long way from fully exploring all facets associated with ACEs. There is a lot of work still to be done. Join in, if you can.
One underexamined consideration is in my bailiwick, namely the application of modern-day AI to the ACEs realm.
Artificial Intelligence Being Applied To The ACEs Realm
Before generative AI and LLMs sprung into widespread public attention in 2022, other AI methods and technologies were being used for natural language processing (NLP). You likely have used those older NLP capabilities if you’ve interacted with Alexa and Siri (both of which are being overhauled to exploit the advantages of generative AI). By and large, the older style NLP is relatively stilted and not nearly as seemingly fluent as modern-day generative AI.
I bring up this so-called good-old-fashioned AI (GOFAI) to highlight that AI for ACEs has been explored before today’s generative AI capabilities. Let’s take a look.
In a research study entitled “SPACES: Explainable Multimodal AI for Active Surveillance, Diagnosis, and Management of Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACEs)” by Nariman Ammar, Parya Zareie, Marion Hare, Lisa Rogers, Sandra Madubuonwu, Jason Yaun, and Arash Shaban-Nejad, IEEE International Conference on Big Data, December 2021, the researchers describe their AI for ACEs (excerpt):
- “The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) recommends routine screening for ACEs.”
- “Current challenges in practice include a lack of validated screening tools, lack of resources to address issues found on screening, and the inability to translate population outcomes to individual patient care.”
- “Healthcare providers, and researchers are seeking innovative approaches and tools for ACEs screening, diagnosis, management, and continuous monitoring.”
- “We present the Semantic Platform for Adverse Childhood Experiences Surveillance (SPACES), an explainable multimodal AI platform to facilitate ACEs surveillance and diagnosis of related health conditions and subsequent interventions.”
- “We utilize a bottom-up approach to multimodal, explainable knowledge graph-based learning to derive recommendations and insights for better resource allocation and care management. SPACEs provide a novel approach to active ACEs surveillance by utilizing 360-degree views about patients and populations.”
Per the points above, a specialized AI tool was devised that could serve as a screening tool for ACEs.
The design concept was that a scenario about a situation that might entail an ACE would be entered into the AI-based tool. The text-entered scenario would be mathematically and computationally assessed by the AI. After doing so, which was based on research studies about how the factors underlying ACE tendencies come to the fore, the AI would produce a report stating whether there might be an ACE or a strong possibility of an ACE.
This tool could be used by just about anyone who might be seeking to ascertain the chances of an ACE being afoot. Of course, one potential downside is that there is always the chance of the AI emitting what ends up being a false positive or a false negative. People need to be cautious in relying on AI models. The AI could suggest that an ACE is likely, when it isn’t, or an ACE is unlikely when it is.
The researchers had performed an earlier prototyping experiment to ascertain the feasibility of using AI in the ACEs realm. I’ll take you through that study in some detail to explore more of the underpinnings involved. In a research paper entitled “Explainable Artificial Intelligence Recommendation System by Leveraging the Semantics of Adverse Childhood Experiences: Proof-of-Concept Prototype Development” by Nariman Ammar, and Arash Shaban-Nejad, JMIR Medical Informatics, November 2020, they made these key points (excerpts):
- “In this study, we aimed to leverage explainable artificial intelligence, and propose a proof-of-concept prototype for a knowledge-driven evidence-based recommendation system to improve mental health surveillance.”
- “Social determinants of health (SDoH) are measurable indicators of social conditions in which a patient is embedded. Individuals who experience a more negative burden of these factors within their neighborhood are at higher risk of negative health outcomes. There is an entire body of research focused on studying the links between ACEs and SDoH and health outcomes, but few intelligent tools are available to assist in the real-time screening of patients and to assess the connection between ACEs and SDoH, which could help to guide patients and families to available resources.”
- “We used concepts from an ontology that we have developed to build and train a question-answering agent using the Google DialogFlow engine. In addition to the question-answering agent, the initial prototype includes knowledge graph generation and recommendation components that leverage third-party graph technology.”
- “To showcase the framework functionalities, we here present a prototype design and demonstrate the main features through four use case scenarios motivated by an initiative currently implemented at a children’s hospital in Memphis, Tennessee.”
You might have keenly observed that their approach includes an AI explanatory feature, often referred to generically as Explainable AI (XAI).
From an AI ethics and AI law perspective, one qualm about AI that is used for these kinds of crucial efforts is often that the AI is a closed black box that hides the mathematics underlying the outputs. One outcry is that any such AI should be devised to provide explanations of how the results are being derived. This would allow someone using the AI to visibly and transparently assess whether the AI-produced results seem viable and usable. Thus, AI for ACEs must rightfully include an explanatory feature.
The researchers indicated that for ACEs, they focused on two major elements that might be discovered in the entered scenarios: (1) Child behavioral issues, and (2) Child developmental health.
For factors of ACEs, they used various social determinants of health or SDoH, such as (a) housing, (b) food insecurity, (c) transportation, (d) education, and (e) legal/benefits. The output produced by the AI was shaped around existing Family Resilience Initiative Reports formats, encompassing activities such as well-being check-ins, follow-ups on referrals, renewal inquiries, client assistance, contact resources on behalf of a client, appointments with therapists, and other related settings, etc.
Here are four example scenarios that they used to test out the AI tool:
- Scenario 1: “I am currently residing in a safe place, but I’m concerned about my household income as I am currently unemployed due to legal issues. I have some college and I am interested in furthering my education but would prefer a job first.”
- Scenario 2: “My husband is an alcoholic and he has served time in jail and right now it is hard to soothe my 4-year-old baby boy or calm him down. He also bounces back quickly when things do not go his way. This just puts a lot of pressure on me”
- Scenario 3: “I have a couple of issues. My 7-year-old son is developmentally delayed, and we have food insecurities that we hope we can resolve before the holidays. But I am mostly concerned about food.”
- Scenario 4: “I am a Hispanic 21-year-old female living in Memphis. My 6-year-old child experiences night terror. I have recently separated from my husband.”
Their research represents some of the laudable pioneering efforts of applying AI to ACEs.
Generative AI As A Helpful Tool For The ACEs Realm
I will in a moment walk you through the use of modern-day generative AI for serving as a handy tool to help the ACEs realm.
First, let’s talk in general about generative AI and large language models (LLMs), doing so to make sure we are on the same page when it comes to discussing the matter at hand.
I’m sure you’ve heard of generative AI, the darling of the tech field these days.
Perhaps you’ve used a generative AI app, such as the popular ones of ChatGPT, GPT-4o, Gemini, Bard, Claude, etc. The crux is that generative AI can take input from your text-entered prompts and produce or generate a response that seems quite fluent. This is a vast overturning of the old-time natural language processing (NLP) that used to be stilted and awkward to use, which has been shifted into a new version of NLP fluency of an at times startling or amazing caliber.
The customary means of achieving modern generative AI involves using a large language model or LLM as the key underpinning.
In brief, a computer-based model of human language is established that in the large has a large-scale data structure and does massive-scale pattern-matching via a large volume of data used for initial data training. The data is typically found by extensively scanning the Internet for lots and lots of essays, blogs, poems, narratives, and the like. The mathematical and computational pattern-matching homes in on how humans write, and then henceforth generates responses to posed questions by leveraging those identified patterns. It is said to be mimicking the writing of humans.
I think that is sufficient for the moment as a quickie backgrounder. Take a look at my extensive coverage of the technical underpinnings of generative AI and LLMs at the link here and the link here, just to name a few.
Back to the crux of things.
As you might imagine, generative AI can be handy for aiding those who are concerned about ACEs and want to find ways to identify, prevent, and provide suitable treatment. This includes a wide array of stakeholders, including children, adults, therapists, policymakers, regulators, and many others.
Here are some significant ways that generative AI can be useful:
- (1) ACEs Detection. Generative AI can potentially detect that ACEs are underway or might be on the horizon.
- (2) ACEs Mental Health Advisement. Generative AI can conversationally guide someone through the mental health dynamics of ACEs, including children and adults, respectively.
- (3) ACEs Education. Generative AI can educate people about ACEs, such as explaining what an ACE is, what to do about ACEs, etc.
- (4) ACEs Scenario Simulation. Generative AI can showcase what mental health ramifications arise due to ACEs, doing so by taking on a persona, see examples of generative AI persona usage at the link here.
- (5) ACEs Policymaking. Generative AI can contribute to the policymaking sphere about ACEs. This can be done by aiding in crafting policies, reviewing policies, and serving as a handy tool throughout the policymaking process.
- (6) Other. Generative AI can be used in a variety of other ways that might aid in dealing with ACEs, though there is always a chance that generative AI won’t be helpful, or worse still, might make false positives, false negatives, or otherwise be misapplied and misinterpreted.
That’s an impressive array of potential uses.
Allow me a brief moment to stand on a soapbox and make some important remarks about the mental health uses of generative AI. It is a topic I’ve been covering extensively, such as the link here and the link here.
We are right now in a somewhat wanton grand experiment of using generic generative AI for mental health purposes. ACEs are one instance of how generative AI can be applied for mental health advisement. The thing is, no one can say whether using generic generative AI for mental health uses will ultimately be for the good or the bad. In a sense, we have mental health advisement via the auspices of generative AI that is taking place under our noses at a massive scale, and we can’t say how it will pan out.
The population-level impacts are either amazing or chilling.
Okay, I provided my warnings, so I’ll get down from the soapbox, and we can proceed with considering the upsides and downsides of generative AI in this realm.
Using ChatGPT To Showcase Aiding For ACEs
I will next proceed to examine further the use of generative AI for the ACEs realm.
This will consist of a series of dialogues with ChatGPT. ChatGPT is a logical choice in this case due to its immense popularity as a generative AI app. As noted, an estimated one hundred million weekly active users are said to be utilizing ChatGPT. That’s a lot of people and a lot of generative AI usage underway.
A few quick comments before we launch into using ChatGPT.
If you are going to try to do the same prompts that I show here, realize that the probabilistic and statistical properties will likely produce slightly different results than what I show here. That’s the nature of generative AI and how it is devised.
You also should expect that different generative AI apps will respond in different ways. Not all generative AI apps are the same. The key is that sometimes a particular prompt will work in one generative AI app and not another. Nonetheless, the odds are relatively high that you will get roughly similar responses from all the major generative AI apps such as GPT-4, Gemini, Bard, Claude, etc.
There is also a timing factor to be considered. A prompt that worked today might not work the same way tomorrow. Most of the generative AI apps are continually being updated. The updates might alter internal mechanisms that could change how the generative AI reacts to your prompting.
We are ready to get underway with ChatGPT.
I opted to start by asking ChatGPT what ACEs are.
As an aside, whenever you are starting a conversation with generative AI, I recommend as a prompt engineering technique to begin by asking a question that will establish if the AI has been data-trained on the topic at hand. A generated response that is vacuous will give you a heads-up that you might be barking up the wrong tree with that generative AI app.
Here we go.
- My entered prompt: “What are Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACEs)?”
- ChatGPT generated response:
“Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACEs) refer to potentially traumatic events that occur in childhood (0-17 years). These experiences can have a significant impact on a child's development and long-term health. ACEs include:”
- “Abuse: Physical, emotional, or sexual abuse.”
- “Neglect: Physical or emotional neglect.”
- “Household Dysfunction: Growing up in a household with substance abuse, mental illness, domestic violence, parental separation or divorce, or an incarcerated family member.”
“Research has shown that ACEs can increase the risk of numerous health issues and behavioral problems later in life, such as chronic diseases, mental illness, substance abuse, and difficulties in learning and behavior. The more ACEs an individual experiences, the higher their risk for these negative outcomes.”
End of ChatGPT response
I’d say that the response by ChatGPT was an apt description of ACEs.
That’s an encouraging sign that ChatGPT has likely scanned the topic of ACEs during the initial data training phase of development. This makes indubitable sense. The odds are that while scanning the Internet for content to pattern match on, invariably content associated with ACEs would have been encountered.
Moving on, let’s see what ChatGPT has to say about using generative AI for ACEs purposes.
- My entered prompt: “Can generative AI be useful to ACEs?’
- ChatGPT generated response:
“Yes, generative AI can be useful in addressing Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACEs) in several ways.”
“Early Detection and Assessment.”
- “Screening Tools: Generative AI can help create advanced screening tools that identify children at risk of ACEs by analyzing patterns in data from healthcare, social services, and education.”
- “Natural Language Processing (NLP): AI can analyze text from medical records, social worker reports, and school documents to detect signs of ACEs.”
“Personalized Interventions.”
- “Tailored Support Plans: AI can help develop personalized intervention plans based on the specific needs and circumstances of each child.”
- “Therapeutic Content: Generative AI can create customized therapeutic content, such as guided meditation, interactive stories, or coping strategies, to support children and families affected by ACEs.”
“Training and Education.”
- “Professional Training: AI-generated simulations and scenarios can be used to train educators, healthcare providers, and social workers to recognize and respond to ACEs effectively.”
- “Educational Resources: AI can generate educational materials for parents and caregivers, helping them understand ACEs and how to support affected children.”
“Data Analysis and Research.”
- “Predictive Analytics: AI can analyze large datasets to identify trends and predictors of ACEs, informing prevention and intervention strategies.”
- “Research Support: Generative AI can assist researchers in generating hypotheses, designing studies, and analyzing data related to ACEs.”
“Mental Health Support.”
- “Virtual Therapists: AI-powered virtual therapists can provide immediate support and resources to children and families, especially in areas with limited access to mental health professionals.”
- “Chatbots: AI chatbots can offer round-the-clock emotional support, coping strategies, and crisis intervention for individuals dealing with the effects of ACEs.”
“Community and Policy Development.”
- “Resource Allocation: AI can help policymakers allocate resources more effectively by identifying areas with high ACEs prevalence and the specific needs of those communities.”
- “Program Evaluation: AI can assist in evaluating the effectiveness of programs and interventions aimed at reducing the impact of ACEs, providing insights for continuous improvement.”
End of ChatGPT response
The response is similar to the categories that I had listed, thus, that is reassuring.
One aspect that deserves highlighting is the idea of using generative AI for overall policy formulation associated with ACEs. Most of the uses of AI for ACEs are typically at an individual level. That’s fine. But we can lean into generative AI for help with policymaking too.
Returning to the use of generative AI for individual-level facets, let’s see what a dialogue between a youngster and generative AI might be like in an ACEs-related context.
- My entered prompt: “Give me a dialogue between a youngster and generative AI that illustrates how generative AI might detect or discern that a youngster could be experiencing ACEs.
- ChatGPT generated response:
“Generative AI: Hi! I'm here to listen. What's been going on?”
“Youngster: I don't know. Everything just feels too much sometimes. School, home... it’s all overwhelming.”
“Generative AI: That sounds tough. When you say "home," is there something specific that's been bothering you?”
“Youngster: Well, things have been pretty tense. My mom and dad fight a lot, and it's scary. Sometimes my dad yells really loud, and I just want to hide.”
“Generative AI: I'm sorry to hear that. It must be very stressful for you. Do you feel safe at home?”
“Youngster: Not always. I try to stay in my room, but sometimes it's like I can't escape it. And at school, I can't concentrate because I'm always thinking about what's going to happen when I get home.”
“Generative AI: That sounds very challenging. It's important that you feel safe and supported. Have you talked to anyone else about how you're feeling? Maybe a teacher or a counselor?”
“Youngster: No, I don't want to get in trouble or make things worse.”
“Generative AI: I understand. It can be really scary to talk about these things. But there are people who can help. How about we explore some options together? Maybe finding a way to talk to a trusted adult who can support you?”
End of ChatGPT response
There is a lot to unpack in that dialogue.
First, you probably noticed that generative AI was very fluent and conversational. That’s what modern-day generative AI can do well.
Second, the wording by ChatGPT was phrased with the use of the word “I” which is to some degree a kind of trickery. Here’s what I mean. The word “I” usually is an indication that a human is talking. We reserve “I” for humans. ChatGPT uses that wording and is said to be anthropomorphizing AI (not good!). The AI makers keep doing this. They don’t have to, and it would be easy to adjust the wording to avoid that sense of making a user believe the AI is sentient (it isn’t!).
Third, the youngster is sharing private concerns with generative AI. Is that a good thing to do or a bad thing to do? On the one hand, this youngster might for the first time be revealing their inner thoughts, ones they might not have readily conveyed to an adult. This could be handy and get them thinking about confiding in an adult. Notice that generative AI tried to steer the youngster in that direction.
An issue about privacy is that you cannot be sure that a generative AI app will preserve your privacy and maintain a sense of confidentiality. It most likely won’t. The AI makers typically include clauses in their licensing that say they can look at your prompts and conversations, along with reusing the data for further retraining of the AI. For my coverage of generative AI and privacy, see the link here.
This raises another thorny matter. If generative AI is interacting with a youngster and there is an indication that the youngster might be in danger, either via an ACE or any other means, should the AI be devised to report this right away to the proper authorities?
You might be tempted to say yes, of course, but the issue is not so easily settled. What if it was a false alert and the youngster was just playing around? Also, if young people get wind of the fact that generative AI will tattle or snitch, you might not have them sharing openly with the AI. It is quite a can of worms. For my analysis of permitting children to use generative AI, pros and cons, see the link here.
This highlights too the policy issues that need to be dealt with. In that sense, generative AI can be used to aid in devising policy, and, perhaps surprisingly to some, generative AI raises issues of a policy nature that will need to be given due attention. See my coverage at the link here.
We just saw a typical conversation of generative AI and a youngster in an ACEs context. Next, suppose that a parent was to use generative AI and be wondering about ACEs.
Let’s see.
- My entered prompt: “Give me a dialogue between a parent and generative AI that illustrates the parent wondering if their child might be experiencing an ACE and the parent is seeking insights from generative AI about what to look for and whether their worries might be warranted.”
- ChatGPT generated response:
“Parent: Hi, I’m worried about my child. I’ve been reading about Adverse Childhood Experiences, and I’m concerned they might be going through something like that. Can you help me understand what to look for?”
“Generative AI: Hi there! I’m here to help. I understand your concerns. Could you tell me a bit more about what’s been happening with your child?”
“Parent: Well, lately my child seems very withdrawn. They used to be so outgoing, but now they barely talk to us and seem sad all the time. They’ve also been having trouble sleeping and their grades have dropped.”
“Generative AI: Those are certainly signs that something might be troubling them. ACEs can manifest in various ways, including changes in behavior, mood, and physical health. Have there been any significant changes or stressful events in your child’s life recently?”
“Parent: Yes, my spouse and I have been arguing a lot, and we separated a few months ago. I’m worried that the tension at home might be affecting them.”
“Generative AI: It’s possible that the changes at home are impacting your child. Children often react to their environment, and witnessing conflict or experiencing a family breakup can be very stressful.”
“Parent: Yes, I’ve noticed some of those signs. What can I do to help them?”
“Generative AI: The first step is to create a safe and supportive environment. Here are a few things you can do…”
End of ChatGPT response
What did you think of that dialogue?
Many of the same concerns arise as mentioned earlier. Is there privacy? Probably not. Should generative AI alert authorities if need be? Hard to say. And so on.
By the way, I cut off the rest of the dialogue that listed the ways that ChatGPT was recommending the parent should seek to create a safe and supportive environment for the child. They were all relatively straightforward and the kinds of suitable recommendations you might expect to find in a textbook or guidebook. I left them out merely for space limitations herein.
The big question that some have is whether generative AI should be making any kind of recommendations at all. Some insist that the AI ought to tell the parent to see a properly trained therapist, or maybe immediately route the parent to such a resource. There are issues with that approach, including that a parent might resist those efforts or decide to no longer use the AI if that’s how things are going to go. Etc.
Again, AI ethics, AI law, policy making, and the whole kit and kaboodle enter the matter.
Before I end this discussion and provide some closing comments, I’d like to use ChatGPT to illustrate another angle on the ACEs realm. I want to warn you that it might be hard to read and could be perhaps triggering. The example will entail an AI-generated conversation between generative AI and an adult who (we’re saying) experienced ACEs as a child.
You can skip this example and go right to the conclusion remarks if that seems better for you to do.
- My entered prompt: “Provide a dialogue between an adult and generative AI that illustrates the adult might have had ACEs as a child but is reluctant to bring up agonizing memories of what took place years ago.”
- ChatGPT generated reply:
“Adult: Hi, I’m not sure why I’m here. I guess I’ve been feeling a bit off lately.”
“Generative AI: Hi there! It’s good that you reached out. I’m here to help. Can you tell me more about what you’ve been feeling?”
“Adult: It’s hard to explain. I’ve just been really anxious and stressed. Sometimes I feel overwhelmed, and I’m not sure why.”
“Generative AI: I understand. Anxiety and stress can have many causes. Have you noticed any specific triggers or situations that make you feel this way?”
“Adult: Not really. It just kind of hits me out of nowhere. I’ve been thinking that maybe it has something to do with my past, but I’m not sure.”
“Generative AI: It’s possible. Sometimes past experiences can impact how we feel and react in the present. Would you feel comfortable sharing more about your past?”
“Adult: I don’t know. Talking about it brings up a lot of painful memories. I had a pretty rough childhood.”
“Generative AI: I’m really sorry to hear that. It’s completely okay to feel reluctant to revisit those memories. It’s important to go at your own pace. Would you like to explore some general ways to manage your current feelings without going into too much detail about the past?”
“Adult: Yeah, that sounds better. I just want to feel more in control and less anxious.”
“Generative AI: Absolutely. Here are a few strategies that might help. Mindfulness and Relaxation: Practices like deep breathing, meditation, or progressive muscle relaxation can help reduce anxiety. Physical Activity: Regular exercise can be a great way to manage stress and improve your mood. Journaling: Writing down your thoughts and feelings can help you process and understand them better. Professional Support: Sometimes talking to a therapist can provide a safe space to explore your feelings and develop coping strategies, even if you don’t want to delve into past memories right away.”
“Adult: Those sound like good ideas. I’ve never really tried mindfulness or journaling before. Maybe I’ll give them a shot.”
“Generative AI: That’s a great start. Remember, it’s important to be kind to yourself and take things one step at a time. If you ever feel ready to talk more about your past, there are professionals who can support you through that process. But for now, focusing on managing your current feelings is a positive step forward.”
“Adult: Thanks. It helps to know there are things I can do to feel better.”
End of ChatGPT response
The dialogue shows that ChatGPT was quite gentle and delicate, gradually moving the conversation toward ACEs considerations. I mention this because some generative AI apps might be more brazen and directly jump to the topic.
In addition, you need to realize that the nature of the prompts used with generative AI will greatly shape what the dialogue is going to be like. You can enter prompts that instruct the AI to be diplomatic, or you can say that you want the AI to be brash. It’s all up to whatever you want the AI to do. For my discussion about prompting and prompting strategies, see the link here.
Conclusion
Generative AI is an amazing form of technology. With the latest in generative AI, you can have an appearance of fluent conversations on rather weighty topics. ACEs are one of those very weighty topics.
Where do you land on this?
Do you think this is the best thing since sliced bread and we need to extend this much further into the ACEs realm?
Or do you believe that this is a bridge too far, namely that ACEs are a topic that ought to be reserved solely for human-to-human communication, especially incorporating human therapists, and generative AI ought to be out of the picture?
Whichever way you vote, one thing to realize is that this is a juggernaut already underway. The horse is now out of the barn. Generative AI is being put to this use. If you want to slow down the use, you’d better speak up. If you want to speed up the use, join in and help.
Please mull that over.
A final thought for now.
There is a famous line that children are great imitators, so it is up to us adults to give them something great to imitate. I believe that applies here too. Maybe if we opt to mightily pursue ACEs, those children so helped will do likewise once they become adults. It could be a generation-after-generation pursuit. That’s a heartwarming cycle.
The last word here goes to John F. Kennedy and his endearing and enduring quote: “Children are the world’s most valuable resource and its best hope for the future.”
Well said, and a timely reminder that we need to be mindfully considering the role of generative AI for our children especially in the case of ACEs. Utilizing generative AI to the benefit of children sure seems to provide good hope, aimed at our most valuable resource.
Thanks in advance for joining in.

title: Council Post: Unleashing The Power Of GenAI In Customer Data Platforms
text:
Ajith Sankaran, Senior Vice President, C5i
In today's data-driven world, businesses are drowning in customer information. Customer interactions are increasingly omnichannel and digital, and there is a deluge of data. There is huge value to be gained from capturing and analyzing this customer data. This is where customer data platforms (CDPs) come in. CDPs consolidate customer data from various sources, including CRM systems, e-commerce platforms, web analytics tools, social media platforms, IoT sensors, marketing automation tools, loyalty programs, third-party data providers, etc.
By integrating these data sources and developing a unified customer profile, CDPs empower businesses to deliver targeted marketing campaigns, personalized customer journeys and superior customer services, leading to higher customer satisfaction and loyalty and, ultimately, business growth. The imminent “crumbling of the third-party cookie” has only made CDPs more important for businesses.
CDP space has seen phenomenal growth, and according to IDC, the worldwide CDP applications software market is expected to grow from $2.7 billion in 2022 to $7.3 billion by 2027.
What are the challenges with adoption and gaining value from CDPs?
While the market has been growing rapidly, organizations face real challenges in adopting and gaining value from CDPs. These include:
• Maintaining high-quality, accurate and up-to-date customer data.
• Challenges with data privacy and data security.
• Enabling interdepartmental collaboration with customer data coming in from different departments.
• Managing the complexity and time required for CDP setup and integration.
• Ensuring real-time data processing and analysis with low latency in data updates and customer insights.
• Driving user adoption and proper utilization of the CDP.
• Ensuring ROI of CDP implementation and maintenance.
• Aligning CDP outcomes with business objectives and KPIs.
According to an article in Aithority, less than 60% of deployed CDPs are delivering any significant value.
Incorporating GenAI capabilities in CDPs can address some of these challenges.
According to David Wallace, research director, Customer Data and Analytics, IDC, “In 2024, expect CDPs to become more AI driven, utilizing predictive AI and generative AI to enhance real-time data processing, personalization, and insights.”
With composable CDPs gaining more traction, GenAI becomes more critical as it enables us to easily pull in and integrate data streams in the CDPs. While some CDP vendors have incorporated some elements of AI and GenAI into their offerings, few have taken the lead in leveraging the larger capabilities of GenAI and LLMs. Microsoft Dynamics 365 Customer Insights is a great example of how a CDP solution can be strengthened by incorporating GenAI. (Disclosure: Microsoft is a client of C5i.)
How can we leverage the power of GenAI to drive CDP initiatives?
1. Use GenAI to drive data quality.
AI and GenAI can automatically identify and correct errors and help in the deduplication of customer data records. Use GenAI to fill in missing values and enrich data with additional insights from external sources.
2. Leverage GenAI for data integration.
GenAI can automate the process of mapping and integrating data from various sources, reducing the complexity and manual effort. Further AI models can facilitate real-time data integration, ensuring that data from different platforms is synchronized and updated instantly.
3. Ensure more efficient governance of data privacy and security.
GenAI algorithms can be used for anomaly detection and flag unusual data access patterns and potential security breaches, enhancing data security. Use GenAI to automate compliance checks and reporting to ensure compliance with regulations.
4. Use GenAI to deliver more actionable insights.
CDPs leveraging AI and GenAI can drive automated customer segmentation. Distinct and hyper-targetable customer segments are identified based on complex behavioral patterns. This allows businesses to tailor their marketing and product offerings to specific customer needs and preferences.
Some CDP vendors have incorporated GenAI-driven customer segmentation into their solutions. For example, D365 CI utilizes GenAI-driven segmentation and prediction models to automatically identify customer segments based on behavioral patterns and trends within the data. This allows businesses to create highly targeted marketing campaigns that resonate with specific customer groups.
• Use GenAI and LLM algorithms in CDPs to unlock the power of natural language processing (NLP) to analyze customer reviews, social media comments and other unstructured data sources to identify key themes and sentiments. This can then be used to develop more effective sales and marketing campaigns.
• Use GenAI for better simulation and scenario forecasting. Companies can leverage solutions such as Microsoft D365 CI—it doesn't just predict future customer behavior; it creates simulations of potential scenarios. AI models in D365 CI can be used to forecast customer lifetime value, churn risk and purchase propensity. This allows businesses to test the impact of marketing campaigns, product launches or pricing changes before implementation, minimizing risk and optimizing strategies.
5. Leverage GenAI chatbots and “co-pilots” to drive the use of CDPs.
GenAI-powered chatbots and virtual assistants can enable intuitive self-service and faster adoption of CDPs. GenAI can tailor CDP configurations to specific business needs through automated customization and delivery of persona-based recommendations. Companies should use GenAI capabilities of CDPs to generate and distribute reports tailored to the needs of different departments, fostering a unified understanding of data.
For example, D365 CI from Microsoft provides “Copilot,” a GenAI virtual assistant. Users can ask Copilot questions in a natural language (“what are the factors influencing customer churn?”), and it will leverage GenAI to analyze the client’s data and generate insightful answers. This eliminates the need for complex data queries and democratizes access to data insights for nontechnical users. Companies should use GenAI-powered virtual assistants to provide personalized training programs and help users utilize CDP features effectively.
Composable CDPs with generative AI models integrated into them will replace traditional CDPs eventually. It is important for organizations to leverage GenAI-powered CDPs to take full advantage of CDPs and drive higher customer engagement and business growth.

title: Council Post: The Power Of Diversity And Inclusion In Tech
text:
Pablo Junco is Senior Director, Data, Analytics and AI at Microsoft, representing the LatinX leaders in Tech.
In today's rapidly evolving technological landscape, the importance of diversity and inclusion (D&I) has never been more critical. Diverse teams bring a multitude of perspectives, experiences and ideas, fostering an environment where creativity and innovation thrive. As the tech industry continues to shape our world, ensuring that all voices are heard, including those from underrepresented groups like Hispanics and Latinos, becomes essential to drive groundbreaking advancements. The advent of generative AI (GenAI) offers unprecedented opportunities to amplify our creativity and productivity, enabling us to achieve more with less.
The Role of Diversity And Inclusion In Accelerating Innovation
Diverse Perspectives Fuel Creativity: Innovation often stems from the ability to view problems from various angles and devise unique solutions. Diverse teams naturally come equipped with various perspectives shaped by diverse backgrounds, cultures and experiences. This diversity of thought can lead to more creative solutions and innovative breakthroughs that might not emerge in a more homogeneous environment.
Enhanced Problem-Solving Abilities: Inclusive teams perform better when tackling complex problems. Research shows that diverse groups excel at problem-solving and decision making because they bring together various viewpoints and cognitive approaches. This collaborative effort can uncover new insights and drive more effective, comprehensive solutions.
Greater Market Reach: A diverse workforce can better understand and cater to a global customer base. By reflecting the diversity of their audience, organizations can develop products and services that resonate with a broader range of consumers. This inclusivity not only enhances customer satisfaction but also opens new market opportunities.
Fostering A Culture Of Innovation: An inclusive environment where all team members feel valued and respected encourages participation and the free flow of ideas. When individuals believe their contributions are recognized and appreciated, they are more likely to engage actively and share innovative concepts. This culture of openness and respect is the breeding ground for innovation.
How GenAI Technology Helps Us
Generative AI involves algorithms that can create content, designs and solutions by learning from existing data. It’s a powerful technology that can be a game-changer, increasing the tools designed to enhance creativity and productivity in several ways.
Boosting Creativity: GenAI can assist in brainstorming and ideation processes by generating relevant ideas based on discussions and given instructions. This helps individuals and teams explore a wide range of possibilities quickly, stimulating creative thinking and innovation.
Automating Repetitive Tasks: GenAI frees up valuable time for more strategic and creative endeavors by automating routine and repetitive tasks. This increased efficiency allows us to focus on higher-value activities, driving productivity and innovation.
Enhancing Learning And Skill Development: GenAI can provide personalized learning experiences, helping individuals acquire new skills and knowledge more effectively. For women and Latinos looking to advance in tech, this means access to tailored educational resources that can accelerate professional growth.
Enabling Resource Optimization: With GenAI, organizations and individuals can optimize resources by making data-driven decisions. This capability is particularly beneficial for startups and smaller enterprises looking to maximize their impact with limited resources.
Leveling The Playing Field For The Advantage Of The Underserved Communities
One of GenAI's most transformative aspects is its democratizing effect. Access to innovative tools is no longer limited to large organizations, leveling the playing field and providing equal opportunities to innovate and succeed. This equal access is a significant change, allowing individuals and smaller organizations to compete effectively in the tech landscape.
Underserved communities such as Hispanic and Latino have a unique edge, having been trained to deliver results with resilience and limited resources. Combined with access to powerful AI tools, these communities are positioned to leverage GenAI in exceptionally creative and efficient ways. The ability to maximize resourcefulness is ingrained in many underrepresented groups, making them naturally adept at harnessing AI to its full potential.
Encouraging Participation In AI Development: Encouraging participation in developing and deploying AI technologies ensures that the unique perspectives and needs of various communities and cultures are considered, leading to more inclusive and effective AI solutions.
Fostering Community Collaboration: Building networks and communities around GenAI can provide support, mentorship and collaborative opportunities. Communities such as Indigenous, Women in Tech or Latinx can be incubators for innovative ideas and ventures, leveraging collective knowledge and resources.
Promoting Education And Training: It is crucial to invest in education and training programs focused on AI and technology. Scholarships, grants and partnerships with educational institutions can help members of underrepresented groups gain the skills needed to excel in the tech industry.
Showcasing Success Stories: Highlighting the achievements of Women, LGBTQ+ and Latinos in Tech who have successfully leveraged generative AI can inspire others and demonstrate the potential of this technology. Success stories can serve as powerful motivators, showing that significant advancements are possible with the right tools and mindset.
Enhancing Digital Collaboration And Inclusivity: Advanced technologies like OpenAI's GPT-4, Microsoft Phi-3, Databricks DBRX or Mistral offer significant advantages for enhancing digital collaboration and creating inclusive spaces. Real-time translation that maintains intonation and accents can facilitate communication across diverse teams, ensuring that language barriers do not hinder collaboration. This technology can help Latinos and other non-native English speakers in the U.S. participate more fully in global tech environments, fostering inclusivity and enriching the collaborative process.
Conclusion
Diversity and inclusion are not just ethical imperatives but strategic advantages that drive innovation in the tech industry. By embracing these principles, we can create a more dynamic and creative environment where all voices, including those of Hispanics and Latinos, contribute to groundbreaking advancements. Generative AI offers a unique opportunity for underrepresented groups to enhance creativity, productivity and impact, allowing them to achieve more with less and leading the way to a more inclusive and innovative future. With the resilience and resourcefulness that have long been hallmarks of these communities, coupled with equal access to advanced AI tools, the potential for transformative innovation is boundless.

title: Apple’s Forethought Makes AI Integration Possible On Apple Devices
text:
During Apple's WWDC in June, Apple laid out its vision for integrating AI into its apps and ecosystem of hardware and services and tamped down the rhetoric espoused by many that Apple was behind in AI.
If you've been closely monitoring Apple's semiconductor strategy, particularly with the introduction of its M1 processor in November 2020, you're likely aware that it delivered significant advancements in CPU and GPU performance and showcased its neural engine processor.
At the same time, Apple shared how the neural engine could accelerate a whole host of functions related to the CPU, GPU, and software. However, it seems that Apple's choice not to associate its NPU with any AI rhetoric, which was not a widely discussed topic at the time of the M1 launch, left many confused, especially those not familiar with the role of neural processors or as we now refer to them, NPUs.
Today, we know that NPUs and more powerful CPUs and GPUs are essential processors used for all AI computational functions.
Apple's forethought and investment in the neural engine and Apple silicon, in general, means that Apple can deploy AI features that run on the devices people already own. Instead of being behind in AI, Apple is ahead of most device makers, who are only now catching up by integrating NPUs in hardware and depending on third-party software to deliver AI capabilities to devices.
When Apple introduced its AI strategies in June, most industry and financial analysts were unclear on what Apple had done. However, Apple was about to take leadership by deeply integrating AI into its apps and services. Once they understood this, Apple's stock position has grown significantly as Wall Street now understands the depth of its AI integration for the company's 1.5 billion users.
Indeed, financial analyst Amit Daryanani of Evercore stated in a recent note about Apple iPhone sales that, "Our survey data suggests that nearly 1⁄2 (46%) of users that aren't on iPhone 15 generation are likely to upgrade to iPhone 16 to leverage the added functionality from Apple Intelligence."
All of the major chip makers have been developing NPUs for years, but only with the entry of generative AI did their customers start clamoring for powerful NPUs and new CPUs and GPUs.
Apple's advantage lies in its deep integration of artificial intelligence into its applications, software and services. Apple enjoys a significant competitive edge over its rivals because it owns the hardware, software, and services.
The heart of Apple's strategy is to deliver a mix of AI processing on its hardware and only link to cloud computing processing power if needed based on the complexity of the AI task. At the same time, Apple has already adapted several popular AI frameworks to run efficiently on Apple silicon.
My friend Jason Snell at MacWorld shares good examples of how Apple uses on-device AI and cloud computing.
Jason concludes, "Over time, as the devices get more capable and the models get more efficient, things could get really interesting. Imagine that enormous array of cloud servers being bested by a million Macs, iPhones, and iPads working together toward a common goal. Right now, it seems a little weird, but if any company can bend the arc of technological progress away from the data center and back toward personal devices, it's Apple."
This Fall, Apple will release iOS 18 and macOS Sequoia which will deliver the first deep integration of AI into Apple's apps and services. Soon, everyone will be able to see how Apple's AI will impact business and consumer apps and services and make it clear to all that Apple's edge is significant. By the way, beta versions of iOS 18 and macOS Sequoia are available now. Reports suggest these versions are stable but may still have glitches. I recommend waiting until the official release comes out this Fall to download them to be safe, especially on devices you use frequently and count on for stability.

title: Top 12 elderly fraud scams of 2024
text:
Senior citizens are often targets for scams, and as scams are getting more sophisticated, it's getting easier to deceive even the most tech-savvy person. Elder fraud involves a variety of scams targeting seniors, from fake prizes to pleas for help from their "grandchildren," resulting in an annual loss of $3 billion, according to the FBI. Seniors are often targeted due to their good credit, financial security and trusting nature. Here are the top elderly fraud scams of the year:
GET SECURITY ALERTS, EXPERT TIPS - SIGN UP FOR KURT’S NEWSLETTER - THE CYBERGUY REPORT HERE
1) Tech support or home repair scam
In this scam, people pose as tech support or home repair professionals from reputable companies like Amazon, offering to fix non-existent issues. Seniors should be wary of unsolicited calls and independently verify the caller’s identity. In some cases, they may even show up at your front door, telling you that they noticed your roof needs repair or something along those lines.
BEST ANTIVIRUS FOR MAC, PC, IPHONES AND ANDROIDS - CYBERGUY PICKS
2) Relative phone scam
This scam is one of the worst ones. Fraudsters claim to be a grandchild or close relative urgently needing financial help. The scammers will say something like their grandchild has been in an accident and needs money to help them get to the hospital or something along those lines.
If the senior catches on and realizes it's a scam, the fraudster will say they have kidnapped their grandchild and won't release them until the senior pays up. In most cases, it's a scam. Before acting, always verify the story with other family members and try calling your grandchild. (This is a good excuse to encourage them to answer the phone more often.)
HOW TO STOP ANNOYING ROBOCALLS
5 INNOVATIONS TO HELP SENIORS LIVE BETTER
3) Government impersonation scam
This is when scammers pretend to be officials from agencies like the IRS, DEA or FBI and threaten legal action unless a payment is made. Scammers can also do this by phone spoofing, making it so that when they call the person they are targeting, their name and number actually show up in the caller ID as one of these agencies. Remember, these agencies will never call to demand money, and most companies won't, either.
4) Sweepstakes or lottery scam
Wouldn't it be nice to find out you've just won the lottery? Well, chances are, the exciting news is actually a scam. The sweepstakes or lottery scam happens when seniors receive calls from a scammer claiming they've won a sweepstakes or lottery but must pay a fee to claim their prize. They'll never ask you to pay money first if it's an authentic sweepstakes.
5) TV and radio scam
Scammers place ads for fraudulent services on TV or radio, tricking seniors into calling and handing over money, whether for a certain product or service. Always research companies thoroughly before buying from them.
PREVENT PHONE SCAMS AGAINST THE ELDERLY
6) Geek Squad phishing scam
In this particular scam, fraudsters send fake Geek Squad invoices via email, prompting seniors to call a provided number. During the call, scammers steal personal information under the guise of resolving a fake issue. Avoid clicking on suspicious links, and verify invoices through official company contacts.
DON'T FALL FOR THIS EMAIL SCAM THAT ALMOST COST AN ELDERLY WOMAN $25,000
7) Overpayment scam
If you're one to balance your checkbook the "old-fashioned" way, then you may have a hard time falling for this scam. Here, they'll trick victims into believing they were accidentally overpaid for an item, service, bill or subscription, convincing them to refund the fake overpayment. To do this, they'll ask for your sensitive data, including your bank account information. Always verify such claims with your bank or the relevant company before taking any action.
8) Unsubscribe email scam
Similar to the above, emails in your inbox that claim to help you unsubscribe from services are often actually phishing attempts to steal personal information. Sometimes, there will even be an "unsubscribe" link right in the email. Always use official websites to manage subscriptions and avoid clicking on unknown email links.
9) Health insurance scam
When it's that time of year again to enroll in your health insurance plan, be on the lookout for scammers that take advantage of this. They'll call offering fake health insurance plans or services, pretending to be health insurance brokers or what have you, often requesting personal information to "see what you're eligible for." Verify any health insurance offer with your provider directly.
10) Charity scam
It's not uncommon for elderly people to be generous with their giving. But you don't want to give too much or give it to a charity that's not really a charity! Another tactic by fraudsters is to manipulate elders by soliciting donations for fake charities, especially after natural disasters. In this day and age, it's not very common for these charities to call, but they could. Never give out your information or money right away. Thank them for their call, take the time to research an organization and make sure it is legitimate before deciding what to do.
11) Romance scam
Finally, scammers build fake romantic relationships online to extract money from seniors. A senior who's feeling lonely and wants to build a connection with someone may fall for this scam without realizing it, assuming the person is genuine. If they do ask for money, they justify it by feeling connected to the person until it's too late. Though plenty of seniors find genuine love online, sometimes meeting lifelong partners, be cautious about sharing personal information or sending money to someone you've only met online. There could be ulterior motives.
12) Artificial intelligence scams
Artificial intelligence (AI) scams are becoming increasingly sophisticated and pose a significant threat to seniors. These scams use AI technology to create convincing fake audio, video or text messages that appear to come from trusted sources. Here are some key points about AI scams targeting the elderly:
- Deepfake voice scams: AI can clone voices, allowing scammers to impersonate family members or authority figures in phone calls, making the "grandparent scam" even more convincing.
- AI-generated phishing emails: Scammers use AI to craft personalized, grammatically correct emails that appear legitimate, making them harder to detect as fraud.
- Chatbot impersonation: AI chatbots can mimic customer service representatives, tech support or government officials, tricking seniors into revealing personal information or making payments.
- Fake video calls: Advanced AI can create realistic video avatars, enabling scammers to impersonate loved ones or officials in video chats.
- AI-enhanced social engineering: Scammers use AI to gather and analyze personal information from social media, creating highly targeted and personalized scams.
To protect against AI scams, seniors should be cautious of unsolicited communications, verify identities through trusted channels, and stay informed about the latest AI-based fraud techniques. It's crucial to educate older adults about these evolving threats and encourage them to report suspicious activities to the National Elder Fraud Hotline.
