title: AI industry is influencing the world. Mozilla adviser Abeba Birhane is challenging its core values
text:
AI industry is influencing the world. Mozilla adviser Abeba Birhane is challenging its core values
“Scaling up” is a catchphrase in the artificial intelligence industry as tech companies rush to improve their AI systems with ever-bigger sets of internet data
“Scaling up" is a catchphrase in the artificial intelligence industry as tech companies rush to improve their AI systems with ever-bigger sets of internet data.
It's also a red flag for Mozilla's Abeba Birhane, an AI expert who for years has challenged the values and practices of her field and the influence it's having on the world.
Her latest research finds that scaling up on online data used to train popular AI image-generator tools is disproportionately resulting in racist outputs, especially against Black men.
Birhane is a senior adviser in AI accountability at the Mozilla Foundation, the nonprofit parent organization of the free software company that runs the Firefox web browser. Raised in Ethiopia and living in Ireland, she's also an adjunct assistant professor at Trinity College Dublin.
Her interview with The Associated Press has been edited for length and clarity.
Q: How did you get started in the AI field?
A: I’m a cognitive scientist by training. Cog sci doesn’t have its own department wherever you are studying it. So where I studied, it was under computer science. I was placed in a lab full of machine learners. They were doing so much amazing stuff and nobody was paying attention to the data. I found that very amusing and also very interesting because I thought data was one of the most important components to the success of your model. But I found it weird that people don’t pay that much attention or time asking, ‘What’s in my dataset?’ That’s how I got interested in this space. And then eventually, I started doing audits of large scale datasets.
Q: Can you talk about your work on the ethical foundations of AI?
A: Everybody has a view about what machine learning is about. So machine learners — people from the AI community — tell you that it doesn’t have a value. It’s just maths, it’s objective, it’s neutral and so on. Whereas scholars in the social sciences tell you that, just like any technology, machine learning encodes the values of those that are fueling it. So what we did was we systematically studied a hundred of the most influential machine learning papers to actually find out what the field cares about and to do it in a very rigorous way.
A: And one of those values was scaling up?
Q: Scale is considered the holy grail of success. You have researchers coming from big companies like DeepMind, Google and Meta, claiming that scale beats noise and scale cancels noise. The idea is that as you scale up, everything in your dataset should kind of even out, should kind of balance itself out. And you should end up with something like a normal distribution or something closer to the ground truth. That’s the idea.
Q: But your research has explored how scaling up can lead to harm. What are some of them?
A: At least when it comes to hateful content or toxicity and so on, scaling these datasets also scales the problems that they contain. More specifically, in the context of our study, scaling datasets also scales up hateful content in the dataset. We measured the amount of hateful content in two datasets. Hateful content, targeted content and aggressive content increased as the dataset was scaled from 400 million to 2 billion. That was a very conclusive finding that shows that scaling laws don’t really hold up when it comes to training data. (In another paper) we found that darker-skinned women, and men in particular, tend to be allocated the labels of suspicious person or criminal at a much higher rate.
Q: How hopeful or confident are you that the AI industry will make the changes you've proposed?
A: These are not just pure mathematical, technical outputs. They're also tools that shape society, that influence society. The recommendations are that we also incentivize and pay attention to values such as justice, fairness, privacy and so on. My honest answer is that I have zero confidence that the industry will take our recommendations. They have never taken any recommendations like this that actually encourage them to take these societal issues seriously. They probably never will. Corporations and big companies tend to act when it’s legally required. We need a very strong, enforceable regulation. They also react to public outrage and public awareness. If it gets to a state where their reputation is damaged, they tend to make change.

title: 5 AI Image Generators For Work To Try In 2024
text:
AI image generators...are they really all the hype that they appear to be?
Since the rise of ChatGPT, nearly every AI work-related solution that you can think of has been invented and developed. From apps that can take meeting notes and brief you on previous meeting conversations, to apps that organize your day and schedule and create thousands of words of content every day, the workplace is being revolutionized by artificial intelligence.
One area that has benefited perhaps the most, due to AI, is content marketing. Social media managers and content marketing specialists can use AI tools and applications to create, update, or enhance quality content in various forms—from blogs, to photos, to illustrations and infographics, to videos—within a fraction of the time it would usually take to deliver this work.
AI image generators have become synonymous with ChatGPT and other AI-powered chatbots. In this month alone (July 2024), analysis of searches for AI image generators (via Semrush) shows a search volume of 673,000.
But why are they so insanely popular, and what's in it for you and your career or job if you work in content marketing?
What Is An AI Image Generator?
An AI image generator is a software application that uses artificial intelligence and deep learning to generate entire images from scratch, or even transform existing images according to specific inputs. AI image generators use GANs (generative adversarial networks) to produce highly realistic and convincingly authentic images and replicas of real objects and people.
Some of the capabilities of such tools and apps include:
- Complete image creation according to given prompts, such as abstract art, celebrities (for fun), and landscapes, or business scenes
- Specific art styles
- Improvement of image quality
- Realistic business headshots and photoshoots (saving you the expense for a photography session, at least temporarily)
5 Popular AI Image Generators
Here are five popular AI image generators you could try for work or for content production:
- DALL-E (well of course, a list of AI image generators would be rendered incomplete without a mention of ChatGPT's visual counterpart)
- Midjourney
- Canva's Free AI Image Generator
- Adobe Firefly
- Freepik AI Image Generator
What You Should Know Before Using An AI Image Generator For Work
Before using an AI image generator, especially for work, there are a few important things you should bear in mind.
First, AI is not perfect. AI image generation is a fairly new art, and although its capabilities are amazing, it is liable to some serious flaws. There have been numerous well-known embarrassing gaffes on social media of AI-generated images, purported to be real, which did not turn out so well, due to them displaying hideous images of people in the background of a crowd, or, as tends to be AI's most common image mistake, showing multiple limbs or distorted fingers.
Therefore always take caution when using AI for work-related purposes and triple-check the quality.
Another important factor to note is that if you want your finished product to actually look real or appear to be of photographer quality, you're better off hiring an actual photographer.
Otherwise, if you want to give your content a creative, unique, and artistic edge not found in any stock photos online, want the product to have a playful vibe, or are looking for a temporary fix to a business photoshoot for your LinkedIn profile photo, you can try an AI image generator.
Finally—and this should go without saying—never abuse your creative freedom to generate images of others and give people the impression that they are real. This is why, many platforms such as Instagram and YouTube, are now requesting users to check a box that labels their content as AI content, to avoid misleading others.
How To Use An AI Image Generator For Work
Using an AI image generator is not a complicated science at all. You simply give it a specific prompt, such as "a Black woman with a braided updo sitting at her desk in a well lit office with woodlands at the window" and it creates a number of images based on what you've described. This can save you time as a designer or other professional creative, and you can go as wild with your imagination and creativity as you desire.
Some effective applications within the workplace include:
- Using an AI image generator to inspire you and get your wheels turning for new art as an artist or interior designer, enabling you to visualize concepts and brainstorm
- Creating unique and engaging content for social media marketing campaigns and blogs
- Logo generation
- Covers and illustrations for published works
- LinkedIn profile headshot
Bear in mind that each AI image generator, whether DALL-E or Canva's free AI tool, will have its own pricing structure, and pros and cons associated with user-friendliness and value for the price. Factor these in and evaluate the quality of the photos generated—not forgetting ethics—before using an AI image generator for work purposes.

title: Alphabet to report double-digit Q2 growth; AI adoption, ballooning costs in focus - ET Telecom
text:
- Internet

Alphabet to report double-digit Q2 growth; AI adoption, ballooning costs in focus
Google is also launching new Pixel devices with AI capabilities next month, moving forward its unveiling event, typically set in fall, after Apple announced in June a slew of AI capabilities and an integration with ChatGPT in the latest iPhones.
By Yuvraj Malik
Google-parent Alphabet is expected to report a nearly 14% rise in quarterly revenue, its fourth straight quarter of double-digit growth, driven by steady demand for its artificial intelligence-powered cloud computing services and an uptick in the ad market.
The search giant's second-quarter report on Tuesday, the first among the Big Technology companies this season, could offer further insight into the uptake of AI services, as well as the rising costs associated with the new technology.
At a developer conference in May, Google widely rolled out AI-powered summaries in Search and beefed up its Gemini AI model to better compete with services from OpenAI and Microsoft.
Google is also launching new Pixel devices with AI capabilities next month, moving forward its unveiling event, typically set in fall, after Apple announced in June a slew of AI capabilities and an integration with ChatGPT in the latest iPhones.
"Investors will be looking for continued success in Search, but also for signs of the company adapting to the new world of AI," said Gil Luria, senior software analyst at D.A. Davidson & Co.
"The company will need to show that AI is driving Google Cloud growth, that there are no share losses in Search as users start leaning more on AI chat, and that the new models being built are competitive."
Alphabet's AI investments will also be closely watched. In the January-March period, the company's capital expenditure jumped 91% to $12 billion, rattling some investors even though CEO Sundar Pichai assured that the AI integrations were boosting demand for its cloud and search businesses.
The company's operating expenses in the second quarter ended June likely rose more than 32% to $27.57 billion, according to LSEG data, the highest jump in over two years.
Investors will also have questions around reports that Alphabet is in talks to buy cybersecurity startup Wiz for roughly $23 billion and how that would affect its bottomline.
Alphabet's core businesses are likely to report healthy growth as an improving macro-economic climate gives customers the confidence to invest in cloud computing and spend on advertising.
"Google search spending still held up fairly well ... we think advertisers need to spend as a key offset to inflation," said RBC Capital Markets analyst Brad Erickson.
Media investment firm GroupM raised its 2024 global advertising growth forecast to 7.8% in June, from 5.3% in December, primarily on account of better-than-expected spending in China and the United States.
Analysts also expect strong performance at YouTube, thanks in part to expanded monetization features in its TikTok-styled video offering, Shorts.
Alphabet's second-quarter cloud computing sales and advertising revenue are expected to grow 26.4% and 10.8%, respectively, according to LSEG data, largely similar to the preceding two quarters.
Ad-dependent peer Meta Platforms will report its results next week on Wednesday, July 31.

Our marketing strategy now leverages AI to predict customer needs and behaviors. We can anticipate trends and adjust our strategy using machine learning algorithms to analyze historical data. This predictive capability enables proactive engagement, offering solutions before customers realize they need them. It enhances our ability to meet customer expectations and stay ahead of market trends. This approach keeps us competitive and aligned with future demands. - Jagadish Gokavarapu, Wissen Infotech

From the perspective of marketing technology, the ability to A/B test the creatives that were clicked and resulted in conversions. title: The Olympic Games' Leap Into The AI Era
text:
At the heart of the Olympic Games lies a spirit of continuous innovation and relentless pursuit of excellence. This spirit transcends the physical boundaries of sports, embracing the advancements of our time. In recent years, a new player has entered the Olympic arena, not to compete, but to revolutionize how the Games are experienced and managed: Artificial Intelligence (AI).
A New Age of Olympic Excellence
Envision an Olympic Games where AI doesn't just augment the experience but transforms it. A realm where the brilliance of human performance is matched by the sophistication of digital innovation. The integration of AI into the Olympics is not a futuristic fantasy; it's the present, unfolding before our eyes. To being with, AI's impact on the Olympics is most visibly seen in athlete training and performance. Trainers use advanced AI algorithms to analyze athletes' techniques, optimize their training regimes, and even prevent injuries. This personalized approach to training is empowering athletes to push the boundaries of what's physically possible. For example, consider the USA Swimming team. For the Tokyo 2020 Olympics, they utilized AI-driven analysis tools to enhance swimmers' techniques and improve their performances. By analyzing thousands of data points, from stroke mechanics to turn efficiency, AI provided insights that were pivotal in fine-tuning athletes' training programs. Next, AI is transforming the sports viewing experience. Through advanced analytics and AI-driven graphics, viewers have insights into sports like never before. This technology breaks down complex athletic maneuvers into understandable segments, allowing fans to appreciate the intricacies of each sport deeply. In the 2020 Olympics, broadcasters used AI to provide real-time analytics and enhanced graphics during events like gymnastics and track and field. These AI-powered insights gave viewers a deeper understanding of the athletes' performances and the nuances of each sport.
AI for Logistics and Security
Beyond the core athletics and broadcasting, AI plays a crucial role in the logistics and security of the Games. From crowd management to event scheduling, AI systems ensure that the Olympics run smoothly and safely. For instance, at the Pyeongchang 2018 Winter Olympics, AI-powered robots were deployed for various tasks, including cleaning, providing information to visitors, and even carrying the Olympic torch. These robots represented a glimpse into a future where technology and human cooperation create a seamless and interactive Olympic experience.
Sustainable Olympics through AI
Sustainability is a critical focus for the Olympics Committee, and AI is playing a pivotal role in making the Olympics Games greener. By optimizing resource allocation, energy consumption, and waste management, AI helps in minimizing the environmental impact of the Olympics. The Tokyo 2020 Olympics showcased this commitment to sustainability. AI was used to optimize energy usage in Olympic venues, contributing to the Games' pledge to be carbon neutral. This approach not only ensured operational efficiency but also set a new standard for future sustainable sporting events. In conjunction, as AI becomes more embedded in the fabric of the Olympics, ethical considerations around its use have become increasingly important. Issues such as data privacy, fairness in AI decision-making, and maintaining the human essence of sports are at the forefront of discussions. As a result, the Olympic Committee has recognized these challenges and is actively working to ensure that AI is used in a way that respects athletes' rights and preserves the integrity of the Games.
Looking Ahead: The Future of AI in the Olympics
The potential of AI in the Olympics is broad and consistently evolving. Imagine a future where AI helps design training programs tailored to each athlete's physiology, where virtual reality allows fans to experience sports from an athlete's perspective, and where AI-assisted officiating ensures fair and accurate competition. This future is not only about leveraging technology for efficiency and entertainment but about creating a more inclusive and accessible Olympic Games. AI has the potential to bring the Olympics to a broader audience, transcending geographical and physical barriers.
The integration of AI in the Olympics represents the meeting point of human athletic prowess and technological advancement. It's a journey that honors the Olympic spirit while embracing the possibilities of the digital age. For athletes, organizers, and fans, the AI revolution in the Olympics is about more than just enhancing performance or streamlining operations; it's about reimagining what the Games can be.
As we stand on the cusp of this exciting new era, let's remember that at the heart of every algorithm, every piece of data, is the Olympic spirit - a celebration of human potential, unity, and the relentless pursuit of excellence. AI in the Olympics is not just about pushing the boundaries of technology; it's about expanding the horizons of what we, as a global community, can achieve together.

title: Future-Proofing Education: AI Will Redefine Learning And Teaching
text:
The education industry is at a crossroads, grappling with outdated systems and the rapid advancement of technology. Teachers are overwhelmed, students are underprepared for the modern workforce, and the integration of artificial intelligence in classrooms is fraught with challenges. Resistance from educators, ethical concerns, and data privacy issues hinder AI adoption, while the potential for personalized and optimized learning remains tantalizingly out of reach.
I met with Kunal Dalal, former educator and now administrator at Orange County Department of Education in California, as well as Aman Sahota and Henry Fu, cofounders of Factors, an education technology platform to explore the current state of education, the evolving role of teachers, and the transformative power of AI. How can we overcome these challenges and harness AI to create a more effective, inclusive, and future-ready educational system?
The Overwhelming Challenges Facing Modern Educators
The current state of education presents numerous challenges, as highlighted by Kunal Dalal who describes the education system as "archaic and struggling to keep up with technological advancements," with teachers often overwhelmed and underpaid. This results in students graduating without the necessary skills to thrive in the modern workforce. Dalal stresses, " Teachers are faced with an impossible task: they must educate students according to their job descriptions and the requirements set by the education system. This includes ensuring that students pass standardized tests, which are often unrelated to real-world skills.”
He observes, at the same time, teachers are responsible for preparing students for the future, a task that is becoming increasingly challenging with the rise of AI. The standards and test scores they are required to uphold often have little to do with the skills needed in the workforce, creating a disconnect between education and employment readiness. Teachers must implement both as part of their mandate but feel it’s impossible to accomplish them simultaneously.
Dalal questions whether the goal of education is to teach academic content or to prepare students for the workplace. It's difficult to do both. However, AI offers the potential to integrate these goals by freeing up time for both teachers and students. This time can be used to focus on valuable academic content while also incorporating workplace skills. AI can help embed practical, job-related skills into the curriculum. Dalal alludes to the efforts are being made Orange County to implement apprenticeship programs for high school students to bridge the gap between education and workforce readiness. “We're really pushing out apprentice programs here now, trying to get students started 10th, 11th, 12th grade well before they would go to college or graduate high school and getting them started working already," he says. This approach prepares students for the demands of the job market and frees up teachers to focus on delivering high-quality, and personalized education.”
Streamlining Educator Tasks and Redefining Educational Goals through AI
Dalal believes the first step for teachers is to streamline their tasks with the help of AI, so they aren't pulled in multiple directions. "You can't think until you can breathe first. And so first you’ve got to let them breathe." AI can assist with parent communications, lesson planning, and administrative tasks, freeing up teachers' time. Once teachers have more breathing room, schools need to address the bigger question of their goals. Dalal suggests that schools should define what a graduate should look like—what skills and thinking abilities they should have—and then work backward to achieve those goals. He notes that schools in Orange County are undergoing significant transformations due to AI, shifting from monitoring students to trusting them more. One district, for example, has abandoned AI detectors that eroded trust and now encourages students to openly share how they use AI in their work. This shift fosters a more collaborative and trusting educational environment.
As AI technology becomes more integrated into education, both teachers and administrators are poised for significant role shifts. According to Aman Sahota of Factors, "The role of the administration will essentially be to vet AI tools and to be able to look at how these tools are working, what type of content they're providing, and how much can you actually steer the AI solution to ensure it's focusing on the topics that you want." Teachers will transition from content creators to facilitators, guiding students through personalized learning experiences curated by AI.
As Henry Fu explains, "the AI is taking on more and more of a role as a copilot instead of an assistant that removes your pain. The teacher can expect it to be more helpful in providing the instruction. This frees up teachers to focus on individual student needs as Aman mentions, ensuring that the content being delivered is aligned with and actually meets those learning objectives." AI can also become a powerful tool for cultivating critical thinking skills. Fu revealed, "We believe the way to do that is by prioritizing problem solving and open-ended thinking early on. Instead of exposing someone to that environment when they're 20, you start doing that when they're six or seven [years old]."
Los Angeles' Ed: A Glimpse into the Challenges of AI-Powered Education
The Los Angeles Unified School District (LAUSD) launched a $6 million AI chatbot named Ed in March, aiming to personalize learning and address learning gaps. In May, a former director, Chris Whiteley, raised concerns about the chatbot's handling of student data. He alleged the system included unnecessary personal information in chats, inappropriately shared data with other companies, and processed it on servers outside the district, potentially violating student privacy rules.
Dalal shares concerns about the rollout of a chatbot, Ed in the neighboring county, citing its failure to protect student privacy. He argues that basic privacy measures like removing personal identification should have been implemented, noting that the software company, AllHere’s approach was careless. When when dealing with student personal information, he professed it's crucial to exercise a lot more caution than just experimenting and hoping for the best.
For Fu, student data privacy is a top concern when it comes to AI in education and emphasizes that AI systems should follow the same principles as traditional systems: data should be deleted when requested and not retained.
However, a unique challenge arises with AI that uses reinforcement learning, a process where the AI continuously improves by learning from data it's exposed to. The problem, as Fu explains, "is that this learning process leaves a residue of the data within the AI model. Currently, there's no way to completely remove this data." To address this concern, Factors takes a two-pronged approach. "We don't do any reinforcement learning," he states. "We do not access the model itself during production." This means they avoid practices that could embed student information within the AI. This prevents individual or sensitive details from being incorporated into the AI, aligning with data privacy laws that restrict unauthorized access to student information.
The AI Parent: Preparing Our Children for a World
Educational technology expert Dalal discussed a troubling trend at a meeting with tech directors: middle school students using character AI in inappropriate ways. "At first," Dalal explains, "the focus was on shutting down character AI altogether." However, the conversation took a more thoughtful turn, shifting to address the underlying issue: "a problem of...epidemic loneliness."
Dalal proposes a solution that leverages the power of AI for good. He suggests, "a healthy AI assistant who could give me healthy advice... It could help me walk through things." I feel like, as a child, [had I had this] I would have felt less lonely." This perspective reframes AI from a source of inappropriate behavior to a potential tool for social-emotional health and positive reinforcement.
Dalal emphasizes the need to equip students for responsible AI use. "One way or another," he acknowledges, "students are going to have AI buddies...We’ve got to teach them how to use it." His approach extends to parents as well. Dalal highlights his book, "The AI Parent," as a resource for parents who want to navigate this evolving technological landscape alongside their children. "My son is going to be so far ahead of his peers whose parents don't use AI at home,” he reflects.
Building Trust in AI for Education
AI offers exciting possibilities, but concerns linger about its accuracy and potential to fabricate information. Fu and Sahota, of Factors, acknowledge the need for safeguards to build trust in AI as an educational tool.
One key strategy is to provide the AI system with clear and specific context. As Fu explains, "If you ask an open-ended question, the chance of it hallucinating is orders of magnitude higher than if you provided the exact context." By carefully crafting the context they provide to the AI system, educators can significantly reduce the risk of inaccurate information being generated. He added, “Imagine asking a student a vague question versus a very specific one. The student with the more specific question is more likely to provide a clear and accurate answer–the same principle applies to AI.”
Another important step in building trust involves alignment with established educational standards. Sahota introduces the importance of ensuring AI-generated content aligns with these standards and ensures that the information students receive is accurate and meets established learning objectives. Each lesson plan would reference curriculum standards to ensure this alignment. Practical applications of AI in schools are already emerging, particularly in administrative functions. Sahota highlights Factors’ success in "providing strategic district improvement plan measurements." AI can streamline data collection and analysis processes, offering educators valuable insights into student performance and learning capacity. AI could be used to analyze qualitative data to identify what academic and social emotional supports are needed.
The future of AI in education, Fu reflects, enables a more optimized learning experience for students. AI can analyze vast amounts of data to identify learning gaps and provide targeted interventions. This personalized approach helps students learn at their own pace and in ways that are most effective for them.
AI Adoption: From Hesitation to Collaborative Learning
Generative AI is transforming the educational landscape. While initial apprehension existed among educators, a shift towards wider adoption is underway. Early adopters faced an uphill battle. Educators, as Sahota acknowledges, were "hesitant" due to unfamiliarity with the technology. School districts recognized this and implemented solutions. By providing professional development, training materials, and frameworks for AI use in classrooms, they addressed the knowledge gap and boosted educator confidence. As Sahota further explains, "more resources were provided by school districts. School districts started coming up with frameworks and guidelines." This investment in education and support empowered teachers to embrace AI as an important tool. The growing presence of AI in everyday applications has also played a significant role. Social media platforms integrating tools like Meta have normalized AI technology. This broader exposure has made AI less intimidating for educators who may not have prior experience.
However, the impact of AI in education extends beyond simply reducing educators' workload. Fu identifies a crucial shift in AI's role. While it initially functioned as an assistant, handling tasks like grading, it's evolving into a collaborative function for teachers. "This next-generation AI as your copilot," explains Fu, “personalizes instruction, tailors learning experiences to individual student needs.
The future of AI in education hinges on its ability to be controlled. Advancements in this area will allow educators to precisely guide AI's role in delivering instruction. In Fu's words, "A teacher can expect it to be more helpful in providing the instruction." This fine-tuned control over AI holds immense promise for the future of education. He imagines a classroom where AI personalizes instruction for each student, working alongside the teacher to create a truly optimized learning environment.
For Kunal Dalal, AI’s inevitability extends outside the classroom into the home and its presence needs to be embraced, albeit cautiously, “Why aren't we empowering parents to utilize AI at home? Imagine a weekly family ritual–a 'Sunday Fridge Photo' –where everyone snaps a picture of what's in the fridge using their phones. Then, during dinner, the family could debate who gets to use the AI-generated recipes for the week's meals. This extends to goal setting! Families notoriously struggle to set goals together. But with AI's help, it can be a breeze.” He adds that everyone can track each other's progress, taking the pressure off and making goal achievement a collaborative effort.
Dalal muses by empowering homes as educational institutions, “We alleviate the immense pressure on schools to be the sole providers of AI education for children. Schools shouldn't feel the burden of being everything for kids, families, AI, and workforce preparedness. Let's empower parents and families to utilize AI's potential within the home environment."

title: The Death Of Chevron Doesn’t Kill AI Regulation
text:
A severe blow to regulatory agencies’ power leveled earlier this month by the Supreme Court could have major ramifications for the United States’ nascent efforts to regulate artificial intelligence.
The Court decided in Loper Bright Enterprises vs. Raimondo to overrule landmark precedent from 1984: Chevron v. Natural Resources Defense Council. Per Chevron doctrine, courts were required to defer to agency interpretation.
When it comes to AI regulation, the Loper Bright decision therefore constitutes a clear but not quite decisive victory for those who believe over-regulation is the greatest danger of AI development and a loss for anyone who thinks the U.S. should pursue — not prevent — AI governance.
In the wake of the Loper Bright decision, it would be up to Congress to explicitly define the scope of authority granted to any future designated AI Agency (or legislation granting an existing agency significant authority to regulate AI).
“The death of Chevron deference makes clear that it’s not for the regulators to decide the scope of their authority; that’s for the courts,” Jeremy Richardson, Partner at Smith, Gambrell & Russell, LLP, explained in an interview. He added that the decision does not favor either political party, since there are federal court judges representing conservative and liberal viewpoints.
Plus, Richardson pointed out, the Administrative Procedures Act, which governs administrative agencies’ rule-making and adjudicative processes, remains in place. Loper doesn’t overrule any enabling statute, he said. Instead, it’s clarifying that if there’s a question on the scope of authority granted by the enabling statute, that’s an issue of law for the court, not the regulatory agency.
As a result, Richardson thinks an empowered AI regulator is possible in a post-Chevron world. “Once an agency to oversee AI is authorized – if that happens – I presume it will have broad (and in light of Loper, explicit) authority to act, and I hope well-informed smart people will answer the call to establish appropriate guardrails,” he said.
Yet Justice Elena Kagan’s dissent takes a different view on the degree to which Loper Bright will curb the consideration of expertise.
“Congress knows that it does not—in fact cannot—write perfectly complete regulatory statutes,” she wrote. “It knows that those statutes will inevitably contain ambiguities that some other actor will have to resolve, and gaps that some other actor will have to fill. And it would usually prefer that actor to be the responsible agency, not a court.”
The implications of the death of Chevron deference therefore depend on whether the courts will be able to fairly assess subjects beyond their skills and training. For most judges, regulatory issues related to science and technology — artificial intelligence the most pressing among them — fall squarely into this category. Justice Kagan’s dissent argues that since certain issues likely to come up in the regulatory context involve technical subject matter, those charged with interpreting them should have sufficient relevant knowledge. “Agencies have expertise in those areas; courts do not,” she wrote.
According to Charlie Bullock, Research Fellow at the Institute for Law and AI, very few people disagree with Kagan’s characterization of the pros of Chevron deference. “But people have different views of the costs,” he said in an interview. Where they fall largely depends on whether they’re more concerned about under-regulating or over-regulating AI.
Bullock said the issue of regulating AI is “the poster child” for Chevron deference, mainly for two reasons: 1) regulators targeting AI benefit from deep subject matter expertise; and 2) considering the rapidly evolving circumstances surrounding AI, regulatory flexibility is paramount. Agencies are more likely than Congress to frequently and quickly update rules.
While the Loper Bright decision doesn’t completely de-fang agencies, it certainly raises the bar for detail when it comes to future legislative language delineating the scope of their responsibilities. The shift could end up increasing pressure on Congress to lay out which agency is responsible for what types of AI regulation with absolute specificity.
In other words, the decision doesn’t go as far as barring Congress from delegating major questions to regulatory agencies. According to Mark Macarthy, Nonresident Senior Fellow at the Center for Technology Innovation at Brookings, the decision could have been more extreme.
“The way the court overturned Chevron still leaves plenty of policy space for agencies to craft measures that protect the public interest, provided only that, going forward, legislatures craft delegations of authority clearly,” he wrote.
That’s a pretty big caveat. Lawmakers have not always delegated regulatory power particularly clearly. The legislative branch’s high level of political polarization won’t make that any more likely.
Plus, Chevron’s application is subject to change depending on a host of factors — the occupants of the White House first among them. If, for example, Trump is reelected and follows through on his plans to make most federal government jobs political appointments, (as he started to do in 2020 via “Schedule F” — and is recommended in the Heritage Foundation’s Project 2025 plan for a second Trump term) Loper could in fact be useful for the development of AI regulation, Bullock explained.
While current political, legal, and technological realities suggest Loper Bright will hinder AI regulation, the political utility of Chevron deference was always situationally contingent.
“Everybody likes Chevron when they have the agencies’ favor but not the courts’ — and everybody hates Chevron when they have the courts’ favor but not the agencies,’” Bullock said.
For now, it seems the United States’ major AI firms have quite a bit of favor from all sides. But there remains, according to Bullock, “a tremendous amount of uncertainty, especially in lower courts, about exactly what Loper Bright means and how big of a deal it is.” Agencies might hesitate to regulate ambitiously, he said, if they’re not sure whether they are exposing themselves to lawsuits.
“We’ve been in a Chevron world for 40 years,” Bullock said. How much power agencies will enjoy under the weaker doctrine of Skidmore deference remains to be seen. The Supreme Court’s decision to overrule Chevron therefore opens up what Bullock called “a whole universe” of previously settled case law.
Given these risks, he expects regulators will adopt a cautious approach. Silicon Valley’s AI firms have shown they have no intention of doing the same.

title: Forget The iPhone 16, Apple Has Something Much Better
text:
Updated July 22 with new display and pricing details.
With the launch of Apple Intelligence, Apple is ready to join the world of AI-first smartphones. While the iPhone 16 Pro will be the workhorse, Tim Cook and his team will ensure the iPhone 16 can match the same promise. But a better iPhone is waiting in the wings that offers value for money, new hardware, and the power of artificial intelligence to Apple’s faithful consumers… the next-generation iPhone SE
The iPhone SE has always been popular, offering the benefits of Apple’s ecosystem and hardware in an attractivly priced smartphone. The tone was set in 2016 with the first iPhone SE based around the iPhone 5S design, the second in 2020 based around the iPhone 8, and the third in 2022 based around the same iPhone 8 design but offering the same chipset as the then-current iPhone 13.
An iPhone SE for 2025 will be just as popular, arguably even more popular than previous models, given the ever-rising price of the Pro iPhones.
Regarding specifications, we’re probably looking at an iPhone 14 form factor, but smaller than the Vanilla and Pro models, which many will welcome. After all, not everyone wants a huge slab of a smartphone. Given the three-year gap between this SE and the previous iteration, you can expect many of Apple’s hardware improvements to be included; there is potential for a larger 48-megapixel main camera, the first use of the notched display in an SE, and for the same fast-charging battery technology expected for the iPhone 16.
The biggest advance may be in the display. While previous SE models have shipped with cheaper and less vibrant LCD panels, the 2025 edition should also have an OLED display.
Update: Sunday July 21.
While the iPhone SE designs have always harkened back to previous models, they have stayed relatively fresh thanks to Apple’s iterative design process that rarely makes any significant jumps in design.
9to5Mac reports that the iPhone SE design could take on a modern look and echo the same rear design as the iPhone 16. Any new iPhone SE will have key identifying features such as the vertically stacked camera and notched screen:
“...In other words, the back sides of both devices may be largely indistinguishable from each other. This isn’t a huge surprise, as CAD renders earlier this year indicated that the upcoming iPhone SE 4 would be the largest SE model yet, with a form factor that mostly resembles the iPhone 14.
There’s also a significant point to consider. The iPhone 16’s twin camera lens arrangement is moving to a vertical arrangement to allow for stereoscopic video recording when held in landscape… video that would be suitable for watching back in 3D on the Vision Pro. Apple is looking to push this out to the iPhone 16 family, and it makes sense that the next iPhone SE will be part of that push.
Update: Monday July 22.
Details on the all-important display sizes are being reported by the MacRumors team. While the iPhone SE has always been seen as the smallest handset in the iPhone range (putting aside Tim Cook’s misguided dalliance with the iPhone Mini), the upcoming SE could match the more expensive iPhone 16’s physical size.
If you assume that the iPhone 16’s display size will be similar to that of the iPhone 15’s 6.1-inch display, then the reported 6.06-inch display for the iPhone SE will effectively offer the same screen area. Given that the iPhone SE should also carry the A18 Apple Silicon chipset and come with at least 6 GB of memory to accommodate Apple’s generative AI additions to iOS 18, it will be a tempting choice.
One final piece of the puzzle being reported is the potential price. 2022’s iPhone SE model launched at $429. Next year’s model will be more expensive, but a price window of $499 to $549 will be competitive.
The iPhone 16, by its nature, has been a compromised device in the past. Apple places the latest and greatest technology available to the company on the Pro models, which will be the iPhone 16 Pro and iPhone 16 Pro Max this year. There has always been a balancing act to keep the vanilla iPhone 16 with a high enough specification to be considered a good enough iPhone while leaving enough space to create the demand for a more expensive Pro model.
In previous years, this has involved using a previous generation of Axx chipsets, reducing the storage options for consumers, and keeping the memory specifications as low as possible. That’s no longer the case, as the need to support generative AI demands the latest Apple Silicon and higher memory to allow for as much processing on a local device as possible.
If the iPhone SE is to support Apple Intelligence, it will need the same base specifications as the iPhone 16, especially in terms of Apple Silicon. Having the iPhone SE sport the same chipset as the main line has happened before, and it’s more than likely to happen with this generation as well.
After all, if AI is the future, then Apple Intelligence needs to be everywhere. And if it is to be everywhere, then it must be supported by the iPhone SE.
There is also the question about the generative AI timetable. The ostentatiously branded Apple Intelligence was previewed at last month's Worldwide Developer Conference and will play its part in iOS 18. However, while iOS 18 will be available to the public when the iPhone 16 and iPhone 16 Pro launch in September, the critical AI componets are not scheduled to appear until the first quarter of 2025.
Apple’s community may be looking for an ‘AI boom’ on iPhone 16 sales as one of the first AI-enabled iPhones, but there’s no sign in the supply chain that Apple is planning to increase the order book. If Apple is waiting until the first quarter of 2025 to kick off the revolution, would it not be better to wait until then to see what shape that revolution will be?
If you want the extra power and the full capability of the iPhone platform, you’re going to go for the iPhone 16 Pro or iPhone 16 Pro Max, and there’s not much point looking at any other iPhone. If you are looking to maximise your value for money, the iPhone SE will be the better deal than the iPhone 16, and thanks to the late arrival of Apple Intelligence, there’s no huge benefit in buying your next iPhone before then.

title: The Urgent Need To Protect AI
text:
The integration of artificial intelligence has been both a boon and a bane for cybersecurity. While AI systems offer unprecedented capabilities for defense, they also simplify and accelerate things from the attacker’s perspective and present new, sophisticated challenges that require immediate attention.
As AI continues to grow more powerful, securing these systems becomes not just a priority but an urgent necessity.
The Double-Edged Sword of AI in Cybersecurity
AI has revolutionized cybersecurity by enhancing threat detection, response times, and overall defense mechanisms. However, the same capabilities that make AI a formidable ally can also be leveraged by malicious actors. This dual-use nature of AI presents a significant challenge: ensuring that while we harness AI for protection, we also safeguard the AI itself from being exploited.
I recently spoke with Dan Lahav, co-founder and CEO of Pattern Labs, about this issue. Lahav is also a co-author of a recent RAND report titled “Securing AI Model Weights: Preventing Theft and Misuse of Frontier Models.” He shared, “We still have a lot of gaps in understanding exactly how these systems work—and how they do what they do. There is a chance that you are introducing new risks that are not going to be fully controllable as an outcome of that.”
Emerging Threats and New Attack Vectors
The integration of AI into cybersecurity frameworks has introduced new attack vectors.
Malicious actors can poison data, manipulate AI models, and use AI to navigate through organizational networks, creating a new dimension of threats. Lahav emphasized that these systems, due to their complexity and dynamic nature, require a unique approach to security.
Traditional cybersecurity measures are insufficient; we need specialized strategies that consider the intricacies of AI technologies.
A Unique Approach to AI Security
Lahav explained that to address these challenges, organizations need to adopt a multifaceted approach that focuses on creating comprehensive security benchmarks, early warning systems, and collaborative research efforts.
He outlined several key initiatives that Pattern Labs is spearheading to protect AI systems:
- Development of Security Benchmarks: Categorize threats and operational capacities of potential attackers. This framework helps organizations prioritize their security efforts by understanding the sophistication of potential threats.
- Early Warning Systems: Continuously evaluate the capabilities and potential threats posed by AI systems with an AI early warning system. These systems assess the skill levels of AI and identify when certain capabilities might pose a risk, allowing organizations to respond proactively.
- Collaborative Research: Collaborate with other research groups and think tanks to map out future threats and necessary defenses. This collaborative effort ensures the ability to stay ahead of emerging threats and develop comprehensive security strategies.
- R&D for AI Security Solutions: Recognize gaps in current AI security measures and invest in research and development to create new solutions. This includes safeguarding AI in unique contexts and developing methods to simulate and mitigate sophisticated attacks.
- Training and Recruitment: Effective AI security requires expertise in both AI and cybersecurity. Focus on training and recruiting professionals with dual expertise, addressing the existing skills gap, and ensuring a robust defense against AI-related threats.
The Potential for AI Weaponization
As AI systems become more advanced, the risk of them being weaponized increases. Lahav noted that the more powerful AI becomes, the greater the potential for it to be used for harmful purposes. This necessitates a reevaluation of security protocols and defense mechanisms, ensuring that we are prepared for the worst-case scenarios.
A Call to Action
The urgent need to protect AI systems cannot be overstated.
As AI continues to evolve, so too must our strategies for securing it. Initiatives like those outlined here provide a roadmap for addressing these challenges. By proactively developing and implementing these strategies, we can ensure that AI remains a powerful tool for defense rather than a vulnerability to be exploited.
AI will continue to evolve, and adoption will continue to escalate. The future of cybersecurity hinges on our ability to protect AI systems. This requires a holistic approach that combines cutting-edge research, practical solutions, and a deep understanding of the evolving threat landscape.
As we navigate this new frontier and learn the potential benefits and consequences of AI, the work being done by companies like Pattern Labs to secure and protect the AI itself will be crucial in safeguarding our digital world.

title: Startup Cloverleaf Raises $300 Million, For Shovel-Ready, Gigawatt-Scale A.I. Datacenters
text:
Startup Cloverleaf Infrastructure announced a huge initial fundraising last week of $300 million from Sandbrook Capital and NGP.
The company won’t say how much equity they handed over in exchange for that growth capital. Cloverleaf co-founder Brian Janous says their objective is to deliver shovel-ready sites for the construction of hyperscale datacenters, specialized to process A.I. queries.
But this is more than just selling land to house artificial intelligences. Before the likes of Google, Meta, Amazon and Microsoft can invest $10 billion into a gigawatt-scale datacenter, Cloverleaf bets they’ll appreciate some help securing sites, prepping permits, and lining up ample electricity supply and transmission. “The ultimate challenge for this industry is not going to be access to GPUs. It’s a power challenge,” says Janous, who was the first VP of Energy at Microsoft.
In the early days a big datacenter used 10 megawatts of power, enough for about 8,000 homes. “We grew up in a time when utilities were seeing declining load growth, like from LED lighting.” Then came cloud computing, and suddenly 200 megawatt centers were in demand. “Utilities were not prepared for the growth of the cloud.” Power usage by datacenters doubled from 2017 to 2021 according to EPRI.
Then the rise of AI changed everything. Demand is exploding. That’s because A.I. models are electricity hungry, using 2.9 watt hours per chatGPT request, versus .3 watt hours for a Google search. Datacenters are the can’t miss growth business, says Janous, who in 12 years at Microsoft orchestrated 15 gigawatts of power supply to support cloud systems like Azure, before leaving a year ago. “Microsoft wants 1 gigawatt. As many GPUs as possible. They want to scale brute force computation,” says Janous.
Data centers now use 4% of U.S. electricity, set to grow to 9% by 2030. Power grid operators are not allowed to redirect electrons from suburban homes to higher-paying datacenter customers. So before grid regulators will allow a new datacenter to be built and power up they have to be convinced that there will be enough additional electric generation coming on at the same time.
“This is a complex power orchestration problem,” says Janous. “It has nothing to do with money, everything to do with physical operation of the power grid and the difficulty of building transmission lines.” Can they build enough to keep up? For example, to provide 1,000 megawatts, or 1 gigawatt of 24/7 power, you would need some 1,000 giant wind turbines on 100,000 acres, or 15,000 acres covered with 20 million solar panels — plus sufficient battery backup to fill the gaps at nighttime and when the wind stops blowing.
A utility might have to upgrade a 500 kilovolt transmission line, which involves getting approvals from regulators, and choosing among other worthy projects. “Consumers are going to be accomodated. Where the rub comes is where utilities have to decide among megaprojects,” like a datacenter versus a factory, says Ken Ryan, who learned the business at Riverstone and Goldman Sachs.
Cloverleaf has ample transmission expertise from CEO and co-founder David Berry, who previously developed renewable energy projects at ConnectGen and Clean Line Energy Partners.
As for Cloverleaf’s potential market — the U.S. will build about 40 gigawatts of hyperscale datacenters by 2028, according to analysts at TD Cowen. Analyst Rob West at research boutique Thunder Said Energy figures that upfront capital costs for those centers will average about $10 million per megawatt of computing capacity. That implies $400 billion of upfront investment in datacenters nationwide.
The profit margins on turning electricity into A.I. data will be enormous, marvels Ryan. “There’s no better business in the world as an energy conversion business,” he says. “Customers will pay a premium. Power and land in the context of the overall cost is tiny.” Cloverleaf aims to site projects where there’s plenty of green power, like Wisconsin, Ohio and Indiana.
Some long-term thinkers are already laying groundwork for new zero-carbon, small-footprint power generation sources to feed their A.I.s. OpenAI cofounder Sam Altman is a big investor in nuclear fusion engine startup Helion, which last year pre-sold 50 megawatts of future green electric generation to Microsoft. Meanwhile Bill Gates has put up $1 billion for the new Natrium reactor, now under construction in Wyoming. Jeff Bezos, of Amazon Web Services, has invested $130 million into General Fusion.
So what does Janous, a longtime observer of energy systems see as the unexpected loser in the A.I. datacenter boom? “It will be hard for hydrogen,” he says, which despite new hype will end up competing directly with A.I. for green electricity required to run electrolyzers to split apart water molecules. “How can you justify turning clean electrons into hydrogen when Google or Microsoft want to buy that power for datacenters?”

title: Business Career Disinformation & How To Exploit It
text:
Business gurus, pundits and thought leaders lead a comfortable life saying things that aren’t true and never saying out loud what they absolutely know is true. They know that “best practices” are mostly irrelevant to the blood sport of “business.” They know that meritocracies are mostly fictional and most employees really don’t like their job, their boss or their companies, and while politicians rant about fake news, companies “lie” all the time about their products, services and numbers, as they easily absorb the tiny fines they receive for misbehaving. Incredibly, research suggests that employees believe that more than 75% of all bosses are “toxic”!
In order to succeed, you have to shed most of what you believe about how business actually works, what your company wants you to believe about loyalty, and traditional career strategies you may have consciously or unconsciously adopted to succeed. What else? Most of what you believe about the relationship between performance and compensation is wrong, and the career momentum you probably feel is fake. Instead, success is about reinvention and career pivots, not long, slow straight lines. You will die-in-place if you follow paths defined by HR, executive coaches, self-help books, organizational hierarchies, traditional mentors or career planners. No, this is about rethinking the way business actually works and how this affects your career. Thinking the right ways about business is essential. Let’s look at just three.
Consultants
How many times have you been disappointed by your organizational and strategic consultants? Even the consultants know their services are less than impactful – but love the second homes their fees buy. How embarrassing – and risky – is outsourcing the “brains” of your company! Why is a stranger’s insights better than yours? You presumably have a talented team that solves lots of problems. (If you don’t, you have a larger problem that no one can solve.) But way too often someone decides that solutions need something more than the ones your team develops, and, well, you know, the ones that just won’t “sell” the way outside ones – with the right imprimatur – sell, which is why I guess God made McKinsey, BCG, Bain, EY-Parthenon, Kearney and Strategy& (among others).
Lots of companies have been on the wrong side of outside organizational and strategic advice – and paid dearly. Not to mention the scandals that have plagued these consultancies over the years. But we still hire them looking past the scandals in favor of cache. So long as the scandal-versus-cache ratios stay favorable, I guess we’re good.
There’s also the cost. Consultants cost a small fortune to engage. They’re also often engaged because they provide air cover to internal decision-makers: they’re blamable when the advice craters. Let’s not forget that companies spend over $1T a year on management consulting. Is all this advice really necessary?
Consulting About Consulting
The first step is to define “brains” versus “brawn” in detail, and make sure the brains stay home. Do you really want to pay someone tons of money to tell you how to think? Make sure you own as much of the substance as you can. Exploit strategic consultancies for what they bring to the table – optics and some brawn – but never completely default to their domain expertise, especially when they tell you what you already know. Internal consultants – your brains – should be supplemented by outside brawn, which is the best use of other kinds of consultants.
The strengths of internal consultants revolve around knowledge of company processes, products and services. What’s the relative benefit of the knowledge of a company’s processes, products and services compared with distant objectivity? Do external consultants have a lock on objectivity and specialty knowledge? (No.) Should employees contribute more – or less – to a company’s strategy? (More.) And what about digital transformation, which is perhaps the most important ongoing work a company can launch? Who should run this? Can we really say that external consultants know more about the strategy, tactics and operations of their clients than the clients themselves? External consultants will reflexively say “yes, of course we do!” But they don’t. They never did. Redraw the line. Use cost as the chalk. Sell internal credibility. Fire the consultants.
AI
As I’ve often argued, AI is coming for you, your company and your industry. Machine learning and generative AI will obliterate knowledge workers and there will be lots of happy people when it happens. If you don’t admit that your career, company and industry are all at major risk, you will somehow, incredibly be surprised when your job is outsourced to a custom GPT. So dig deep into the biggest career threat in a generation. If you live in a company where “AI” is just an assistant, you’re already losing the game. AI is destined to become a full partner and in many areas your boss.
AI for Fun & Profit
You should understand how AI works and its potential to reimagine whole industries. Unless you’re close to retirement, you have no choice. You better understand what large language models (LLMs) are, how GPTs work, how to prompt and how to leverage the most powerful technology in a generation. If you understand more than most at your company – and trust me, that’s not hard to do – you can monetize that knowledge into an AI leadership position that will significantly increase your compensation. The problem is that even though you’re now an AI guru, your company may discount your contributions because you’re already there. Perhaps the best way to monetize AI knowledge and experience is to leave your company for a ton more money than they’re paying you now. Go to a competitor all dressed up as your company’s AI guru. They will welcome you with open arms and lots more compensation than you’ll get at home.
Cybersecurity
I’ve asked this before. Remember SolarWinds? All you probably remember – now that I jogged your memory – is that it’s linked to some kind of cyberattack, but you can’t explain exactly what happened, what was hacked or what happened after the attack. It was only a couple of years ago, right? Or was it more recent? Maybe longer? Do you know what actually happened? Were the Russians involved? What did they do? Was Microsoft involved? What did they do? Do you know if the US government still uses SolarWinds software?
All everyone talks about is how the number of cyberattacks is increasing and that companies need to spend more and more money on cybersecurity. Yes, the number and severity of cyberattacks is increasing – nothing new here – but is more money the answer?
Look what happens when a company is breached. While the company’s reputation suffers somewhat – because breaches are so commonplace – impact to their reputation is minimal and short-lived. The auditors then arrive to inspect everything and declare that the company did its best (or not) to prevent the breach. Sometimes there’s a fine, even a large one, but often there’s not, but the fines are generally a tiny percentage of annual revenue – and then the insurance company writes a check.
Cybersecurity Passes
If you know that your company will likely have to pay a fine of less than 1% of your revenue for a major breach, and that your customers will return and the price of your stock will recover, how much should you really care? If you also know no matter how much you spend you’re still vulnerable to attack, how much should you spend? Is just the right amount of underspending an acknowledgement that this is an unsolvable problem with manageable consequences? Of course it is! If you do what you must to satisfy the auditors, the Board, the executive team and the insurance company, but swim upstream when everyone calls for massive new spending, you should convince the team – with data – that enough is enough. This knowledge can save your company a ton of money and make everyone less nervous about breaches. You should quantify the savings – and brand yourself a cost management guru. Let PR worry about the messaging for a week or two.
There’s More
There’s a ton of misinformation and disinformation out there about business processes, models and strategies. Some of the areas we believe we understand, we really don’t. Some examples? Here are eleven more:
- Teams don’t work, but individual contributors with money do
- The calculous of compensation: where more is easy
- Leaders are often incompetent, dishonest and mean – so queue up
- Digital transformation always fails, so fake it like everyone else
- Your people are expendable, so why are they’re still here?
- Social media and disinformation are permanent facts of life, so use them
- Enterprise software is a trap you cannot escape, so enjoy it
- Innovation is a myth, so look outside for stimulants
- Strategies are just pretty tactics — despite what you’re told
- Personalities and networks rule – work it
- Leadership is rigged, so rig it back ...
Now What?
Look around very carefully. What do you see? Step back and “see” business for what it is – not what you’re told it is. There are circles, layers and distractions everywhere. At the end of the day, perhaps the best skill is shapeshifting.

title: Will AI Really Revolutionize Every Industry? A Critical Analysis
text:
Every day, it seems, we hear bolder and more grandiose claims about how AI is poised to change the world. Most specifically, we’re told, it will affect every industry and change the way we work.
Famously, Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai said that he thinks AI will be more transformative than fire or electricity.
It’s very easy to get caught up in the excitement. But here’s the problem: Most of this buzz and hype is coming from multi-billion or trillion-dollar companies – like Alphabet - that have a vested interest in selling us on an AI-powered future.
To what extent are these hyperbolic predictions realistic, and how much is simply marketing hype?
Is it really set to change every business and industry? Or is it just another money-spinner for some of the world’s richest and most powerful corporations?
In this article, I’ll try to cut through the noise to take a hard look at how well some of these claims really stand up.
Don’t Believe The Hype?
We’ve become used to hearing wild and sensational predictions about the impact that AI will have on business and the economy. For example, PwC predicts that AI will add over $15 trillion dollars of value to the global economy by the year 2030.
To put that into perspective, that’s equal to the impact of four new nations, each the size of Germany, emerging within the next five years.
In healthcare alone, the market for AI products and services is forecast to reach $208 billion by 2030. AI advocates claim that AI can outperform doctors at diagnosing illnesses and will revolutionize the process of drug discovery.
In financial services, it’s claimed that benefits could be around $1 trillion, as professionals in the industry use AI to automate fraud detection, investment and trading algorithms, numerous back office functions as well as customer service.
In manufacturing, AI-powered “lights-out” or “dark” factories, it is claimed, will operate without human involvement, as robots and automated systems operate production lines around the clock.
In retail, we are told, we will see a rise in cashierless stores, as well as continued growth in online shopping, largely driven by the adoption of AI technology. This will enable businesses to provide us with more personalized retail experiences as well as interactive, tech-driven innovations such as virtual fitting rooms and smart mirrors.
But what about industries where it seems difficult to imagine manual human skills being replaced? Construction, for example?
Well, many processes around design, architecture, engineering and project planning and management will be automated, we are told. But so too will building skills themselves, as autonomous robots become capable of carrying out the work of bricklayers, pipe fitters and electricians.
It certainly seems like big changes are ahead, but how does this all stack up with reality?
Reality Or Marketing?
While the picture being painted points to an imminent revolution across all industries, in reality, the impact is likely to be more iterative and nuanced.
Many of the predictions are based more on the potential of AI, than its actual capabilities. Meanwhile, in the real world, there are a huge number of hurdles that will need to be overcome before this potential will be reached.
For a start, there’s the question of trust, which is essential for the broader adoption of AI. For example, the technology to create self-driving cars already exists, but despite the efficiency and convenience benefits they promise, they aren’t yet a common sight on our roads.
This is because regulators and the wider public don’t yet trust the technology. In fact, trust seems to be declining – one study found that 53 percent of us are ready to put our trust in AI today, compared to 61% five years ago.
Predictions of astronomic leaps in value that AI will add to industries may be achievable in theory. But challenges around regulation and data privacy, as well as technical challenges such as overcoming AI hallucination and bias, may not be simple to solve.
In retail, for example, all of the technologies mentioned – cashierless stores, smart mirrors, virtual fitting rooms – have been trialed and prototyped in recent years, but none of them have yet been adopted by the mainstream.
However, in financial services, we can see that there is evidence that AI is already generating change. When I recently spoke to Mastercard CTO Ed McLaughlin, he told me that it had stopped $20 billion worth of fraud thanks to AI in the past 12 months while simultaneously massively reducing the number of false positives that result in genuine customer transactions being declined.
Overall, this means that while I believe AI will have truly profound implications for business, jobs and industry, the pace of this transformation may well be slower than some of the hype and hyperbole suggests – in the short term, at least.
Looking Further Ahead
If we look to a longer timescale, then it’s very hard to imagine a future where AI isn’t hugely transformational.
For evidence of this, I believe we should look at the outcome of previous technological quantum leaps.
As with fire, electricity or nuclear power, AI isn’t going to go away, whether we like it or not. It’s only going to get better, faster and more powerful.
To me, it seem to be very unlikely that technical challenges won’t be resolved, along with the legal, societal and ethical hurdles.
In fact, betting against AI being transformational would be a little like betting against the internet being transformational 30 years ago. While it might be difficult for us to imagine the profound changes it will bring, that doesn’t mean they aren’t going to happen.
So, to sum up, I believe that all the evidence points towards the fact that although the AI revolution is underway, the dramatic changes we have been promised may not happen overnight. And the journey to mainstream adoption may take longer than those who are selling it would like us to believe.
However, the end result is likely to be significant advancements and efficiencies that will radically change the way we work and do business. Don’t count on it happening tomorrow, but equally, don’t pretend that AI is a fad that will be forgotten about any time soon.

title: The Skill Code: Preserve And Enhance Your Workplace Value
text:
With all the hubbub about artificial intelligence, do you sometimes worry that your skills will become obsolete?
Fear not. Our world will always have plenty of opportunity for people who are willing to learn. Sure, AI can seem intimidating. But as with many other things invented by humans, we can use AI as motivation to expand our own capacity.
The current handwringing reminds me of a favorite story. After working for years in a factory, a guy decides to go out on his own. He starts a consulting practice. A couple of weeks later he receives a call from the factory where he was previously employed. An important machine has stopped working and nobody can fix it. So he shows up with a bag of tools. He examines the machine carefully, then removes a small hammer from his bag. He gently taps the machine with the hammer, and it suddenly springs to life and hums right back into action. The factory foreman is delighted, and he asks the consultant for an invoice. He receives an invoice that reads, “Machine repair: $1,000.” The foreman is stunned by the amount and demands an itemized bill. The consultant writes out another that reads, “Tapping machine with hammer, $1. Knowing where to tap, $999.”
Somewhere, sometime, that guy acquired some skills that preserved his value in the marketplace.
An excellent examination of that issue is found in The Skill Code: How to Save Human Ability in an Age of Intelligent Machines.
Author Matt Beane earned his Ph.D. at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and now teaches technology management at the University of California, Santa Barbara. He’s regarded as one of the world’s top researchers on work and technology.
“The Skill Code is the DNA of how we build our skill at work,” Beane says. “It consists of three ‘Cs’—challenge, complexity, and connection. Work near your limits, engage with the bigger picture, and build bonds of trust and respect. Like the four amino acids are to genetics, the three Cs are the basic building blocks of how we learn our most valuable skills.”
Beane explains the “See one, do one, teach one” approach to learning, then tell us why that approach is in jeopardy in today’s workplace.
“Think about your most valuable skill. The thing you can reliably do under pressure that delivers results—and looks like magic to those nearby. How did you learn it? Decades of research suggest that you achieved mastery the same way: by working with someone who knew more than you did. More specifically, by watching an expert for a bit, getting involved in easy, safe parts of the work, progressing to harder, riskier tasks with their guidance, and then finally starting to guide others. In surgery, this is called ‘see one, do one, teach one.’”
But regardless of what we call it, Beane says, “whether we even know it’s going on, it’s the same process—in pipefitting, midwifery, or carpentry, in an elementary school classroom or a high-energy-physics lab. And we have clear archaeological evidence of this process going back at least to the invention of language and the bow: about 160,000 years ago.”
What can be done to preserve the skill code in a hybrid work environment?
“Once people understand that intelligent technologies allow us to get better results with less help, they can get that we’re in a ‘novice optional’ economy, and that this breaks the skill code, for experts and novices alike,” he says. “The knee-jerk (and understandable) reaction here is to just mandate that folks head into the office. I think that’s neither practical nor wise as a first-priority strategy. It’s the moral equivalent of trying to put toothpaste back in the tube.”
The key, Beane says, is to look at how work is currently being done, assess the “health” of the three Cs, looking for where and how people are succeeding at staying healthy in a hybrid environment. “They’ve discovered new tactics that others can use to get skill without throwing out the benefits of hybrid working arrangements,” Beane says. “In some cases, this will mean bringing people back together, perhaps when they’d prefer to work remotely. But that often won’t be necessary or desirable.”
What does Beane see as some of the short- and long-term consequences of intelligent machines in the workplace?
“In the short run, when we use them we often get a productivity boost,” he says. “There are arguments about how big that boost is, and for whom. Economist Daron Acemoglu believes it’s very small and won’t grow much. Others are presuming it’s large and will get much larger. But part of the way we get that improvement—again, the right way—is by becoming more ‘self-serve’ in our work. We can reach farther, faster, on a focal task. That can compromise our own skill development. Part of healthy progress in that regard involves challenge and complexity, but also will mean we’ll need less from others, in particular those who have less skill. Longer term, that means we’re knee-capping our organizations and professions by limiting skill development for the next generation.”
As this age of AI continues to evolve, what will be the key to successful mentoring relationships?
“If we care about saving human ability in an age of intelligent machines, we should focus on the expert-novice connection, not on mentorships,” Beane says. “Most of us never get a mentor and are never mentors. That’s a very special, focused relationship that stretches over a long period of time and transcends personal and professional boundaries. Mentors are role models, not just experts who help novices build skill. It's the expert-novice relationship that we all take for granted, that’s under severe threat for 2.6 billion of us right now, and that is existential. The key there is to invest in it. Spend money, time, and attention understanding how it functions, how to amplify and extend it, and in particular how to make AI part of the solution there.”
Beane says there’s a human side to that investment—one that’s agnostic about technology. “The skill code itself gives us a lens on what that looks like when it’s healthy, and what we can do to ensure that. But there’s a technological side, too. In the new world we’re building, we need to build a network of human experts, novices, and AI, focused on building human and AI capability right in the middle of work. This goes way beyond AI-assisted matches between experts and novices who happen not to work in the same physical space or organization. This is literally a new fabric for the expert-novice connection—where simply by engaging with it, both humans and AI learn faster than they could on their own, enhancing human relationships and our sense of fulfillment along the way.”
How can people at every level in an organization collaborate in saving the skill code from extinction?
“To collaborate, we need general guidelines that will help make skill a consequence, not a casualty as we drive new technology into fields and professions around the globe,” Beane says. “A healthy set of guidelines isn’t far away from the skill code—all we have to do is shift from the three Cs to the three Ds, a set of mutually reinforcing activities that nurture human skill and adaptability: discover, develop, and deploy. First and foremost, we have to discover the specific approaches that preserve the health of the skill code in our contexts—whether that’s a team, an organization, a profession, or an industry. Then we need to develop organizations and technologies that foster both productivity and healthy challenge, complexity. and connection. Robotic bomb disposal turned out better for skill building than robotic surgery because it was the trainee who controlled the robot, not the expert. That was driven by the features engineers used when they were working together, and the processes developed in the organizations that purchased these technologies. Finally, we have to consider how we deploy technology: how we alter various work processes, who we involve in that, and how we configure technologies to suit.”
Beane says any solution “must address both the technical and the social sides of the ledger if we’re going to preserve skill while securing the productivity boons promised by new technology. If we do that, not only will we have a skills solution, but it will be self-improving, because we’ve repaired the learning mechanism at its core.”
