Alphabet to report double-digit Q2 growth; AI adoption, ballooning costs in focus
The search giant's second-quarter report on Tuesday, the first among the Big Technology companies this season, could offer further insight into the uptake of AI services, as well as the rising costs associated with the new technology. At a developer conference in May, Google widely rolled out AI-powered summaries in Search and beefed up its Gemini AI model to better compete with services from OpenAI and Microsoft.
Google-parent Alphabet is expected to report a nearly 14% rise in quarterly revenue, its fourth straight quarter of double-digit growth, driven by steady demand for its artificial intelligence-powered cloud computing services and an uptick in the ad market.
The search giant's second-quarter report on Tuesday, the first among the Big Technology companies this season, could offer further insight into the uptake of AI services, as well as the rising costs associated with the new technology.
At a developer conference in May, Google widely rolled out AI-powered summaries in Search and beefed up its Gemini AI model to better compete with services from OpenAI and Microsoft.
Google is also launching new Pixel devices with AI capabilities next month, moving forward its unveiling event, typically set in fall, after Apple announced in June a slew of AI capabilities and an integration with ChatGPT in the latest iPhones.
"Investors will be looking for continued success in Search, but also for signs of the company adapting to the new world of AI," said Gil Luria, senior software analyst at D.A. Davidson & Co.
"The company will need to show that AI is driving Google Cloud growth, that there are no share losses in Search as users start leaning more on AI chat, and that the new models being built are competitive."
Alphabet's AI investments will also be closely watched. In the January-March period, the company's capital expenditure jumped 91% to $12 billion, rattling some investors even though CEO Sundar Pichai assured that the AI integrations were boosting demand for its cloud and search businesses.
The company's operating expenses in the second quarter ended June likely rose more than 32% to $27.57 billion, according to LSEG data, the highest jump in over two years.
Investors will also have questions around reports that Alphabet is in talks to buy cybersecurity startup Wiz for roughly $23 billion and how that would affect its bottomline.
Alphabet's core businesses are likely to report healthy growth as an improving macro-economic climate gives customers the confidence to invest in cloud computing and spend on advertising.
"Google search spending still held up fairly well ... we think advertisers need to spend as a key offset to inflation," said RBC Capital Markets analyst Brad Erickson.
Media investment firm GroupM raised its 2024 global advertising growth forecast to 7.8% in June, from 5.3% in December, primarily on account of better-than-expected spending in China and the United States.
Analysts also expect strong performance at YouTube, thanks in part to expanded monetization features in its TikTok-styled video offering, Shorts.
Alphabet's second-quarter cloud computing sales and advertising revenue are expected to grow 26.4% and 10.8%, respectively, according to LSEG data, largely similar to the preceding two quarters.
Ad-dependent peer Meta Platforms will report its results next week on Wednesday, July 31.

title: Target Employees Hate Its New AI Chatbot
text:
The retail company, which is suffering from stagnant sales, has made AI part of its growth strategy. But staff said that ‘Help AI’ is a poorly designed tool and a waste of resources.
By Cyrus Farivar, Forbes Staff
Last month, Target officially plunged into the AI bubble. Like many of its peers in the retail industry, the company went with something simple and accessible — a ChatGPT-esque bot. But instead of focusing it on customer support, Target focused it on employees.
“We're continually experimenting with new tools to make it even easier for our team to do their jobs and to bring more of what guests love about shopping at Target to life,” Target CIO Brett Craig enthused in a press release, touting a “transformative GenAI Technology" that would arrive in the all of the company’s nearly 2,000 stores by August.
“Help AI,” would be a sort of “store process expert and coach,” helping new and seasonal team members learn on the job. It would also “answer on-the-job process questions, coach new team members, support store operations management and more,” making “teams’ jobs easier and allow them to work more quickly and efficiently.”
But that hasn’t proven to be the case.
“Why don’t they spend the time applying AI to something actually useful?”
Target employees told Forbes that “Help AI” struggles to provide decent answers, is frustrating to use and is more distraction than anything else. Many described it as a waste of company resources.
“This tool feels like something [Target] can say: ‘Oh look at we’re so innovative,” one Target employee who wished to remain anonymous for fear of professional reprisal told Forbes, adding that Help AI felt like a bad version of OpenAI’s ChatGPT, but with more restrictions. Said another: “We call it the shitbot because it gives shit answers.”
In examples shared with Forbes, Help AI appeared adept at answering some questions but was befuddled by others. It instructed an employee asking how to handle an impolite customer to “stay calm,” and “engage politely.” But when asked the same question about an ornery coworker, it refused to respond. Another employee said the bot failed to explain basic store terms, describing its answers generally as “incomplete and mostly unhelpful.”
“Why don’t they spend the time applying AI to something actually useful?” another employee asked. “Why aren’t they using machine learning to identify trends in the items that get canceled from order pick-ups?
Worse, when a Texas employee asked Help AI how to handle an active shooter in the store, it told him to confront the attacker if he was near a weapon, specifically suggesting he use a baseball bat.
“It’s just not a good idea, just go hide,” the employee told Forbes. “If you’re in a break room, stay there, don’t go find a weapon.” Department of Homeland Security guidance suggests “evacuate,” and “hide out” as first and second options before taking action “as a last resort.”
Target spokesperson Brian Harper-Tilado did not respond to questions about the chatbot’s guidance around an active shooter situation. He said in a statement that the company is “committed” to making employee jobs easier” as a way to “better serve our guests” and was open to feedback about the bot.
“Given the transformative nature of this technology, we’re focused on testing, learning and iterating while gathering valuable feedback and insights from our team to continue making this tool even more impactful over time,” Harper-Tilado said.
“Is it bottom-line improving customer satisfaction and driving sales? I think that is a TBD.”
Earlier this year, Target said in its annual report that AI would be part of its growth strategy. The $70 billion retail giant is struggling with floundering sales, which recently dropped for the first time since 2017. It’s slashed prices on some items to remain more competitive with Walmart. At about $150 per share, its stock price has nearly been cut in half since its peak in 2021.
Help AI appears to be the tip of the spear on its AI efforts. In the press release announcing the chatbot, Target chief stores officer Mark Schindele touted it as a tool that “frees up time and attention for our team to serve guests with care and to create a shopping destination that invites discovery, ease and moments of everyday joy.”
While Target is hardly the first company to embrace AI chatbots — others include Apple, Klarna, and Morgan Stanley — it claims to be “the first major retailer” to do so for internal work purposes.
Industry observers say it’s too soon to evaluate the company’s return on investment.
“At the end of the day, is it useful?” Duleep Rodrigo, a retail analyst at KPMG, told Forbes. “Is it bottom-line improving customer satisfaction and driving sales? I think that is a TBD.”
Sky Canaves, an analyst at eMarketer, agreed that “it’s challenging to determine the exact impact of the chatbot on sales given other recent initiatives that Target has launched to turn around its decline in sales.”
But some Target employees are wondering why the company invested resources in a tool like Help AI when they could be better used elsewhere.
“Have you had to wait in a long line at Target recently because they closed self-checkout and there was only one person on the register?” she asked. “Target spent God knows how much on this practically useless tool while stores are struggling with unreasonable expectations and unmanageable workloads. [Why didn’t it] spend the time applying AI to something actually useful?”

title: Council Post: How AI Empowers Small Business Owners
text:
Minna Hu, Founder of AI Bookkeeper, committed to helping small business owners get their books done on time and with minimal effort.
Once upon a time (well, in 2018 to be precise), I made a bold move. I waved goodbye to my nine-to-five grind and dived headfirst into the unpredictable world of real estate investing. My mission? To carve out more time to nurture my business. But you know what they say about the best-laid plans ...
Instead of basking in newfound freedom, I found myself buried under a mountain of tasks for a good six months straight. From marketing to business development to playing customer service rep, I was doing it all. And let’s not forget the joy of crunching numbers for bookkeeping.
As time rolled on, I crossed paths with fellow small business owners who shared similar challenges. We were drowning in work, struggling to find reliable folks to delegate to; instead of creating our dream business, we landed ourselves multiple part-time jobs.
The traditional small business playbook tells you to grind it out until you can afford to hire help. But what if there was another way? Enter the superheroes of the modern age: AI models like GPT and Gemini.
With these AI allies by our side, small business owners can finally reclaim their focus, streamline operations and unlock their full potential without maxing out their staff rosters. So how exactly can AI level up our game? Here are three areas:
Let’s start with customer service.
Picture this: You’ve just purchased an idyllic little inn in 2020 (because, why not?). Fast forward a year, and you’re scrambling to outsource after-hours support. Cue the tedious task of crafting knowledge documents and training your outsourced team from scratch. Exhausting, right?
But what if I told you there’s a better way? Thanks to AI’s knack for understanding natural language, all you need to do is feed it the specifics of your business. Voilà! Your very own chatbot is born, ready to tackle FAQs and leave you free to handle the tricky stuff like customer complaints.
For small business owners, leveraging AI customer service tools can be a game changer. Key features to look for include seamless integration with your website through plugins compatible with platforms like Wix and GoDaddy. These tools should allow you to upload your own knowledge documents, equipping AI customer service agents with information specific to your business.
It's also crucial to choose software that includes safeguards against AI-generated errors, or "hallucinations," and ensure that the information provided is accurate. Additionally, effective AI customer service tools should identify when an issue needs to be escalated, automatically notifying you or involving you directly in the conversation.
Let's talk about the superhero powers of AI bookkeeping.
If you're tangled up in the chaos of learning QuickBooks, wrestling with your accounts and dashing to your accountant come tax season, rest assured, you're in good company. Imagine a world where the mountain of invoices and receipts that currently drowns you becomes a thing of the past. Welcome to the era of AI bookkeeping.
AI bookkeepers glide through piles of financial documents with ease, transforming them into neatly organized, searchable data. Gone are the days of desperate searches for that one elusive receipt lost in a sea of paperwork or buried in your email abyss.
While AI bookkeepers don't replace the human touch, they excel by automating the mundane—think data entry and reconciliation. This shift doesn't just boost accuracy; it can slash the time and energy you invest in keeping your books up to date.
When scouting for the right AI bookkeeping tool, don't settle without a test drive. Check the precision of its receipt and invoice scanning—try it on different invoice formats and with varying tax details. Explore how much time it saves on reconciliation and what it does when it hits a snag; does it alert you or guess at categories?
Best of all, AI bookkeeping usually costs a fraction of traditional methods. It's a double victory for small business owners eager to streamline back office operations and save money, freeing you up to focus on what truly matters—growing your business.
Now let's look at communication and coaching.
Ever found yourself agonizing over the perfect language for that email to a client? Say hello to your new best friend: AI. Just give it a prompt like this and watch as it whips up a response faster than you can say “procrastination.” Here is an example prompt:
I am a business owner. I have this issue ... Please write a response in a professional and polite tone, highlighting the following points: ...
In today's digital age, we're swimming in a sea of info. Need to crack a problem? Just hit up Google or scroll through social media. But here's the kicker: Too much info can leave you overwhelmingly stuck, like a deer in headlights.
Real progress comes from putting that knowledge to work, solving real-world problems and making a difference. That's where AI swoops in like a business coach.
Imagine you struggle to create more revenue for your business; here is an example prompt you could use:
I am a business owner running a restaurant. My business has been around for two years. Could you help me increase my revenue by $5,000 per month?
Be specific about your problem, but avoid specifics that could identify you. AI can take that information into consideration and provide you with tailored solutions.
You can go back and forth and have a conversation with your AI coach until you pinpoint practical steps to achieve your goals.
So there you have it. With AI in our corner, the sky’s the limit for small business owners looking to work smarter, not harder. It's time to embrace the future of customer service, bookkeeping, and communication and coaching and watch our dreams take flight.

title: Are There Jobs That AI Can’t Replace?
text:
Recently, a worried college graduate asked me if there were any jobs that AI couldn't replace. While I understood his concerns, I realized the question needed some tweaking. Instead of asking about specific jobs, it’s more helpful to identify the functions across industries that AI cannot perform.
The AI takeover seems mostly unfounded. According to the World Economic Forum’s latest Future of Jobs Report, 50% of organizations expect AI to drive job growth. That said, the most competitive professionals in the future will be those who possess uniquely human skills that AI cannot replicate. Here are some of those skills and how they can be applied.
Offering Empathy
When you think about jobs requiring empathy, therapists and social workers may be the first roles that come to mind, but in fact, empathy is a key trait for so many professions. I think about one of my college professors, and the way she calmly listened to our frustrations when we couldn’t solve a certain problem. I think about the nurse who made one of my sons feel less scared of getting a shot.
An empathetic person is a source of comfort and reassurance that can’t be replaced by an AI-powered tool. One study looked at people’s feelings of “being heard” after receiving a response from either AI or a human. The researchers found that initially, people felt more heard by the AI-generated messages, indicating that AI can provide emotional support. However, once the participants realized responses were AI-generated, they felt less heard, suggesting that more than anything, people want emotional support from humans.
It’s safe to say that roles requiring high degrees of empathy are safe from AI.
Engaging In Complex Negotiations
In 2021, Walmart Canada began using AI-powered tools to negotiate contracts with many of its 100,000 suppliers. This raised some alarm bells about whether AI would take over business and legal negotiations, but as Martin Rand, CEO and co-founder of Pactum, who helped lead the implementation of AI-based negotiation for Walmart Canada told Forbes, “Instead of replacing human employees, we are eliminating the mundane, low-input aspects of a procurement executive’s job, freeing up time for strategic negotiations.”
AI can handle straightforward negotiations over boilerplate contracts. Humans are still necessary to decide on the constraints and acceptable terms, and review the negotiations once completed. But sophisticated, dynamic negotiation processes will remain safely within the purview of humans. That includes real estate agents, attorneys, event planners, sales executives, project managers, and more.
Creativity And Creative Direction
Wharton professor Christian Terwiesch is an advocate for using ChatGPT to generate ideas.
“It’s cheap. It’s fast. It’s good. What’s not to be liked? Worst case is you reject all of the ideas and run with your own. But our research speaks strongly to the fact that your idea pool will get better,” said Terwiesch.
ChatGPT and other LLMs are a great resource for brainstorming. You can use them to come up with a killer headline. You can use them to help identify profitable startup ideas. But at the end of the day, humans are uniquely capable of doing meaningful creative work and making final decisions about that work.
AI might be able to imitate Dostoevsky’s voice, but it couldn’t have written Crime and Punishment. It might be able to write music based on musical theory, but it couldn’t independently create the ominous music that made Jaws so scary.
It’s a matter of taste, experience-based expertise, and point of view—all things that AI cannot replicate.
Leading (Other Humans)
AI is objective. It doesn’t play favorites. It can quickly synthesize massive amounts of information and make data-based projections. You could say that AI possesses leadership qualities. But when employees are looking for guidance, motivation, or inspiration, a human leader has a leg-up every time.
In a survey of 600-plus employees across multiple industries, researchers found that humans prefer to be led by other humans, even though people can be flawed and messy. The majority of people surveyed said they had limited trust that AI could understand human behavior at work. 69% agreed or strongly agreed that they were concerned about using AI to make decisions about hiring, promotions, and work assignments.
AI may be able to carry out certain tasks typical to leaders, but ultimately, people want other people to lead.
Final Thoughts
Once you have a grasp of the job functions that AI tools can’t perform, the best way to prepare for the future workplace is to continue developing the associated skills.
For roles that require empathy, I’d practice active listening, patience, and questioning my own assumptions. For negotiating, I’d focus on learning how to create value. To become more creative, I’d consume as much creative material as possible. And to become a great leader, I’d try to cultivate the most authentic version of my leadership style. I’d think about leading in a way that reflects my values and vision. And I’d practice trying to know and understand my colleagues in order to work more effectively with them.
Professionals who develop these and other human-centered skills will be best positioned to future-proof their careers.

title: Council Post: Gain The Data Advantage With Web Scraping
text:
Amit Chaudhary: Co-founder & CEO of Grepsr, empowering businesses with managed data extraction services. Proudly fostering talent in Nepal.
Large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT and Gemini are at the forefront of the AI revolution. But even the most advanced AI requires a critical ingredient to function and grow: Data.
The explosion of web data has directly powered the rapid development of AI, just as it empowers search engines like Google through crawling and indexing. By strategically harvesting targeted datasets from the web, you can train your machine learning (ML) models to create your own unique and powerful AI technology.
Web scraping is a powerful tool that empowers this targeted data acquisition. It allows you to go beyond search results and collect the specific datasets executives need for in-depth insights, driving strategic decision-making.
This targeted data collection can lead to significant competitive advantages, but there are many considerations when looking to utilize this tool and strategy.
To Build Or Not To Build: Technical And Ethical Challenges
Technical Considerations
Web scraping offers a tempting solution for data collection, but it comes with technical challenges. Building your own scraper requires coding knowledge, often in Python with frameworks like Beautiful Soup. The process involves crawlers that navigate websites by interpreting their structure (usually HTML) and scrapers that extract specific data.
However, websites can be complex puzzles. Many rely heavily on Javascript for dynamic features, which can require additional tools or techniques beyond parsing HTML. The mix of languages used on a website can make scraping more challenging, requiring you to adapt your approach based on its unique build.
Ethical Considerations
Remember, it’s crucial to focus on publicly available data and respect website terms of service. Ethical scraping also means avoiding overloading servers and following robots.txt guidelines. When unsure, consult a legal professional to ensure your data collection stays squeaky clean.
The Applications Of Web Scraping
To put it simply, web scraping enables you to convert websites into data that you can feed into your systems for analysis. The applications of web scraping are wide and varied. Let’s look at some of them:
1. Price Monitoring
E-commerce prices are known for their dynamism. Businesses can leverage web scraping to track competitor prices and stay informed about market trends.
This data helps them maintain competitive pricing strategies and avoid selling below a retailer's preferred price point. Additionally, price monitoring data can be used for broader research purposes like understanding consumer price index (CPI) trends by analyzing price fluctuations over time.
2. Search Engine Optimization
Ranking high on search engines like Google is crucial for online success. Web scraping can help with SEO by allowing you to analyze your competitors' strategies. By monitoring the keywords they target for relevant products, you can gain valuable insights to optimize your own SEO approach.
You can use web scraping to collect search engine results page (SERP) data for specific keywords over time. This data can help identify competitor strategies and develop a competitive advantage in search rankings.
3. Sentiment Analysis
The power of online reviews and social media allows businesses to understand customer sentiment. Web scraping helps gather this valuable user-generated content (UGC) data, including product ratings and reviews.
By analyzing this data, businesses can gain insights into customer sentiment and make informed decisions for product improvement.
4. Market Analysis
By scraping job postings, news articles and industry reports, businesses can analyze market trends, identify competitor strategies and better understand customer needs.
For instance, a university can analyze job openings to see the demand for big data skills and adjust its course offerings accordingly. This demonstrates the power of web scraping for uncovering hidden gems in publicly available web data.
5. AI Development
The vast amount of web data available today fuels the advancements in AI. LLMs like ChatGPT and Gemini leverage this data to function.
Web scraping can allow you to gather and curate web data to train your own proprietary AI models, potentially creating a competitive advantage in various fields.
Let’s say you are building an AI that analyzes customer reviews. Web scraping can help you to gather a huge amount of real-world reviews from various websites, giving your AI a vast training ground to understand different opinions and writing styles.
The more data you feed your AI, the better it gets at recognizing patterns, making predictions and, ultimately, performing its intended tasks.
It’s All About Interpreting The Data
Web scraping is a powerful tool, but the real magic lies in interpreting the data it gathers. Remember, ethical data collection is crucial, so respect privacy regulations when scraping.
Here's a great example: A healthcare client needed to understand the purchasing power of a specific population. Income data wasn't readily available, but by thinking creatively, we identified a connection: Higher income often leads to higher rental prices.
By scraping rental data and combining it with geographic information, they could get actionable insights without compromising privacy.
The web is a vast resource, and with careful analysis, you can unlock valuable datasets to solve complex business problems. Web scraping can help you gain that small but crucial edge you need to stay competitive.
In Conclusion
Web scraping offers a powerful tool for data acquisition, particularly for training AI models. By strategically harvesting targeted datasets, you can gain valuable insights that inform decision-making and potentially lead to a competitive advantage.
However, ethical considerations and technical hurdles are important factors to keep in mind. Responsible web scraping practices ensure the continued viability of this valuable tool for the foreseeable future.

title: Council Post: The Critical Role Of Data Platforms And Observability In LLM Success
text:
Vaibhav Dobriyal Dobi is the Co-Founder at LUMIQ, a firm specializing in Data & Analytics and helping accelerate the data maturity journey.
Generative AI and large language models (LLMs) have become the talk of the town, promising revolutionary advancements. However, as enterprises rush to invest in these powerful models, I see many leaders and institutions overlooking significant risks: The necessity of proper context and the availability of reliable data and metadata.
Without these critical components, I believe investments in building LLM-based solutions are doomed to fail, leading to generic and suboptimal outcomes as well as wasted resources.
This article covers why your LLM investments might fall short without the proper context, highlighting the critical role that data and metadata play in ensuring LLM success.
The Basics: Understanding LLMs
LLMs are sophisticated AI systems designed to understand and generate human-like text. These models are typically pre-trained on vast amounts of data and can perform a variety of tasks with impressive accuracy.
However, even the best foundational LLMs are not ready to fully deliver meaningful results and operate effectively in an enterprise environment and context.
The most critical and often missing requirement is the "relevant context," which includes specific business definitions, KPIs, other domain-specific information and, most importantly, quality data. Without this context, LLMs can misinterpret queries and generate suboptimal responses.
What Is Relevant Context?
To understand the importance of relevant context, let’s explore a scenario that breaks down the stages of how a real-world insight is generated.
Consider the query a user asks the LLM: "What are the top-performing mutual funds in the last quarter?"
1. User Query Acceptance
• The process begins when a user submits such a query to the LLM.
2. Interpretation of the query
• The LLM interprets the query to understand the user’s intent and the specific information being requested.
3. Contextual Data Retrieval
• The LLM retrieves relevant contextual data to inform its response. The domain context for the LLM includes anything that contributes to its data understanding: Dictionaries, business glossaries and metadata to accurately comprehend the underlying data.
• When it comes to our example query, it would gather data on mutual fund performance, quarterly financial reports and relevant market conditions.
4. LLM Processing
• The LLM processes the query using the retrieved contextual data.
• The model uses specific metrics and definitions to understand and calculate "performance" and "ranking." This domain context includes KPI metrics and other definitions.
• In our example, then, it would analyze the performance data to identify the top-performing mutual funds.
5. Response Generation
• The LLM generates a response based on its analysis.
• In our example, it would create a list of the top-performing mutual funds for the last quarter, complete with performance metrics.
• A final response to our query might read something like this: "The top-performing mutual funds last quarter were Fund A with a 12% return, Fund B with a 10% return, and Fund C with an 8% return. These funds outperformed due to their focus on technology stocks which saw significant gains. Performance has been calculated as the last three year’s return as defined KPI."
6. Response Output Serving
•The generated response is served to the user in a clear and understandable format.
• As a result, the customer receives a detailed report outlining the top mutual funds and their performance metrics for the last quarter.
To summarize, without the proper context and an understanding of how data is stored, where it is stored, what it means and how the business interprets performance (e.g., the KPI definition), the LLM might provide generic, irrelevant or even misleading advice. This highlights the importance of each step in this process.
Implementing LLMs : Two Stages When Readying Foundational LLM For Deployment Within An Enterprise
Working with proprietary or open-source LLMs involves two crucial stages:
Stage 1: Implementation (Readying The Foundational LLM)
During the implementation phase, the foundational LLM is fed with metadata (both technical and business metadata) and large datasets to learn patterns and develop its language understanding capabilities. This metadata and data provision allows the pre-trained LLMs to learn enterprise-specific nuances.
Stage 2: Deployment In Production
Once the LLM is ready, it is deployed in a real-world environment to process live user queries. To maintain high-quality and relevant responses, it is crucial to continuously provide the model with updated, relevant and reliable metadata and data.
In both stages, the integration of context and high-quality data is paramount to the LLM’s success.
The Missing Parts: Data Platform And Observability For LLMs
Along with proper context and an understanding of data, data platforms and observability are integral to both training LLMs and their deployment in production. Observability ensures that the data being used is of high quality and that metadata provides the necessary context.
Key Points For Success With LLMs
• Traditional data platforms must be enhanced with observability tools to provide context (metadata) and ensure data quality. Observability tools help monitor data flows, detect anomalies and maintain data integrity, which is crucial for both the training and deployment phases.
• I find that the lack of proper observability and reliable, high-quality data often leads to failures in LLM implementations.
Conclusion
For LLMs to truly deliver on their promise, they must operate within a unified ecosystem that includes robust data platforms and comprehensive observability. The interplay between LLMs, data platforms and data observability ensures that the models are not only trained with the right context but also continue to receive high-quality, relevant data in production.
By addressing these critical components, enterprises can maximize their LLM investments, achieving better outcomes and driving innovation forward.

title: Council Post: How To Be Ready For AI, Responsibly
text:
Marco Argenti is the Chief Information Officer at Goldman Sachs.
When companies ask how they should implement AI in their enterprise, I respond with a few questions: Do you have your data story right? How about your cloud strategy? Do you have the guardrails and mechanisms in place that will enable you to safely and effectively leverage generative AI?
I’ve worked in technology for decades and have been through the development of a variety of disruptive technologies like the internet, mobile and cloud. Compared to previous tech waves, this one feels different.
With most of those previous disruptions, we largely continued to do the same things, just in different ways. For example, with the cloud, we no longer needed to own data centers and were able to access virtually unlimited compute and storage almost instantly, but the fundamental building blocks remained largely the same.
Interacting with an AI feels very different than interacting with a computer the way we’ve been used to. The interaction is closer to that with a human: It happens primarily via natural language, is conversational and allows for a certain level of ambiguity, versus the strict semantics required by computer languages. You won’t get a syntax error from an AI; it may just be a request for clarification. While this leads to an interaction that feels more natural, it also opens up new risks.
AIs, the way they're constructed today, are rewarded for finding the next word in a sentence that’s most probable, not necessarily the most accurate. They'll also very seldom say, "I don’t know." Rather, they’d eagerly provide an answer that’s the best approximation based on the prompt, training and available data.
For AIs to be effectively implemented in an enterprise, there needs to be an apparatus around them to protect from inaccuracies, biases and “hallucinations” (i.e., completely made up, yet very plausible answers). That comes down to a combination of human factors, systems, controls and data.
Responsible AI
Responsible AI is more than a phrase; it's a fundamental business priority. We know that AIs can make mistakes, and they’re good at presenting incorrect outputs in a believable way. Responsible AI for us at Goldman Sachs means that we are aware of its limits and are focused on developing mechanisms, training and other controls to ensure the technology is used in a careful and controlled manner.
Companies need to first create a governance framework—a sort of scaffolding around AI—that establishes the necessary guardrails to ensure safe experimentation and implementation. Such governance has to account for the foundational limits of AI—like the extreme susceptibility to poor quality data—hence the importance of understanding and internal education when designing controls and policies around it.
While taking the time to develop that scaffolding may slow you down at first, it’ll ultimately give you more velocity. It may be because of my background in control engineering, but I have always thought of controls as velocity enablers. Think of a highway where the whole system is designed to allow you to proceed safely at higher velocity, not slow you down. Take the time to create your own interstate system of data on-ramps, off-ramps and controls around AI. It will pay off in the long run.
Foundational Technologies
We are in a sort of technology trifecta of AI, data and cloud. They’re the three legs of the stool taking the industry forward, and I’m a firm believer that to have a strategy around AI, you need a strategy around all three.
The first layer is cloud. The cloud plays an important role in achieving agility and velocity by helping provision resources in a more efficient, controlled way, abstracting away much of the infrastructure management and complexity and allowing the team to focus on what’s important for the business and its safety.
The other layer is data. There is no AI without data, and in order to capitalize on the opportunities this technology presents, it’s imperative to have a strong foundation centered around data quality. AI is the ultimate amplifier of your data governance—good or bad.
If you build on top of a bad foundation, your building will eventually fall. If you build AI on top of bad data, the AI will try to layer it with a veneer of congruency and plausibility to eventually hallucinate to the point of becoming useless, at best, or dangerous, at worst.
That’s why the focus we’ve had on our data strategy over the past decade-plus is so important. A strong foundation built on quality data, presented in a way that an AI can understand, creates a source of ground truth that enables companies to capitalize upon the opportunity in a safe and responsible way.
AIs are closer to human memory than to databases. Some argue that AIs are better at reasoning around data than at storing facts, which is why they need to be fed with the correct information in the form of context, documents or direct access to data sources. Like most humans, they’ll provide accurate answers if given the tools to reference check their sources when in doubt.
Current generations of AIs are somewhere between lossy data stores and reasoning platforms, which come with unique safety, compliance and IP protection considerations. That’s why what’s "around them" to ensure data quality and accuracy is so important, especially in a complex enterprise environment where data is the lifeblood of the business.
"Parenting" AI
We’re in the early stages of the development of this technology. Much like parenting a child, humans are responsible for ensuring that AIs, which are in their infancy, act responsibly, accurately and without biases.
Whether you’re training a model, leading the AI charge at a company or working on a breakthrough development of the technology, responsibility is paramount. As a humankind, we’ve just taken the first step in the development of AI. Now, it’s time to shape the functional ecosystem around it. We all play a role in how this technology develops or "grows up." It’s our responsibility to help it do so well.

title: Council Post: Revolutionizing Property Listings With AI-Driven Virtual Refurnishing
text:
Joshua Lamerton, AI Thought Leader & Co-Founder at PropTexx.
In the digital era, the real estate industry is undergoing a profound transformation driven by advancements in deep learning and AI. A pivotal innovation in this industry is the integration of AI-powered virtual refurnishing and renovation tools. These systems are revolutionizing how potential property buyers interact with property listings, providing a level of personalization and engagement that is reshaping the market.
AI-Driven Virtual Refurnishing And Renovation
Potential buyers can now engage with AI-driven tools that allow them to visualize spaces with customized furniture and décor rather than merely viewing static images. These systems employ advanced computer vision algorithms, such as convolutional neural networks (CNNs), to accurately render realistic images of interior spaces. For instance, a user could upload a photo of an empty room and see it transformed with various styles of furniture, wall colors and decor in seconds. Generative adversarial networks (GANs) are utilized to generate diverse styles and furnishings, enabling users to experiment with different configurations in real time.
An example of this in action could be a platform that allows potential buyers to switch between a modern minimalist theme and a cozy rustic style with just a few clicks. Another practical application could involve adjusting the layout to see how different furniture sizes affect the sense of space in a room. These interactive experiences not only enhance user engagement but also help buyers make informed decisions by visualizing potential changes before making a purchase.
Enhancing User Engagement And Conversion Rates
The ability to experiment with different styles, colors and layouts creates a tailored experience that significantly enhances user engagement. This personalized experience is powered by deep learning models trained on large datasets of interior design images and user preferences, ensuring that the suggestions are both aesthetically pleasing and relevant to the user's tastes.
Predictive Modeling And Return On Investment (ROI)
One of the most compelling use cases for AI-powered virtual renovation tools is the ability to perform predictive modeling at scale. By analyzing market trends, property values and renovation costs, these tools can provide potential buyers with a visual representation of a renovated space and an estimated return on investment (ROI). This predictive capability is achieved through a combination of regression models and reinforcement learning algorithms, which continuously learn and adapt to new data inputs.
Advanced Analytics And Marketing Integration
From a marketing standpoint, the insights generated from AI interactions are invaluable. Detailed analytics on user preferences, favored styles and most viewed configurations allow for highly targeted marketing campaigns and personalized follow-ups. This data-driven approach ensures communications are relevant and engaging, increasing the likelihood of conversion and enhancing overall marketing efficiency. Techniques such as clustering and segmentation are used to categorize users based on their interaction patterns, enabling more precise targeting.
Operational Efficiency And Automation
Operationally, AI-powered virtual styling tools streamline the lead capture process. Automation reduces the need for traditional staging and extensive photo shoots, leading to significant time and cost savings. For enterprise-level clients, these tools offer seamless integration into existing systems, enhancing scalability and operational efficiency. The API-based architecture of these solutions allows for easy incorporation into diverse platforms, ensuring a cohesive tech ecosystem while leveraging cutting-edge capabilities.
Technological Advancements And Capabilities
The AI algorithms powering today's virtual refurnishing tools embody a significant advancement in technological capabilities. Central to these developments are advanced deep learning models such as convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and generative adversarial networks (GANs). CNNs excel in image recognition tasks, crucial for understanding and interpreting user-uploaded photos of spaces, while GANs facilitate the generation of photorealistic images, enabling real-time rendering of highly customizable environments.
One of the groundbreaking trends in this field is the rise of open-source AI models. This technology democratizes access to powerful image generation capabilities, allowing developers to create highly detailed and diverse visual content without the high cost typically associated with proprietary systems. Furthermore, these tools leverage parallel computing resources, including GPU clusters, to process large datasets swiftly. This not only enhances the performance and scalability of AI-driven applications but also ensures that the end-user experiences are both personalized and instantaneous, transforming how users interact with digital content in the realm of interior design.
Future Implications And Industry Impact
The integration of AI-powered virtual refurnishing and renovation tools is redefining real estate marketing and sales strategies, offering unprecedented levels of personalization and engagement for buyers. These innovations allow potential buyers to vividly visualize and customize properties, driving higher conversion rates and enhancing operational efficiencies.
Whilst these advancements are transformative, they also prompt thoughtful consideration regarding privacy and data security. It is essential to manage personal data responsibly to maintain trust and ensure a positive user experience. Additionally, as these technologies become more widespread, ensuring they remain accessible across various market segments will help prevent disparities in technological advantage.
Concerns about potential market homogenization can be addressed by designing algorithms that encourage diverse aesthetic and cultural expressions. Moreover, the precision of ROI predictions can continually improve as AI models evolve and adapt to new data, thus enhancing their reliability.
By proactively addressing these considerations with robust data protection measures and equitable technology access, the industry can leverage AI to not only drive innovation but also foster a more inclusive and dynamic real estate market.
In conclusion, the integration of AI-driven virtual styling tools represents a critical evolution in real estate technology. Leveraging advanced deep learning models and predictive analytics, these platforms can significantly boost user engagement, elevate the quality of leads and streamline business operations. The fusion of personalization capabilities with predictive ROI modeling equips the industry to offer more intuitive and satisfying buying experiences. This sets a robust foundation for ongoing innovation and growth, heralding a new era where technology profoundly enhances how properties are marketed and sold.

title: Council Post: Tap Into GenAI Without Sacrificing Your Brand Values Or Compliance
text:
Assaf Baciu is President and co-founder at Persado, which provides specialized generative AI used by some of the world's largest brands.
The benefits enterprises are realizing with AI tools are impressive, but they're not without unintended consequences. I previously outlined the perils of a fragmented GenAI ecosystem and proposed a solution. Now, I'm zeroing in on the risks associated with the content produced by GenAI tools—notably in the martech stack for illustration—and the data used to generate it, as well as ways to ensure governance for responsible enterprise AI use.
GenAI tools have become synonymous with efficiency. However, while marketers are basking in their own productivity, they need to be cognizant that GenAI may be rewriting their brand voice—or worse, putting the brand at risk of copyright infringement, noncompliance or going viral for the wrong reasons. In some cases, misgoverned GenAI could be taking brands off the rails.
Distracted AI Use
No matter the industry—financial services, travel, retail, telecom or even professional services—every piece of content marketers produce and distribute contributes to customers' brand experience. This includes anything from campaign emails and text messages to web copy or social media posts. While messages may vary from customer segment to segment, it's important that AI-generated content keeps customers squarely in the brand's lane.
Consistent brand values are essential for standing out in a crowded market, conveying your value proposition(s) and maintaining a strong customer experience throughout the customer life cycle. In every piece of content your customers see, your brand values should be prevalent.
While GenAI tools can take the effort out of writing emails, updating web copy and posting to social media, this hands-off approach introduces risks such as plagiarizing copyrighted language, inadvertently creating copy with biases and, of course, diluting your brand voice.
This risk isn't inconsequential: In heavily regulated industries like banking, the stakes are higher than simply maintaining a consistent brand experience. Governance is the cornerstone of responsible AI, and enterprises can't afford to risk noncompliance. Keeping content consistent and free of biases averts ambiguity or even penalties and fines.
Keeping Your Hands On The Wheel
Fears of brand or regulatory governance issues shouldn't be a reason not to implement or, at the very least, pilot GenAI solutions for content creation. There are practices and technology capabilities that can help ensure easy, low-risk, round-trip AI use that also fuels business growth.
GenAI Tools With Built-In Guardrails
An increasing number of GenAI solutions for marketing are equipped with guardrails to ensure content outputs are accurate, relevant, on-brand and free of biases. These purpose-built GenAI solutions allow you to input specific guidelines so that the output is tailored to your specific brand voice, legal restrictions and so on. In some cases, you can easily plug in your brand values, tone and language style, input control copy or campaign details, and watch as the platform churns out accurate, on-brand content compliant with global regulations and adheres to ethical standards.
Guardrails can be as precise as the sentence structure your brand employs, your preferred punctuation, symbols/emoji usage, tone or even your audiences' reading abilities. Guidelines can be applied across channels and segmented if you cater to a range of audiences—all while maintaining your overarching brand identity and values.
While human marketing and brand teams should always have a hand in these solutions, such guardrails mean your teams will spend less time reviewing and editing content that got lost in translation and more time engaging customers in a consistent voice. It's a step toward a more efficient and cost-effective content supply chain that will drive your brand strategy forward.
Human Oversight—AI Is A Companion, Not A Replacement
Today's AI is most effectively used as a human copilot rather than an auto-pilot, with continual checks for quality assurance and brand/regulatory compliance. This is the bare minimum for brands using GenAI for external content. Remember, even professional copywriters must have their content reviewed by another human.
GenAI tools seem so easy and self-sufficient that you could take your hands off the wheel, but you should have at least one team member regularly checking the content you generate. Not only will this maintain brand voice and legal/regulatory compliance, but it may also provide co-collaborators with valuable learnings about how to craft more specific prompts for your AI to speed up getting on-brand copy into market across channels.
Maintaining Stringent Data Practices
Privacy is a fundamental right. Regardless of integrated guardrails, make sure you're upholding stringent data privacy measures with your marketing content.
• To reduce the risk of data breaches, collect and process only data that is absolutely necessary for the functioning of your platform (sometimes called data minimization).
• Anonymize personal data to protect user identities and ensure compliance with regional privacy regulations like GDPR and CCPA.
• Obtain user consent and allow your customers to easily manage their data preferences.
GenAI tools equipped with guardrails and protocols to uphold data privacy can be a helpful copilot for marketing teams, reducing risk while maintaining the efficacy of your content. Detailed logging of decisions and data input to support audits and regulatory oversight can minimize the risk of infringing on third-party copyrighted content.
The Road Ahead
GenAI is transforming how we work, handling repetitive and laborious tasks and maximizing efficiency. However, without human oversight and guardrails, GenAI tools can quickly take your brand—and your customers' experiences—off the rails.
Customers, competitors and regulatory agencies have instant access to any public content your brand is distributing; mistakes, copyright infringement, shifts from brand voice and compliance blunders won't go unnoticed. Enterprises should use tools that not only boost outputs but also deliver peace of mind.
Depending on the size of the marketing team, human oversight alone may be enough. However, if you're hoping to spend even less time backtracking on AI-generated content, explore solutions designed to keep your brand voice consistent and prioritize compliance with the highest industry standards. Your reputation may depend on it.

title: 4 Reasons Why AI Hype Outpaces Investments And Adoption
text:
Everywhere we turn, there's a flood of information — articles, statistics, books and boardroom discussions — all highlighting the impending transformative impact of artificial intelligence on our world. While the excitement and anticipation are palpable, there’s a mismatch between the hype and the actual rates of AI adoption.
Despite the substantial investments and the media's narratives, when compared to the rates that businesses are adopting artificial intelligence, the math simply isn’t adding up. One plus one is not equalling two; it’s closer to .01.
U.S. based companies have invested nearly $290 billion in AI, with optimistic projections estimating a total of $1.2 trillion to $3.8 trillion to be applied toward research, development, and across a variety of applications and industries such as driverless cars, healthcare, commercial banking, and the federal government.
According to Goldman Sachs Research, the U.S. is the market leader in AI technology, with American companies likely to be early adopters and China investments to be likely smaller and more delayed. This makes sense, when 83% of 333 million U.S. companies claim they will be using AI in their business strategies.
While the promise of AI is undeniable, only 5.4% of U.S. companies have actually leveraged AI as of February 2024, according to the U.S. Census Bureau. While AI usage is growing, rising from 3.7% in the fall 2023 to 5.4%, the total expected rise is only estimated to be single digits, 6.6% by fall 2024.
In comparison, China has the highest rate of AI adoption, with 58% of its companies leveraging AI. So while their investments are reportedly smaller compared to that of companies in the U.S., their efficacy and use of their investments are 974% greater.
The main question now is, why. What is the root cause and driving force between the mismatch in investments versus adoption?
While there are many speculations, some are clear:
- Fear: Knowledge workers and employees are resistant to embrace new AI technologies in fear it will replace their jobs. Employees are understandably concerned about the impact on their livelihoods, and this fear can be a significant barrier to the widespread acceptance of AI within organizations.
- Inability to calculate business value: The total cost of ownership associated with implementing and maintaining AI systems often fails to provide a compelling return on investment, making it challenging for organizations to justify the substantial financial commitment required. The true value of AI, which may lie in its potential to enhance productivity, improve decision-making, and unlock new business opportunities, is not always easily quantifiable, making it a hard sell to company leaders.
- It’s complicated: The technological complexity involved in integrating AI into existing IT ecosystems presents a significant hurdle. Many Fortune 1000s are still grappling with the challenge of reducing their technical debt and modernizing their overall technology infrastructure. Adding AI technology on top of this existing infrastructure can be akin to building AI on top of a house of cards, creating a precarious and unstable foundation.
- Too many strategic priorities: The tension between managing current strategic priorities and exploring innovative technologies like AI can be a barrier to widespread adoption. Organizations are often torn between the need to focus on driving market growth, expanding margins, and improving operational efficiency — their immediate and pressing concerns — and the desire to experiment with and invest in cutting-edge technologies that may yield long-term benefits. This balance is delicate, and the limited availability of resources, both in terms of funding and personnel, can make it challenging for organizations to allocate the necessary attention and resources to AI initiatives.
While there are plenty of logical reasons for the mismatch between AI investments and adoption within the US market, its impending transformative impact however is clear. The technology is here to stay and will likely be embedded in our day-to-day lives without us even knowing it. The question remains, when (not if) the adoption will catch up to the investments.

title: Curating Cleaner Data In Messy Multimodal Modals
text:
AI is messy. We can suggest that artificial intelligence is “messy” because a proportion of it is developed within inappropriate guardrails leading to security concerns. In some of the messiest cases, poorly managed AI models lead to decision bias and so-called AI hallucinations. We might also say that AI can be a little messy because user trust is embryonic and still nascent in many areas; we have as many machine intelligence scaremongers as we do AI evangelists. But perhaps our best validation for claiming that AI is messy comes down to the fact that its data streams are increasingly complex, varied and multimodal… and that makes AI data unstructured.
Some of the problem here lies in the challenge of processing unstructured data in large quantities and attempting to put these information streams through AI analytics algorithms. Software architects and engineers are all too aware of the missing link between structured data technologies and the newer AI workflows, which might now typically be based in modern programming languages like Python. Although Python does have its own processes for data cleansing and categorization, its use is emblematic of the issue we are seeking to explain here... so let's go on.
What Is Multimodal Data?
While the (older) analytical often databases provided plenty of control over data quality, unstructured multimodal AI data (such as text and images or video) prove much harder to assess and improve at scale.
To address these issues we need to start thinking about data more directly as a moving and morphing entity, not as some static set of values that resides in some repository or database, even if that data store is designed for real-time streaming data. We need to think about data in a lifecyle, data inside workflows and data as a chain of operational records.
Intelligent Data Curation
Iterative, the company dedicated to streamlining the workflows of AI engineers and creator of open source projects in MLOps has a product designed to create impact at precisely this level. DataChain is a tool for processing and evaluating unstructured data. In a world where less than a quarter of firms are using generative AI in real world business applications according to McKinsey’s Global Survey on the state of AI published in early 2024, the proliferation of sophisticated AI foundational models increases the call for cleaner (and more intelligent) curation and data processing.
“The biggest challenge in adopting artificial intelligence in the enterprise today is the lack of practices and tools for data curation and generative AI evaluation that can ensure the quality of results,” said Dmitry Petrov, CEO of Iterative. “As the next step, we need AI models that can evaluate and improve AI models. So far this has only happened at the industry forefront – take a look at DeepMind's AlphaGo training against itself, or OpenAI’s DALL-E3 curating its own dataset. Our goal is to change this.”
The Iterative boss says that the absence of simple solutions to wrangle unstructured data using AI models in easy-to-manage formats keeps the technology barrier high. In practice, most AI engineers are still building custom code for converting their JSON model responses, adapting them to databases and running models in parallel with out-of-memory data.
“DataChain democratizes the popular AI-based analytical capabilities like large language models, judging LLMs and multimodal generative AI evaluations, greatly leveling the playing field for data curation and pre-processing,” said Petrov and team. "DataChain can also store and structure Python object responses using the latest data model schemas - such as those utilized by leading LLM and AI foundational model providers.”
A Cleaner Data World?
The progression to develop this type of tool is interesting and admirable enough, but it is arguably unlikely to be Swiss Army Knife enough to clean up all messy unstructured data and help AI model developers to curate from a completely clean pipe of pure information streams for our intelligence engines for all use cases.
That being said, this is the type of tool that larger industry behemoths like to aquire and build into their wider enterprise platforms, so if Iterative does enjoy continued interest and success it will either need to scale intelligently itself or get ready to become part of a Salesforce, Snowflake, IFS, SAP or other (insert major enterprise software vendor platform company of your choice) going forwards.
Either way, we do know now that data can often be unstructured, a bit messy and occasionally dirty. Now, wash your hands.

title: A New Study Shows That AI Adds To The Workload And Stress Of Employees
text:
Many companies quickly embraced AI, expecting that it would increase the productivity of workers and make their jobs easier. But a reality check with employees who are using the technology shows it has had the opposite effect.
Reality Check
A majority of surveyed workers say that AI has actually made their jobs harder.
The survey for the Upwork Research Institute and Workplace Intelligence found that:
- 77% of employees reported that AI tools added to their workload.
- 39% said they spent more time reviewing or moderating AI-generated content.
- 23% invested more time learning how to use AI tools.
The survey of 2,500 employees freelancers, and C-suite executives in several countries was conducted by Walr, a data collection company, between April 16 and May 5, 2024. The results have a confidence level of 95%, according to the researchers.
In addition to making their work lives harder, the use of AI could lead to other undesirable results. The surveyed full-time employees said that because of AI:
- 71% were burned out.
- 65% struggled with the productivity demands of their employers.
- 1 in 3 will likely quit their jobs in the next six months because of burnout or being overworked.
Falling Short of Expectations
“Our research shows that introducing new technologies into outdated work models and systems is failing to unlock the full expected productivity value of AI,” Kelly Monahan, managing director of the Upwork Research Institute, said in a press relese
“While it's certainly possible for AI to simultaneously boost productivity and improve employee well-being, this outcome will require a fundamental shift in how we organize talent and work,” Monahan warned.
A informal survey of executives at companies that are using AI reinforced the key findings of the research project.
‘Can Be Overwhelming’
“The implementation of AI tools often requires extensive training. Employees must learn to use new systems, which can be time-consuming and detract from their regular responsibilities,” Stephanie Alston, CEO of BGG Enterprises, said via email.
“Our team has found that the time spent on feeding data into AI tools, ensuring data accuracy, and troubleshooting AI-related issues can be overwhelming. This shift in focus from core job functions to AI maintenance can lead to burnout as employees find themselves juggling multiple responsibilities,” she observed.
“In some cases, AI tools are expected to solve complex problems instantly, leading to unrealistic expectations from management. When AI fails to deliver immediate results, the burden falls back on employees, who must compensate for the gap, increasing their stress levels. While AI has the potential to revolutionize various aspects of our business, it is crucial to recognize and address the challenges it brings,” Alston pointed out.
‘An Unintended Stressor’
“Where the AI system offered an efficient solution theoretically, it still required continuous monitoring and validation by our staff to ensure the activities it recommended would apply to the unique needs of our operations,” Lucas Botsen, an HR expert and CEO of Rivermate, an HR services company, said an emailed message.
“This oversight responsibility fell to staff who already carried significant workloads, stressing them and edging them closer to burnout. Rather than reducing those employees' workload, the AI system became an unintended stressor and illustrated the lesson in providing proper training, support, and realistic expectations with AI integration,” he commented.
‘The Biggest Challenge’
“The biggest challenge we've faced is during the learning stage when a new AI tool is introduced,” Stefano Lodola, an Italian language coach and founder of Think Languages, said via email.
“Training the team to use these tools adds an additional task to their already busy schedules, leading to frustration and increased workload. Not everyone adapts to new technology at the same pace; some team members are tech-savvy and pick up the tools quickly, while others struggle and feel overwhelmed.
“This disparity can lead to feelings of frustration and burnout, especially when deadlines are tight, and the pressure to master the new tools is high. Despite my team being composed mostly of young individuals who generally adapt well to new technology, the initial training period remains a significant source of stress,” he observed.
‘Perfectionism Paralysis’
“On my own team, one issue I have seen is what I would describe as ‘perfectionism paralysis,’” Stephen Greet, CEO and co-founder of BeemJobs, said via email.
“Being leaders of an AI-based resume builder [company], our goal is to offer the best optimization available. But if used excessively, tools that endlessly polish documents can cause an ineffective cycle.
“This is a lesson I have carried forward: even if continual improvement is commendable, perfection paralysis usually results from ignoring human priorities. Technology must serve people, not the other way around,” Greet concluded.

title: Council Post: How Customer Support Businesses Can Survive In The Age Of AI: Seven Tested Tactics
text:
Nataliia Onyshkevych is COO at EverHelp, a customer support outsourcing company. Experienced in all support roles.
AI assistants keep turning the impossible into reality. Virtual agents can now book flights, reserve a hotel room and even arrange a shuttle bus—all in five minutes.
Because of that, customer support professionals often feel overwhelmed, and that's a pretty normal reaction to something new. But what if customer support companies can still thrive by using the right tactics?
My team has learned a big lesson on our AI journey: Staying proactive is key. And the numbers prove it—we've grown 185% in just a year. That's not because we're the biggest or have the fanciest AI tools.
I'm happy to share action-proven strategies beyond mere motivation that brought results for my team and helped with feeling more confident in a world dominated by AI.
1. Learn about AI and customer trends from all angles.
Simple strategies often work best. What helps me and my team greatly is proactively following industry trends via different channels, preferably from firsthand sources.
Here's how you can actively seek out industry trends:
• Organize your curated newsfeed. I follow top AI experts and bloggers to always stay in line with the latest news. I check out what AI leaders, such as Ian Goodfellow or Sam Altman, are saying on X and LinkedIn to get their take on things.
• Hunt for upcoming conferences. When I'm on the lookout for what's next, I check out customer support events like All4Customer or big conferences like VivaTech. The best thing? I find out my team isn't the only one who's frustrated. I learn what helps businesses like my company, and that's what motivates me to take action!
• Turn FOMO into proactive action. To not feel left behind, my team regularly visits lots of online webinars, both free and premium, on the latest customer trends. Also, I recommend you actively look for customer industry research and benchmark papers, where you can learn data-driven insights about the latest customer expectations. Then, work actively to implement relevant insights into your strategy.
By using multichannel resources for learning firsthand, you can significantly minimize FOMO and take proactive steps.
2. Don’t hurry with AI: Run deep tests first.
When AI is done right, it increases revenue.
But the opposite scenario also exists. So, take your time to test new customer support tools in real-life projects. Establish teams to run tests and see what works and what doesn't. After that, you can decide whether to implement tools into the daily workflow.
At my company, we also have integration experts who follow the latest tech trends that are worth trying. The strategic work includes performing a competitive analysis (researching how our competitors are using AI) and evaluating AI solution providers to choose the best strategic partner.
And, another thing that helps is the golden rule—rolling out only one AI solution at a time.
3. Create an open communication culture within your team.
Your team members set the tone for everything. That's why I suggest you prioritize an open and honest culture. If someone's struggling with a specific AI tool, they can speak up safely and get the training they need ASAP. Also, be transparent about your plans to give everyone on the team the confidence they need.
What I've seen is that clear communication drives out fear and builds trust within teams.
4. Invest resources in internal and external training.
The success of AI implementation starts with having the right skills on your team. So, regularly check in on your team's skills to see where you need a boost.
Then, invest heavily in both internal and external training programs. For example, our employees attend webinars, lectures and industry schools to improve their skills. Additionally, brainstorming sessions help everyone think creatively and come up with new ideas.
5. Focus on three competitive skills.
As never before, I think customer support representatives should be focused on emotional intelligence, advanced personalization and proactive anticipation.
• Emotional intelligence and empathy: Train agents to not just hear but listen to what customers say and respond without clichés (e.g., “I’m so sorry to hear that.”) It, indeed, helps to stand out from AI-driven conversations.
• Personal touch: AI is great, but humans are still better at understanding each other on a deep level. Aim for more thoughtful interactions that don't feel scripted. Just like when Chewy's customer agents send flowers to people who've lost their pets—it perfectly shows that the company cares.
• Proactive anticipation: Try to predict what customers might need, and fix problems before they happen. Proactive maintenance can help cut customer complaints and increase satisfaction scores.
6. Go above and beyond what customers anticipate.
I've noticed this is a tactic used by many Michelin star restaurants. For instance, customers want quick and tailored help. Aim to give them fast, 24/7 support. I also recommend giving them the choice between getting quick chatbot answers or connecting with real agents, and, beyond that, add personalized emphatic answers and different language options. Beyond that, continually look at data to find ways to speed up your responses.
7. Don't resist change.
So, what did I learn from the last two years?
Every customer support business needs to stop resisting AI, no matter how big or small. And my experiences prove that mixing technology with a human touch leads to happy customers and growth. No AI solution can empathize like humans. No AI solution can send flowers for grieving customers to support.
We, as humans, still have that power. And we always will.
And just like all other businesses, we in customer support have two options—adapt and take action, or risk falling behind.

title: Council Post: Understanding The Impact Of Industry 5.0
text:
Gisela Carere, MBA, President and Principal of Benchmark Benefit Solutions Inc.
The next phase of the industrial revolution, Industry 5.0, is upon us. Throughout the last four industrial revolutions, breakthroughs from penicillin to the microwave to the internet fundamentally changed and shaped healthcare and society, respectively. I believe that recognizing and unlocking the potential of those "eureka" moments is true cognitive efficiency at play.
Embracing The Future
Embracing change is hardly easy, but neglecting it carries a higher risk. Industries 1.0 through 4.0 happened whether we were ready (and liked them) or not. Industry 5.0 will happen, as well, so it is important that we, as business leaders, get ready!
Industry 5.0 is focused on harnessing the synergy of human brainpower and artificial intelligence (AI) to create a robotic workforce that is perceptive and responsive to human goals and desires. For example, by leveraging big data analytics, real-time data points can be used to generate insightful predictions to make meaningful and quick strategic organizational decisions.
AI has been referred to as “the new electricity” that could be used to make our lives easier and more efficient. AI can alter the way we live, work and learn, but this also has raised concerns about whether all of those alterations will be positive. Rather than looking at AI as a threat, however, I believe we should look at it as a factor of positive economic and societal transformation.
The exponential growth of AI is faster than previous technological cycles, including the internet. So how do we scale it? I believe the answer is in how we innovate and differentiate our companies.
Adapting To Industrial Transformations
Every industrial revolution has fundamentally reshaped the nature of society, the way we work and how it is carried out. I have found that the keys to adapting to these changes lie in adaptation, agility and strategic foresight.
In Canada, we have “poor” AI adoption rates compared to our U.S. counterparts. A TD Economic report suggests that generative AI could increase Canada’s GDP by 8% over the next ten years should it be widely adopted in the economy. As a business owner, I see the advantages of adopting AI for highly repetitive manual work to help enhance the productivity of our team. Google LLC estimates that generative AI could save the average employee 100 hours per year. Companies have a great opportunity to evolve, and as job disruption is top-of-mind for many workers, team communication should be a significant part of your strategic planning. I also recommend investing in skills training, which can help you promote an environment that allows team members to be more creative and strategic-thinking.
Data privacy and security are also important considerations in this new era. As per Alain Francq, director of innovation and technology at the Conference Board of Canada, “AI is very much about trust, and trust and data cut across everything from security to data analytics to privacy to ethics.” We need to continue pushing for the creation of a regulatory environment that establishes safety standards, ethics, environmental sustainability and guidelines for the use of these new technologies, as these are important for wider acceptance and adoption of AI.
Productivity Unleashed
Productivity is an important part of economic growth that functions without triggering inflation and stable interest rates. In my experience, improvements in technology often lead to increased productivity and play an important role in closing the gap in human capital. Our goal as leaders should be to improve workers' productivity, such as by investing in education and skill development opportunities.
By automating repetitive manual processes, we can free our team members from “boreout” and feeling under-challenged. Leaders are left with the important task of bringing forward human value rooted in an organizational culture of advancement and innovation. In working with many diverse organizations, I've experienced how these "human-centric" approaches, when managed and applied well, can empower collaboration and overall business success. Job crafting, for example, can allow employees to redesign their work experience based on their strengths and interests. In turn, it gives workers the opportunity to proactively tackle more complex challenges and give organizations a competitive edge.
AI: Redefining Global Perspectives
Thus far, the big winners of AI seem to be America’s “Magnificent Seven” tech firms: Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, Tesla, Meta, Nvidia and Apple. As technology spreads quickly, however, western countries will not be the only ones to benefit. AI is also set to assist emerging countries in the development and adoption of key industries such as healthcare, agriculture, manufacturing and finance.
Industry 5.0 is value-driven. In the age of AI, the emphasis remains on human value and potential. I believe that “work inertia” needs to be a thing of the past, left behind. Instead, we as business leaders should look forward and collaborate with “robot colleagues” to help humans focus on creativity and experimentation. Regardless of what industry you are in, adaptation and agility can keep you competitive while you capitalize on new opportunities brought on by technological advancements.
