title: Council Post: How To Ensure AI Sovereignty While Launching A Generative AI Chatbot
text:
Brian Jackson, Principal Research Director, Info-Tech Research Group. Author of Info-Tech's 2024 Tech Trends report.
The initial fear of AI solution providers stealing sensitive business data has evolved into more of a healthy paranoia in the 18 months since ChatGPT hit the web.
Many organizations initially warned employees not to use consumer-facing generative AI tools. Since then, many have also set to work on mitigating the risk so that employees can harness their capabilities without exposing sensitive data.
The fear that intellectual property could be scooped up and threaten an organization’s business model is well-founded. After all, we’ve all seen the copyright-related legal disputes that generative AI-focused firms are facing. Further, many of these consumer-facing tools openly state in their terms of use that users’ prompt data is fair game for future model training. So, when organizations considered adopting generative AI from a third-party provider, data confidentiality was the first concern.
Yet it’s not the only concern, as I’ve seen with the launch of Info-Tech Research Group’s own chatbot initiative. Quality is another area of consideration. Models sometimes generate errors. The bias of output is a related concern and is sometimes harder to detect. Quality factors also span into technical performance such as latency. Then, there are metrics to consider related to the specific job you want your AI agent to handle.
Finally, cost considerations are also pertinent, with cloud-based models offering metered usage on a price-per-token basis. Cost projections require organizations to estimate the scale of use and API price rates.
Put these three considerations together—data confidentiality, performance and quality—and you get AI sovereignty. Organizations will want to keep control over these three aspects within limits that are acceptable to them. Harnessing generative AI may require some level of trade-off. Finding the right balance between the three isn’t a question of identifying the right answer for everyone but the answer that best aligns with your own organization’s goals.
In 2022, my company, Info-Tech Research Group, was like many organizations when it issued a policy asking employees not to use generative AI. By the summer of 2023, while a BlackBerry survey reported that three-quarters of organizations worldwide were weighing a ban on generative AI apps, Info-Tech was already evolving its approach.
After evaluating the benefits, we pushed ahead with generative AI use cases for both employees and customers, including the launch of a generative AI chatbot to provide customers with assistance finding relevant research content and entering into dialogue about business challenges. Based on this implementation, let’s explore how to ensure AI sovereignty is successfully implemented into the launch of your generative AI chatbot.
Data Confidentiality
For us, the purpose of launching the chatbot started with a focus on improving the customer experience. Supporting customers in a trusted environment means that security and data confidentiality are prerequisites.
To ensure this, we conducted testing for prompt injection attacks using various publicly available tools and libraries. Additionally, guardrails were put in place to keep the chatbot on topic and prevent any unwanted usage. Next, the quality has to be top-notch. The chatbot’s success will be based on how well it’s used by customers, with metrics like recurring usage and content referrals tracked to indicate such.
Quality And Performance
When developing a chatbot, consider testing several different foundation models and evaluating the quality of responses from a variety of prompts. We began with a minimum viable product based on retrieval-augmented generation using Info-Tech’s website index. Early users were asked to test queries and provide detailed feedback, which was crucial for refining the system. Areas for improvement should then be identified, and plans should be made to address them to enhance the overall performance and accuracy of the tool.
For us, selecting the LLM was done by providing a list of standard questions we developed to simulate typical user queries. The quality and consistency of behavior should be highly valued.
Cost Management
For organizations starting the process, it’s essential to balance cost with quality and security. Our testing revealed that one LLM cost 150 times more than other comparable models without offering significant additional benefits in quality or security. While cost might not be the primary consideration, it still plays a role in decision making. Many organizations are opting for more cost-effective solutions that satisfy security and quality requirements, too.
Furthermore, the overall impact on costs will depend on how frequently the tool is used and which model is chosen. Higher usage of a more expensive model will lead to significantly increased costs, whereas selecting a cost-effective model can help manage expenses more efficiently. Therefore, organizations must consider both the initial investment and the ongoing operational costs when making their decisions.
Conclusion
As you chart your roadmap for the launch of your generative AI chatbot, consider improvements that extend beyond this project using a roadmap of initiatives, including cross-checking answers and adding additional content for pretraining.
It’s a long way to go from issuing a policy to protect against a threat to putting in place mitigations to seizing the opportunity promised by generative AI. That’s what AI sovereignty is all about. Each organization has to weigh its own balance between confidentiality, performance and cost. There’s no right answer for everyone, but there is a right answer for your scenario. How will you translate a healthy paranoia into creating value for users?

title: Gamuda Berhad BrandVoice: Transforming Digitally To Excel Globally
text:
The construction industry, often overlooked in this fast-paced world, stands as a silent giant, shaping the very foundation of our global economy and society. Its impact extends far beyond bricks and mortar, influencing everything from economic growth and employment to innovation and sustainability.
But the construction industry is not merely an economic engine; it is a hotbed of innovation. New technologies such as artificial intelligence (AI) and advanced data analytics are transforming the way the industry designs and builds. This shift is fueled by several factors, according to the 2024 State of Digital Adoption in Construction Report by Deloitte and Autodesk, including the need to improve efficiency, reduce costs, and meet the growing demand for sustainable and resilient infrastructure.
Despite its potential, AI and data analytics adoption in the construction industry is often fragmented and reactive, driven by isolated initiatives or regulatory compliance rather than strategic integration.
According to McKinsey, fragmentation, low IT spend (relative to other industries), and entrenched analog ways of working are some of the challenges to the digitalization of the construction industry today.
The GET Mission
Recognizing this industry-wide challenge, Gamuda has distinguished itself as a pioneer, fostering an “innovation first” philosophy. The company has consistently championed technology as a cornerstone of its operations, emphasizing the importance of holistic integration throughout the organization.
Gamuda's relentless pursuit of innovation has propelled the company to develop groundbreaking technologies, such as the world's first autonomous tunnel boring machine (TBM), Gamuda Digital Operating System (GDOS), as well as its next-generation digital Industrialized Building System.
From highways and underground tunnels to mass rapid transit railways and data centers, Gamuda consistently prioritizes digitalization and data analytics in its solutions.
Driving its digitalization ambitions is the Gamuda Excellence Transformation (GET) program. Launched in 2021, the GET program is a digital transformation initiative aimed at elevating digital excellence through the deployment of technology across the group.
GET brings together previously dispersed innovation teams into a cohesive and specialized unit. By focusing on key themes such as AI, data, Building Information Modeling, augmented reality, software development and tunneling, GET fosters collaboration and knowledge sharing, driving long-term technological strategies for the group.
“In the past, many of our grassroots teams were innovating in silos. The GET program created structure and institutionalized the importance of systemic innovation within the group. GET consolidates talent, data and systems, and disseminates best practices throughout the group,” says John Lim Ji Xiong, Group Chief Digital Officer of Gamuda Berhad.
GET's innovations have generated substantial benefits for the group, primarily by securing order book wins. Notably, the award-winning autonomous TBM has served as a technological advantage, accelerating the group's expansion into new markets like Singapore and Australia.
Furthermore, digital systems have significantly contributed to construction excellence and margin protection. A prime example is the RM2 billion (US$424 million) water supply plant project in Rasau, Selangor, where the implementation of GDOS resulted in the early identification of over 2,600 design issues. This translated into RM26 million (US$5.5 million) in savings and the efficient processing of over 16,000 forms, leading to a 91% reduction in time consumption.
The GET program has also proven instrumental in retaining Gamuda's top talent by offering alternative career paths, particularly for those with a passion for technology.
Partnerships, The Key
Driving Gamuda's digitalization efforts are two pivotal partnerships: construction software leader Autodesk, providing its collaborative construction platform, and Google, contributing its AI and cloud computing expertise.
Gamuda utilizes Autodesk Construction Cloud (ACC) as a key part of GDOS, which drives the collaboration and data collection from projects. ACC unites teams across design, health and safety, contracts/commercial and project delivery onto a single technology platform. Through Autodesk Platform Services (formerly Forge) APIs, Gamuda continues to integrate and enhance the value of the platform through its in-house tools.
As recognition for Gamuda’s global innovativeness, the company is a member of Autodesk’s Construction Executive Council (CXC), an exclusive group of forward-thinking companies in the built environment that guides product development through interaction with Autodesk’s top leadership. Lim was also awarded Autodesk Construction Champion 2023.
“Gamuda is a valued member of the Autodesk Construction Executive Council, helping the industry innovate with collaborative product development and learning. Digital technologies are addressing the major challenges facing the construction industry by lowering costs, improving efficiency and driving growth. Gamuda is helping to be a part of the solution says Jeff Larrick, Senior Director of Asia-Pacific and Japan Sales at Autodesk.
Gamuda has strategically chosen Google Cloud as its preferred Cloud partner for its diverse workloads. This robust foundation supports the GDOS, a unified enterprise data platform that consolidates project data from across the entire organization.
Furthermore, Gamuda leverages Gemini Pro, Google’s powerful foundational model, to empower BotUnify. This innovative in-house marketplace provides generative AI bots trained on Gamuda's proprietary enterprise data. Users can further personalize these bots by incorporating their own documents, ensuring that the AI assistants are finely tuned to their specific needs within a secure and isolated environment.
Gamuda recently launched the Gamuda AI Academy, a pioneering initiative to address the growing demand for AI skills in the workforce. Leveraging the power of Google Cloud to build and deploy solutions quickly and Gamuda's innovative use cases, the Academy offers comprehensive training in full-stack AI.
"We are fully sponsoring digital and AI upskilling pathways for students, aiming to forge a new generation of skilled professionals and AI innovators. The three-month immersive, project-based learning will equip participants with the relevant skills that are highly valued in the tech industry," Lim says. This initiative aligns with the national digital transformation roadmap and reinforces Gamuda's position as a digital adoption and innovation leader.
“AI is becoming a way of life, even in the age-old construction industry,” says Patrick Wee, Country Manager, Malaysia, Google Cloud. “Gamuda exemplifies how embracing digitalization and generative AI at scale can transform traditional paradigms, merging diverse data streams to solve real-world challenges while saving time and costs. The company is setting a powerful example for enterprises seeking rapid innovation by modernizing its infrastructure, data analytics, security and AI convergence.”
The Future Is Bright
The construction industry is going through a major inflection point but Gamuda believes the best is yet to come. The company is already ahead of the digitalization curve, thanks to the establishment of its GET program.
“With increased proliferation of AI and advance data analytics, the company is demonstrating how the industry can experience the same evolution the automotive industry is going through with electric vehicles, becoming more software- and data-driven. As Gamuda faces this future, we are confident that we can face any challenges that come our way. The sky is the limit as to what we can achieve in the coming years,” says Lim.

title: How Uplimit Harnesses AI To Drive An Enterprise Learning Revolution
text:
As generative AI becomes ubiquitous in every industry sector, worker skills are becoming obsolete at an accelerated rate. The way to address this overwhelming surge of worker disruption is by upskilling employees. By 2030, McKinsey Global Institute estimates US workers will require 12 million occupational transitions affecting 7.5 % of the current workforce.
Up to 1.4 million workers will need reskilling by 2026, and for many workers if their job is not automated, it will be entirely re-designed due to gen AI. BCG data shows 68% of workers are aware of these coming disruptions and they are willing to upskill to remain employable. Are companies doing enough in making upskilling a priority?
As Thomas Friedman says, we are all going through a collective “Promethean moment.” This Promethean moment is not driven by a single invention, like a printing press. Rather, it is technology supercharged. It’s a moment in time when major disruptions occur all at once and change how we digitize, process, learn, communicate, share, and act, all with the help of AI.
Kraft Heinz, GE Healthcare, Procore, and Databricks are all navigating their “Promethean moments,” by harnessing Uplimit, the AI powered cohort-based learning platform for employee technical and non-technical learning, as well as customer education. What is unique about Uplimit is its ability to leverage gen AI to easily author content, provide AI coaching support, and streamline course management while driving course completion rates 15-20X higher than conventional asynchronous online self-paced courses. Julia Stiglitz, CEO and Co-founder of Uplimit and a former early executive team member at Coursera, created Uplimit to solve the enterprise learning problem of expensive and time-consuming course updates and lack of personalization in online self-paced learning courses.
Uplimit, recently closed an $11M Series A funding, led by Salesforce Ventures to drive the AI enterprise revolution in learning. As an example of the power of AI to drive new types of personalized learning experience, Uplimit just released AI role plays, which provide learners with the ability to practice leadership, sales, and call center conversations using AI and get personalized feedback on their strengths and areas for improvement. This type of interactivity was not possible a few years ago. This is just the beginning of what the next generation of online learning will be like.
Companies that are leading the way in using AI to personalize the learning experience will have a competitive advantage in attracting and retaining talent. The Gallup American Upskilling Study found 61% of workers surveyed say upskilling opportunities at their company are an important reason to stay in their current job.
So how are companies like Kraft Heinz, GE Healthcare, Procore Technologies, and Databricks using AI powered learning for employee development and customer education?
#1 Build Gen AI literacy
LinkedIn’s 2024 Workplace Learning Report finds four out of five workers say they want to learn more about AI and how it can be used in their role, but just 38% of U.S. executives say they’re currently helping workers build AI literacy.
Kraft Heinz, under the leadership of Pamay Bassey, Chief Learning and Diversity Officer, focused the company’s Ownerversity Day— an annual 24-hour global learning event - on the theme of “Revolutionizing Creativity and Collaboration Through the Power of AI.” This learning event, sponsored by the company’s corporate university, Ownerversity, followed the sun so all employees could easily participate, and was organized around three topics:
- What is AI and what are its power and challenges?
- How is AI used at Kraft Heinz and what are some internal projects underway at the company?
- What does AI mean personally and professionally for each of us?
Bassey, author of Let’s Learn Our Way Thought It, Shall We?, believes in the power of journaling to help us navigate the disruptive and powerful opportunities AI will have on our lives. Following the AI Learning Day, Bassey started piloting AI and ChatGPT for Everyone, a synchronous online course giving learners a hands on introduction to a range of AI tools that went beyond the AI Learning Day and set up Kraft Heinz employees to be curious about exploring how AI will impact their role within the company. GE Healthcare also piloted AI and ChatGPT for Everyone and, according to Kristy Callahan, Head of Learning & Development, “One of the key takeaways for learners who completed the course and received a badge was the requirement to identify what gen AI could do for them and then develop a roadmap to accomplish this.”
#2 Personalize the learning experience in the context of the business
The goal to personalize learning has been around for decades, but often this is focused on how personalization can increase learner engagement. Rebecca Scales had a different goal, one of building learner proficiency skill levels for employees of Procore Technologies, a leader in construction management software. Rebecca, a former K-12 teacher and now Director of Capability Development, is a believer in aligning all learning skill levels to the business needs of the organization. Her first step: develop a skills framework for both technical and non-technical jobs which identify key skills and define specific sub skills at four levels: beginning, approaching proficiency, proficient, and advanced levels. Then using the Uplimit AI powered cohort learning platform, Procore developed a range of learning programs, some created by AI, which align to the specific needs of the business. Learning is personalized giving learners a clear pathway to their success and integrating assignments and exercises along the way, with evidence of completion. Says Scales, “At Procore, we build learning programs with measurable outcomes rather than delivering a NPS on a course or our department.”
#3 Expand upskilling to customers and measure the impact
The audience and investment for learning is rapidly expanding beyond internal workers to stakeholders such as current and prospective customers. Databricks, a global data, analytics, and artificial intelligence company, launched Databricks Customer Academy to drive education and upskilling for customers and users. Databricks is rapidly growing its customer base to currently more than ten thousand companies, across industries ranging from publishing to oil and gas. This is requiring learning to be scaled beyond small intact cohorts of customers to large cohorts without losing the human touch of personal interaction. The solution was to “flip the classroom,” a concept first espoused by Salman Khan in 2012, and put into action by Databricks Customer Academy. In this blended learning approach, Databricks’ customers first engage in range of content, videos, and exercises, and then, collaborate online in a series of synchronous sessions with a live instructor. According to Rochana Golani, Vice President of Learning & Enablement at Databricks, “Our customers benefit from real time human instruction alongside personalized AI coaching support. Course completions have exceeded 75%, and learning sessions have scaled from 20 to 1,000 learners without additional cost.” This combination of flipping the classroom and scaling synchronous learning to a cohort based online format is allowing Databricks to deliver a personalized learning experience to thousands of current and prospective customers around the world.
Investing in upskilling powered by gen AI is not just about staying ahead of the technology curve. Companies that are early adopters in developing enterprise-wide AI literacy for both employees and customers are able to unlock greater efficiency, increase productivity, enhance innovation, and better attract and retain employees.

title: Adobe Rolls Out More AI Generative Tools To Illustrator And Photoshop
text:
Adobe continues to roll out more AI tools across its Creative Cloud family of apps with the announcement that Adobe Illustrator and Photoshop now have accelerated creative workflows that give users more control.
Everything from the initial conception of an idea through to final production is getting a helping hand from AI. The latest version of Illustrator now has new ways for designers and illustrators to quickly bring their visions to life, whether that’s product branding, development of graphics and logos, mocking up product packaging, producing patterns and much more.
The latest release of Photoshop also features new ways for creative professionals to more easily produce design concepts and asset creation for complex and custom outputs featuring different styles, colors and variants.
To accelerate creative workflows, Illustrator now has new tools including an all-new beta Generative Shape Fill so designers can quickly add detailed vectors to shapes by entering text prompts directly in the Contextual Taskbar. The Generative Shape Fill tool is powered by the latest beta version of Firefly Vector Model which offers extra speed, power and precision.
Other innovations in Illustrator include the Dimension Tool, Mockup, Contextual Taskbar, Retype, plus enhanced selection tools. There are also Text to Pattern, Style Reference and more workflow enhancements that can seriously speed up tedious design and drawing tasks enabling designers to dive deeper into their work.
Photoshop also has new and intuitive features to accelerate core creative workflows and streamline repetitive tasks by using the Selection Brush Tool, Adjustment Brush Tool and enhancements to the Type Tool and Contextual Taskbar. Adobe says these tools can unlock new levels of productivity and precision, as well providing better control when selecting, compositing, adjusting images or simply working with type.
Photoshop also has new ways to create with Generate Image, powered by Adobe’s Firefly Image 3 Model. Whether you’re a graphic designer, fashion designer, interior designer or professional creative, Adobe says the new releases will speed up tedious workflows, freeing up more time to have fun creating and playing with concepts.
The new tools will also help across all design workflows whether that’s creating variations of advertising and marketing graphics or mocking up digital drawings and illustrations. For example, it’s now easier to add patterns to fashion silhouettes for mood boards.
Designers can also test product packaging with multiple patterns and design options, exploring ads with different seasonal variations and producing a range of designs across product mockups in endless combinations.
Adobe Firefly is the technology powering the new generative AI innovations in both Photoshop and Illustrator. And with great power comes responsibility so Adobe says it wants to be a trusted partner for creators in a way that is respectful and supportive of the creative community.
The company says it’s committed to taking a creator-friendly approach and developing AI following the company’s AI Ethics with principles of accountability, responsibility and transparency. This includes respecting creators’ rights and never training the development of AI by using customer content.
Adobe also says it will deliver AI technology in a way that supports the creative community with Adobe Firefly by providing high-quality, creator-centric generative AI models that are designed to be safe for commercial use, trained only on licensed content, such as Adobe Stock and public domain content.
Availability: The latest Firefly Vector Model (beta) is now available in Adobe Illustrator powering Generative Shape Fill (beta), Text to Pattern (beta) and Style Reference. Additional innovations including Mockup (beta), Dimension Tool, Retype, Enhanced Pan and Zoom and Contextual Taskbar are also available today in the Illustrator app.
More info: blog.adobe.com

title: The Dawn Of AI In Agriculture Is Harvesting The Future
text:
In the verdant fields and vast farmlands, a quiet revolution is unfolding. It's a revolution not marked by uproar but by the gentle hum of technology merging with the ancient art of farming. This revolution is powered by artificial intelligence (AI), and it's changing the landscape of agriculture in profound and inspiring ways.
AI: A New Companion for the Farmer
Gone are the days when farming solely depended on manual labor and traditional wisdom. Today, AI stands as a companion to the farmer, a tool as vital as the plough and the hoe. It's transforming how farmers interact with their land and crops, promising a future of increased efficiency, sustainability, and yield. At the forefront is precision agriculture. By using AI algorithms, farmers can now analyze a wealth of data, from soil conditions to weather patterns, to make informed decisions. John Deere, a name synonymous with farming equipment, is leading the way with AI tractors and equipment that can plant seeds and apply fertilizers and pesticides with astonishing accuracy, reducing waste and increasing efficiency.
AI in Crop Monitoring: The Watchful Eyes
Monitoring vast fields is a herculean task, but AI makes it manageable and precise. Companies like Plantix offer AI mobile applications that allow farmers to identify crop diseases and nutrient deficiencies just by taking a photo. This technology is not only saving crops but also empowering farmers with knowledge and solutions at their fingertips. In conjunction, predictive analytics through AI has boon a major in forecasting better harvests. One of the most significant challenges in farming is the unpredictability of nature, insect infestation, and the volatility of climate conditions. AI is changing that through complex predictive analytics. By analyzing data, AI can forecast weather patterns, predict pest invasions, and even suggest the best planting and harvesting times. For instance, the Climate Corporation provides digital agriculture solutions that leverage AI to help farmers optimize their efforts and anticipate challenges to maximize resources and crop yields.
Automated Farming: Robots in the Fields
The image of robots tending to crops is no longer futuristic. Automated farming is here, and it's making agriculture more efficient. Companies like Blue River Technology have developed AI robots that can thin and weed crops, doing the work faster and more accurately than human hands.
Sustainable Farming: AI as a Steward of the Earth
Sustainability is not just a buzzword in agriculture; it's a necessity. AI is playing a crucial role in promoting sustainable farming practices. By optimizing resource use and reducing waste, AI is helping to create farming systems that are kinder to the planet. For instance, IBM's Watson Decision Platform for Agriculture integrates AI, weather data, IoT, and blockchain to provide comprehensive solutions for sustainable farming. Initiatives in Africa are leveraging AI to identify specific seeds to use based on local topsoil conditions and nutritional needs. Moreover, some organizations are tapping into platforms like FutureView that tap into the convergence of AI, cognitive science, and the Metaverse to perform complex scenario planning to help people identify the optimal use (balancing profitability, local community impact and environment impact) of land.
The Future is Bright and Green
As we stand amidst this technological renaissance in agriculture, it's clear that AI is not just a tool; it's a catalyst for a new era of farming. An era where efficiency, sustainability, and productivity go hand in hand. AI is empowering farmers to feed the growing global population while taking care of the earth. This journey of AI in agriculture is just the beginning. It's a path leading to a future where hunger and environmental degradation are relics of the past. In this future, every seed planted, and every crop harvested tells a story of hope, of a world where technology and nature coexist in harmony. The hybrid intelligence combination of person and machine will yield greater crop yields using less resources, like topsoil and water consumption. More important, it’s the path to producing an abundance of food so that no one on Earth needs to go hungry. Let's embrace this future, for it holds the promise of a world fed not just in quantity, but with the quality and care that only the union of human ingenuity and AI can provide. The fields are ripe, and the future is waiting. Let's harvest it together.

title: Google Stock Could Rise On Q2 Cloud Growth Despite Busted Wiz Deal
text:
Wiz, the fast growing Manhattan-based cloud security startup, rejected Google’s $23 billion acquisition bid, reported Forbes.
Wiz plans to keep growing to $1 billion in annual recurring revenue before considering whether to go public, according to a letter to employees from CEO Assaf Rappaport reported in Forbes.
The collapse of this deal leaves Google’s Cloud unit struggling to keep up in the race for AI-driven cloud services. As Microsoft Azure grows faster than AWS and Google Cloud, the deal’s collapse takes away a potential growth pillar which might have propelled Google stock.
This leaves many questions unanswered:
- What is Google Cloud’s AI cloud services strategy?
- Would Wiz have boosted Google Cloud’s revenue growth?
- Why did the deal to acquire Wiz fall apart?
- What will Google Cloud do now to win a bigger share of the AI cloud services market?
My hypotheses include:
- Google Cloud’s strategy is not clearly articulated; however some of the company’s AI applications — for enabling developers to customize large language models and an AI-powered coding assistant — hold some potential to boost Google Cloud’s growth, according to my new book, Brain Rush.
- Wiz would have boosted Google Cloud’s revenue growth — although Wiz’s $350 million in 2023 revenue would add a mere 1% to Google Cloud’s $33.1 billion revenue last year. Moreover, the growth synergies for acquiring a cloud security platform are not as significant as Microsoft’s partnerships with OpenAI and other popular LLM providers, noted Brain Rush.
- The Wiz deal probably fell apart due to fear of the deal facing antitrust problems, noted the Financial Times. Based on my interviews with Rappaport about his time at Microsoft following the software giant’s acquisition of his first company, Adallom, my guess is he would not be thrilled to go from being CEO of Wiz to a cog in Alphabet’s wheel.
- Google Cloud’s strategy in the short-term is unclear. A key challenge the company must overcome is retaining the generative AI talent it has so expensively recruited, according to Brain Rush.
With Google’s earnings to be reported after the market closes on July 23, investors may find themselves asking how the search giant will post expectations-beating growth in the future.
I have requested comment from Google and Wiz and will update this post if I receive a reply.
Why Wiz And Google Went Their Separate Ways
There is no definitive answer to why the companies ended their merger discussions. While Wiz walked away from the deal, first reported July 14 by the Wall Street Journal, Rapport’s letter did not reveal the reasons the deal fell apart.
The appeal of the deal for Google was fairly clear. Wiz’s cloud security products — including prevention, active detection and response — “appeal to large firms and would have helped Google compete” with Microsoft’s security software, according to CNBC.
In rejecting Google’s offer, Rappaport wrote, “Saying no to such humbling offers is tough,” according to his memo to employees. When my students and I met with Wiz in January 2023 in the company’s Tel Aviv headquarters, he struck me as intensely humble.
We were listening to a presentation by Wiz’s chief technology officer when Rappaport walked into the meeting. He sat down quietly in order not to interrupt the CTO. Our guide — who had not previously met Rappaport — looked at him and asked, “Who are you?” Rappaport respectfully said, “I am the CEO.”
Wiz’s founders previously built security startup Adallom, raised money from Sequoia and Index and sold the business to Microsoft for $320 million in 2015 where he headed the company’s cloud security business, according to a March 2021 Forbes post.
Rappaport cofounded Wiz in 2020. After 18 months, the company hit $100 million in annual recurring revenue after 18 months, and last year reached $350 million worth of ARR. The $23 billion deal with Google would have nearly doubled the company’s most recent private-market valuation of $12 billion, according to CNBC.
Why did Rappaport walk away from the deal? “A person familiar with Wiz’s thinking cited antitrust and investor concerns as part of the reason for abandoning a potential deal,” noted CNBC.
A separate report also cited anonymous sources who fingered regulatory risk as the reason the deal fell apart. “Some members of both the Alphabet and Wiz boards of directors had been sceptical the deal would get past regulators,” the Financial Times reported. Referring to the chair of the Federal Trade Commission, “Lina Khan killed another deal,” said one of the people involved in the deal, Financial Times reported.
Can Google Cloud Grow Faster?
Google Cloud’s market share lags that of AWS and Microsoft Azure. AWS — which has led the cloud services market for over a decade — controlled 31% market share in the first quarter. Microsoft and Google Cloud control 25% and 11% respectively, noted CRN.
However, in the first quarter of 2024, Google Cloud grew faster than AWS as Azure outpaced both rivals. AWS’ revenue grew 17% in Q1, according to CNBC, compared to Azure’s 31% growth in the quarter, CRN noted.
Google Cloud — which generates sales from the Google Cloud Platform (GCP), platform services, infrastructure, collaboration tools like Google Workspace and from other IT services for customers — enjoyed 28% growth in the first quarter, CRN reported.
Google Cloud’s revenue growth rate could surpass Azure’s. How so? Alphabet forecast Google Cloud revenue would reach $12.5 billion in the fourth quarter of 2024, said CEO Sundar Pichai in April 2024 — implying a 36% growth rate, according to Acceleration Economy.
Google Cloud’s growth has resulted from building off of the company’s “strengths across AI, infrastructure, databases and analytics, and cybersecurity,” noted Acceleration Economy.
To be sure, the company has also struggled to retain its world-class AI talent. For example, generative AI was enabled by a paper about Transformers — which improved the predictive accuracy of neural networks used to respond to user prompts.
All but one of the eight co-authors of that paper have left Google. “Six started their own companies, and one joined OpenAI,” as I wrote in Brain Rush. One co-author, Aidan Gomez, left to become CEO of AI rival Cohere. Gomez said Google’s “structure does not support [product innovation]. And so you have to go build it yourself.”
Wesley Chan, who founded Google Analytics and left to co-found FPV Ventures, said Google’s “code red,” which Pichai issued after ChatGPT’s success, meant “Our guys got too lazy,” noted Brain Rush.
Will Google Beat And Raise In Its Second Quarter 2024 Report?
Google stock has outpaced Amazon and Microsoft. As of July 22, the search giant’s shares have risen 32% — far better than the 24% and 20% rise in the stock prices of Amazon and Microsoft respectively, according to Google Finance.
Investors expect Google to report strong growth in the second quarter report to be released on July 23.
Highlights include:
- Q2 2024 revenue analyst estimate: $84.35 billion — up 13% from the year before, according to Bloomberg.
- Q2 2024 earnings per share analyst estimate: $1.85 — up 28.5% from Q1 2023, notes Bloomberg.
- Q2 2024 Google Cloud revenue estimate: $10.1 billion — up 26.3%, reported Yahoo! Finance.
- Q2 2024 Google Cloud operating income estimate: $982.2 million — up 148%, Yahoo! Finance noted.
It remains unclear when AI will start to generate revenue for Google’s Cloud or ad businesses. “It is still too early to count on AI benefits as most [companies] remain in pilot mode, and material AI [revenue] is more likely a 2025-26 event,” Jefferies analyst Brent Thill wrote, according to Yahoo! Finance.
Despite Google’s many challenges, the company could beat and raise when it reports results after the bell. That would benefit investors in the search giant.

title: New Research Reveals 5 Concerns About Gen Z’s Relationship With AI
text:
Gen Z is diving headfirst into AI, weaving it into their lives in every possible way—from prepping workout and food plans to crafting job applications and using AI tutors. New research out today questions how this tight-knit bond will impact the workplace. Young adults are already getting flak for their inability to collaborate and communicate, and hiring managers say Gen Z are the worst to work with and manage.
Andrew Roth, founder and CEO of dcdx, told me his company’s goal is to help other business leaders demystify Gen Z work culture. Many believe the younger peers, feeling vilified and misunderstood, are getting a bad rap from previous generations and business leaders. Gen Z are criticized for having too many rules, refusing to comply with corporate demands, being oppositional and lacking etiquette, reliability and flexibility.
Gen Z’s desire for immediate feedback and flexible work environments often clashes with traditional practices, further exacerbating workplace tension and reducing overall productivity. A new study released today asks if relying too much on AI will make Gen Z rely less on people and diminish their social skills. Findings from the latest TalentLMS survey of 1,000 Gen Z employees (ages 20 to 27) in the U.S. sheds light on five concerning gaps on the horizon:
Gap 1. Seek Guidance From AI More Than Managers Or Colleagues
Almost half (46%) of Gen Z professionals say they get better guidance from AI than their managers. An additional 46% also report that they prefer asking AI about work-related questions rather than their colleagues or managers. This data points to a concerning pattern: When seeking support and guidance at work, the youngest workforce turns to AI over people. This shift can put collaborative workplace dynamics, such as mentorship, teamwork and knowledge sharing at risk.
The researchers explain this concern as the result of the major life milestones Gen Z has undergone in the isolated and remote world of the pandemic years. “Missing out on in-person interactions on campus and at work, they immersed themselves in screens, feeds, and technology,” the researchers state. “So when AI showed up, they embraced it. For Gen Z, AI isn’t just a new tech tool. It’s their 24/7 sidekick, helping them navigate work and life.”
To gauge AI’s impact on work relationships, the researchers asked Gen Z employees if they interact less with their colleagues because of AI. A slightly higher percentage (41%) report that using AI at work has not made them communicate less with their peers. Still, the researchers say they are worried that as many as 39% of Gen Zers interact less with colleagues because of AI.
According to the study, Gen Z responses signal that AI could curb collaborative dynamics in the workplace. “Even though they don’t appear to want it, young adults need guidance from their coworkers,” the researchers insist. “AI can answer questions but it can’t mentor them, give meaningful feedback, guide their development, or help them adapt to new environments. Turning to AI may be easier than navigating the complex world of human relationships.”
But the study authors emphasize that this easy fix comes with a cost. “It can strip young professionals of the opportunities to learn how to communicate and collaborate well with others. Less time spent in interactions with people will inevitably lead to underdeveloped people skills. Despite all the advantages, AI fluency can’t bridge the communication gap.”
Gap 2. Believe AI Has Negatively Affected Their Skills
The investigators wanted to know if Gen Z’s heavy reliance on AI builds their skill sets or strips them away. Although a majority (66%) believe using AI positively impacts their skills, close to 10% feel it has a negative impact and 15% say there’s no impact. Despite these positive findings, the investigators caution that the minority of Gen Z who are negatively affected still need support.
Gap 3. Lack Of Interest In Developing Soft Skills
Soft or interpersonal skills can be an antidote to disconnection and isolation of the digital age. Surprisingly, it turns out that a whopping 63% of Gen Zers think AI integration in the workplace should be accompanied by training on soft skills. These results indicate young professionals’ awareness on the mixed impact of AI. While recognizing AI is elevating their growth and development, they’re aware of the growing communication gap.
But the researchers identified a catch. The worrying findings they noted in the first concern—Gen Z’s preference to interact with AI over people at work—implies that Gen Z understands the importance of developing soft skills, but they don’t seem motivated to practice them. A confirmation of this conclusion is reflected in Gen Z’s ranking of the most impactful skills. Digital (52%) and hard/technical (46%) skills topped the crucial list, and interpersonal (35%) and emotional intelligence (31%) skills bottomed the list, underlining their strong connection with technology.
In the light of Gen Z’s lacking collaboration and communication skills, the authors say they feel unsettled to see Gen Z interpersonal skills and emotional intelligence at the lowest ranks. “AI can do wonders for Gen Z employees, but at the same time it throws a wrench into their development in terms of teamwork, communication and building workplace relationships.”
Gap 4. Miss Out On Learning Opportunities To Grow From
The researchers wanted to know if AI is hindering or propelling Gen Z growth opportunities. They identified a mixed patchwork with 62% of Gen Z employees saying AI has positively impacted their learning and development at work. Although that’s a strong statistic, the authors wanted to know about growth opportunities from various tasks that are now delegated to AI.
When they asked if AI has stripped Gen Z of growth opportunities, the sentiment was almost evenly split. On the positive side, a slightly higher number (42%) think AI hasn't held their growth back by doing tasks from which they could have learned. These respondents don’t see AI as an obstacle to their growth.
However, the data also shows a flip side—that 40% of Gen Z employees believe AI has hindered their growth by doing tasks from which they could have learned. A large portion of respondents feel like they’re missing out on learning opportunities, spotlighting what the researchers call the double-edged sword of AI efficiency.
“Just like smartphones weaken the intellect by making the brain dependent, any new tech that replaces the process of human discovery will have the same impact,” the authors point out. “Employees, especially the more inexperienced, may neglect their judgment and work on autopilot, missing chances to develop their problem-solving and critical-thinking skills.
Gap 5. Depend On AI To Complete Daily Work Tasks
The data indicates that while 38% of Gen Z employees are dependent on AI for completing their daily work, 44% are not. Still, the survey authors underscore the fact that 38% of Gen Z employees are dependent on AI is a caution light to keep an eye on. Furthermore, 68% see benefits of smart tech in their day-to-day work, finding AI helpful with their daily workflow and tasks.
The list of areas where AI helps young pros:
- 59%: improves decision-making
- 55%: aids onboarding at a new job
- 50%: assists with landing a new job
- 50%: bridges communication gaps with colleagues or other departments
Final Takeaway: Redefining The Workplace
The report interprets this new data to indicate that as Gen Z takes over the workplace, they’re putting human interaction on the back burner and gravitating toward technology. “AI can do wonders for Gen Z. But at the same time, it throws a wrench into their professional development,” the authors argue. “Especially when it comes to teamwork, communication and building workplace relationships.”
They explain that this interplay between the up-and-coming generation and machine minds in the workplace will redefine the workplace. “To help employers successfully navigate the transition, we have identified 5 takeaways—critical gaps that the survey data brought to light,” they conclude. “AI has the potential to elevate organizations that foster a strong people-centered culture. In contrast, it may erode the skill sets of those that remain in business-as-usual mode, lulling them to sleep.”

title: Chinese Companies Use AI To Bring Back Deceased Loved Ones, Raising Ethics Questions
text:
With just one minute of high-quality video, a Chinese company claims it can bring your loved ones back to life - via a very convincing, AI-generated avatar. “I do not treat the avatar as a kind of digital person, I truly regard it as a mother,” Sun Kai tells NPR, in a recent interview. Kai, age 47, works in the port city of Nanjing and says he converses with his mother - who is deceased - at least once a week on his computer. Sun works at Silicon Intelligence in China, and he says that his company can create a basic avatar for as little as $30 USD (199 Yuan). But what’s the real cost of recreating a person who has passed?
Through an interpreter, Zhang Zewei explains the challenges his company faced in bringing their “resurrection service” to life. “The crucial bit is cloning a person's thoughts, documenting what a person thought and experienced daily,” he says. Zhang is the founder of Super Brain, another company that’s using AI to build avatars of deceased loved ones. For an AI avatar to be truly generative and to chat like a person, Zhang admits it would take an estimated 10 years of prep to gather data and to take notes on a person's life. In fact, although generative AI is progressing, the desire to remember our lost loved ones usually outpaces the technology we have, Zhang shares. He says, “Chinese AI firms only allow people to digitally clone themselves or for family members to clone the deceased.”
Ethics Question: What’s the Real Risk?
The idea of digitally cloning people who have died is nothing new. AI girlfriends and online companions are prevalent - offering either the best or the worst of machine learning, depending on your point of view. Or your investment portfolio.
Turning to simulation for stimulation is a risky business for end users, but a profitable one for tech companies. Is it right to try and cheat death, or are we cheating ourselves, with these resurrected avatars? How do we move on, in the grieving process, if we use AI to short-circuit it? On an unrelated subject: how does my AI girlfriend really feel about me, and why does that question even matter?
Today, for these Chinese companies, science fiction is becoming fact. Chinese LLMs (large language model) AI companies like MediaTek and Baidu have created tools like BreeXe and ERNIE. According to reports, these LLMs are similar in capability to ChatGPT. And, like ChatGPT, the real extent of their capabilities (or potential damages?) remains a mystery.
Heartbreaking, or Heartwarming? AI-Generated Avatars
In 2017, Microsoft created simulated virtual conversations with the deceased, and filed a patent on the technology but never pursued it. Called “deadbots” by academics, avatars of deceased family members have raised questions about the ethics of “resurrecting” the deceased in electronic form.
For these Chinese companies, and their executives, there is hope that technology will offer some relief around the grieving process in China. There, mourning is extensive and can be quite elaborate. (Note that while “professional mourner” is a career path in China, expressions of daily grief are discouraged). According to in-country reports, a cultural taboo exists around discussing death.
As terrible as death can be, using AI to short-circuit the circle of life can be a slippery slope. For leaders, the ethics of AI remain an uncharted area. And a place where the pursuit of profit is resurrecting new concerns.

title: Council Post: Tech Experts Detail 12 Ways Pop Culture Misrepresents AI’s Abilities
text:
Artificial intelligence isn’t new to the industrial world—or to the realm of pop culture. AI has played a starring role in movies, TV shows and books for decades, but what’s portrayed on page and screen often bears little resemblance to the reality of AI’s influence and capabilities.
While it can be fun (or scary) to consume creative content that speculates about AI’s current or future impact on society, it’s important not to continue to suspend our disbelief when the show’s over. Below, 12 members of Forbes Technology Council detail some of the ways pop culture misrepresents AI’s potential and capabilities, as well as the truth of its current state and likely future.
1. It’s A ‘Set It And Forget It’ Solution
Popular culture often portrays AI as a “set it and forget it” solution without exploring how AI must be developed and trained. This leads to a lot of hype among the general public in terms of what AI can do. While AI has substantial and exciting applications, in reality, it also has many shortcomings. AI requires an active, informed and, indeed, skeptical user to achieve optimal benefits. - Patrick Smith, Certara
2. It’s Not For Everybody
Twenty years ago, I rented Terminator 3 at Blockbuster. AI is not the Terminator, and AI will not take your job—but someone who uses it better will. After watching NVIDIA’s astonishing, meteoric rise, here’s the real truth: Generative AI is changing every company and every industry on the planet. Companies will either embrace that fact, or they’ll become the next Blockbuster. - David Yunger, Vaital
Forbes Technology Council is an invitation-only community for world-class CIOs, CTOs and technology executives. Do I qualify?
3. It Can Develop Human-Like Emotions And Consciousness
Popular culture often portrays AI as having human-like emotions and consciousness, but in reality, AI is just advanced algorithms that process data and perform tasks without any understanding or feelings. AI is not even close to being as smart as humans. - Edin Deljkic, Klika
4. It Will Replace Us
AI is often portrayed as a futuristic, menacing technological advancement that replaces humans. However, AI’s best value is in augmenting human and machine interactions. This doesn’t mean chatbots. Rather, the best use of AI—the use that will produce increased adoption—is incorporating it into tools so that users are unaware of it, yet find that their experiences with systems are suddenly more intuitive, personalized and satisfying. - Lalitha Rajagopalan, ORO Labs, Inc.
5. It’s Always Right
One of the biggest mistakes popular culture makes about AI—the Generative Pre-trained Transformer type (such as ChatGPT)—is that it is always correct. In reality, GPT models can produce totally wrong answers based on the prompt, but present the answer with the highest level of confidence. If you don’t know what the right answer is, you could be way off the mark. Always verify what Copilot, Genesis or ChatGPT say. - John Bruggeman, CBTS
6. It’s Capable Of Autonomous Thought And Decision-Making
AI is frequently portrayed in popular culture as a sentient entity with human-like cognition and emotions that’s capable of autonomous thought and decision-making—an example is Ultron from the Marvel film. In actuality, AI is emotionless and lacks self-awareness. It is incapable of independent thought and acts solely with the help of algorithms and preprogrammed reactions. - Ashok Manoharan, FocusLabs
7. It May One Day Destroy Humanity
Many people have unconscious fears that artificial intelligence may destroy humanity in the future. The classic science fiction theme is human-robot wars. In reality, AI lacks consciousness and only works with big data based on given algorithms, which it can do faster than humans. The only danger we currently face from AI is that we will become overreliant on it and stop thinking critically ourselves. - Filip Dvorak, Filuta AI
8. It Can Help Us Become Immortal
In the 2014 movie Transcendence, AI is shown transferring human minds into computers, making people live forever digitally. This is a rare and incorrect idea. In reality, we can’t transfer human consciousness into machines. AI can handle data and imitate some human actions, but it can’t copy the full complexity of human thoughts and personalities. - Margarita Simonova, ILoveMyQA
9. It Provides Instantaneous Results
Whether it’s Mission: Impossible - Dead Reckoning or Stealth, one thing movies always get wrong about AI is that it’s instantaneous. Getting the best results out of AI requires deep thought and a lot of back-and-forth between the human and the AI app; it’s never a magic djinn that’s going to solve all your problems lickety-split. - Syed Ahmed, Act-On Software
10. It’s Creative
Movies and TV shows frequently show AI as highly creative, capable of autonomously producing original art, music or literature. The truth is that AI can only generate content based on patterns in the data it has been trained on; it lacks genuine creativity. Human intervention is crucial for guiding AI to produce meaningful and contextually appropriate outputs, limiting its creative abilities. - Jagadish Gokavarapu, Wissen Infotech
11. It Has Intrinsic Goals And Motivations
AI is frequently shown going rogue and turning against humanity. While it’s crucial to develop AI responsibly and institute proper safeguards, the reality is that AI inherently lacks human motivations, such as a thirst for power. Its “goals” are to optimize for the objectives it was programmed for. But bias in training data can lead to flawed models, so rigorously testing for safety and fairness is vital. - Marc Fischer, Dogtown Media LLC
12. It (True AI) Actually Exists
Popular culture doesn’t misrepresent AI; the reality is that true AI is the domain of science fiction. AI—actual artificial intelligence—doesn’t exist. What does exist are increasingly fast and well-trained models that are capable of generating real-time responses to prompts and rapid business intelligence. The rift between reality and AI is cultural. We choose to call real-life tools “AI” to drive interest. - Lewis Wynne-Jones, ThinkData Works

title: Artificial Expectations? Time To Get Real About AI
text:
When generative AI first came on the public scene a couple of years back, it was hard to contain peoples’ excitement about its possibilities. Now, a somewhat cooler reality has set in — AI is a powerful tool, but also capable of great misuse and abuse. Oh, and it’s often more expensive to implement than the problems it’s designed to solve.
The latest pushback against AI may even be a selling point. For example, Jonathan Bell, founder of Sprout, a platform for sustainable website development, recently announced his company will have nothing to do with AI, as the technology consumes too many resources and “might only add minimal value to our platform and it doesn't align with our values. We're not going to hop on the bandwagon just for the sake of a buzzword.”
Conversations about generative AI “are more earnest, moving from excitement and hype to more realistic assessments,” an analysis out of Bain & Company reports. “Concerns about security and conversations around implementation are more deliberate and informed as companies have a better understanding of the challenges based on learnings from their pilot programs.”
The consensus among the industry leaders and thinkers we queried is that AI is indeed a powerful tool, but needs to be approached with clear-headed thinking.
“In many ways, the hype around AI reminds me of the hype around the Internet during the dot-com era,” said Benjamin Lee, professor of computer and information science at the University of Pennsylvania. “At the time, there was a lot of excitement around investment in technology and infrastructure with the expectation that the Internet would be transformative. Indeed, it was but perhaps at a longer timescale than many had thought.”
AI has already proven to perform well in a number of domains, “such as software engineering and text summarization,” Lee continued. “But the rate and depth of adoption has been slower than many have anticipated."
For instance, getting to high-functioning AI will require a significant information technology infrastructure overhaul, requiring “massive investments in GPU and datacenter infrastructure,” Lee said.
Along with software engineering, AI is delivering impressive productivity gains and capabilities in areas such as sentiment analysis, fraud detection, search, and machine translation. But there are many areas where it has not moved the needle yet.
“AI struggles to do math or engage in multi-step logical reasoning, leading generative AI systems to create errors that seem obvious to humans,” said Michael Allen, chief technology officer at Laserfiche. “In these areas, AI is falling short of expectations that have been recently inflated by the success of AI in other areas.”
Robotics is another area where AI is not well-developed, Allen continued. “AI control of robotics still appears to be in its early stages,” he said. “The ability for AI to safely understand and navigate complex physical environments has been ‘just around the corner’ for years.”
An issue that has been a showstopper for AI at many levels is security and privacy. “Since AI tools are generalized, the challenge is allowing employees to use them without feeding private intellectual property data into their models,” Cliff Jurkiewicz, vice president of global strategy at Phenom, illustrated.
“Picking and choosing where to employ AI tools in an organization is another hurdle,” Jurkiewicz continued. “A big company with 50,000 employees isn’t going to turn AI tools on for everyone.”
Selecting the best applications across an organizations for AI requires a strategic plan that will help “decide where the tools will be most effective and can be measured and tested for their effectiveness,” said Jurkiewicz. Information flow is probably the best indicator. “Start with email,” he advises. “The tools are actually quite good at helping people craft better, more personalized, more engaging emails.”
Always keep the human in the loop, Lee urged. “For example, AI might be a great research assistant as long as the human user expects rough drafts and is prepared for multiple rounds of human review and revision.”
Deployment of AI models without immediate human oversight, such as coding assistants, “requires specialized tools and processes to monitor for errors and system performance that most enterprises have not yet developed to a high level of maturity,” Allen agreed. Those organizations that have already been working with traditional machine learning models are already ahead of the game, he added.
As well-functioning AI tends to be expensive and resource-intensive, is the return on investment worth the costs and efforts? At this point, “I think it unlikely that companies training and deploying models such as OpenAI are making significant returns from subscriptions given the capital costs of training and serving models," said Lee. Even the large technology providers, such as Apple and Amazon, “seem to be in a broad, exploratory phase.”
Once AI is embedded into commercially available tools and products — versus building and maintaining one’s own large language models — greater returns will likely finally be realized, Allen believes. “Where AI has been incorporated by vendors into existing tools, the benefits are usually realized very quickly and the feature is typically available at a predictable and relatively low cost,” he said.
It’s important to keep in mind that people are just starting to understand the best uses of AI for their roles. “Although the underlying technology is advancing at remarkable speed, knowledge workers will need time to understand the capabilities and its eventual impact on workflows,” said Lee. “It took decades for the Internet to transform the way we work and live. AI will be similarly transformative, but we are only a year or two into this process.”

title: How AI Has Made The Networking Market Exciting Again
text:
The networking infrastructure market is more dynamic and interesting than it’s been in decades—and AI is going to make it more interesting.
AI is a voracious consumer of data, whether that’s in the hyperscaler cloud, fueling the machinations of a large language model (LLM), or at the edge, where private infrastructure must gather and securely transmit data to any type of destination to be used for a variety of applications. This means more demand for network connections.
What’s interesting about AI is that not only will it create new market for networking infrastructure hardware and software, but it will also boost traditional networking markets such as datacenter and enterprise, because of the new demands for data.
All of this has dozens of networking players positioning for new markets that have been relatively static for decades. Cisco has dominated the networking market since the Internet bubble days, with estimates of 50%-60% market share in enterprise and datacenter networking markets. This lack of competitive dynamics has made the market a big dull. But that’s started changing in recent years, with competitors such as Arista Networks taking share in the cloud hyperscale markets. The looming merger of Juniper Networks and HPE also provides a twist, with that combination possibly taking the number two spot in networking. With Juniper ramping up its AI networking roadmap, it will become a more strategic asset for HPE. At the same time, Nvidia, the leader in chips for AI infrastructure, has also built its own full networking stack optimized for AI, jumping in front of the networking incumbents for AI workloads for hyperscaler LLMs.
Networking innovation also abounds. Startups such as Arrcus and DriveNets are attacking AI with a disaggregated hardware and cloudscale network operating system (NOS) approach. Hedgehog and Aviz Networks are leveraging the open-source Software for Open Networking in the Cloud (SONiC) NOS as well as cloud tools such as Kubernetes. And because AI requires more connectivity to more data, you can expect it to give a boost to multicloud networking, which features hot startups such as Alkira, Aryaka, Aviatrix, Graphiant, Itential, and Prosimo, among others.
This will all be great for the market. Networking buyers have more options than ever before. And they’ll be able to choose between many approaches, whether that’s a full networking stack provided by AI infrastructure leader Nvidia, best-of-breed networking with established companies such as Cisco and HPE/Juniper, or innovative startup solutions.
We’ll add more on the competition later, but first let’s look at the analysis of why networking for AI has different requirements.
Why AI Networking Is a New Market
It looks like AI applications will take many forms, ranging from huge cloud LLMs to other use cases, including small language models (SLMs) used in private clouds for specific vertical applications. For example, AI can be used to train a generalized chatbot to help with chat and writing, but it can also be used to develop drugs using customized data—or to optimize a manufacturing site.
The first thing to understand is that AI networking often has different requirements from traditional networking. The transition from general-purpose computing to accelerated computing requires new software and distributed networking architectures to connect, move, and process data at lightning-fast speeds, with very low latency and almost no tolerance for data loss. This isn’t networking in your local coffee shop.
The arms race to build huge LLM clouds has also spurred demand for specialized processors such as SmartNICs, IPUs, and DPUs to boost performance of networking, security, and storage functions of AI networks. But there are more areas to watch: Networking players will use a variety of architectures, software, and components to build more economical infrastructure to access AI models, whether those are at the edge or in the cloud. Whether connecting chips within supercomputers, interconnecting servers in AI clusters, or linking those clusters to the network edge, existing technologies must evolve to sustain the performance demanded by AI applications.
Futuriom recently spent months examining the end-user requirements for AI workloads in a detailed report on AI Networking. The market is already starting to segment, and it falls into two categories:
1) Training. This is the step in which LLMs such as ChatGPT, Llama, Claude AI, and Mistral are trained by repeatedly running billions of parameters against neural networks to forge a system that recognizes words, images, sounds, etc. These LLMs are fundamental to AI applications. SLMs will also require unique networking solutions.
2) Inference. This is the process of adapting an LLM or SLM to work with specific sets of data to create an AI application that delivers information, solves a specific problem, or completes a task. A bank, for instance, may adapt Claude AI to streamline customer service at ATMs by running the model against anonymized data from multiple transactions. This is often referred to as the “front end” of AI, and it also requires processing and networking capabilities closer to the customer.
Training and inference both call for features not present in traditional or general-purpose client-server networks or, for that matter, in high performance computing (HPC) networks based on that paradigm.
The new needs include the following: higher capacity (scaling to 400 Gb/s and 800 Gb/s), higher throughput, lower latency, high reliability, faster access to storage, optimized clustering, and high compute utilization—to only name a few.
Let the Competition Begin!
With AI continuing to capture the business world’s imagination with its potential for productivity gains and new digital products, it’s understandable there is excitement about the AI infra buildout. However, with the revenue and productivity gains still elusive, this is a multi-year cycle—if not a multi-decade cycle—in which changing business models and architectures are to be expected.
The AI networking market, which is estimated to be about 10%-15% of the total AI infrastructure budget, will certainly be billions of dollars, but it is starting from a low level. Arista Networks CEO Jayshree Ullal is on the record expecting $750 million networking revenue directly connected to AI buildouts in the next year, but that number is expected to grow fast.
The market for AI networking has thus far been described as InfiniBand vs. Ethernet, because of Nvidia’s early lead in connecting GPUs with networking has been focused on InfiniBand technology, which has special low-latency and lossless characteristics. However, Ethernet solutions are now coming to market, and Nvidia also has Ethernet-based technology with its Spectrum-X platform. As more Ethernet-based solutions come to market, the AI networking will broaden out. SLMs can be run by a wide variety of vertical businesses and don’t require the full horsepower of LLMs. They could even be implemented in private datacenters and infrastructure. Ethernet is broadly deployed, well understood, and can benefit from the economies of scale of widely available components.
To this end, Ethernet is being adapted to handle AI networking needs for lower latency and lossless communications—in a sense making it more InfiniBand-like, while at the same time taking advantage of Ethernet economics. A raft of vendors has teamed up and formed the Ultra Ethernet Consortium (UEC), which is tasked with introducing upgrades to the Ethernet standard to make it suitable for demanding AI environments, whether large or small. Ethernet has already been adapted with Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) over Converged Ethernet (RoCE) to make it more AI-class. And it’s going to further evolve. Most networking vendors support RoCEv2, which adds a variety of enhancements to RoCE, including DCQCN (Data Center Quantized Congestion Notification), a technology that combines PFC (Priority Flow Control) and ECN (Explicit Congestion Notification), as well as smart queuing and buffer management. Some vendors also have added AI and ML to RoCEv2 to improve overall performance.
There’s a lot to be said for open networking as well, whereby customers can opt for building their own networks by mixing and matching vendor NOSs and hardware. A strong portfolio of commercial silicon offerings from chipmakers Broadcom, Marvell, and Intel enables networking experts to use off-the-shelf hardware and pair it with the NOS of their choice, including the open-source SONiC.
Large, established networking vendors such as Arista, Cisco, Broadcom, Juniper, HPE, and Nokia have joined the UEC to pursue these goals. In this group, the forthcoming merger of Juniper and HPE looms large, giving the combined networking company more scale that is expected to make it the number-two by market share to Cisco.
AI networking also offers additional opportunities for startups. These include vendors with technology rooted in SONiC, such as Aviz Networks and Hedgehog, as well as startups focusing on scale-out, disaggregated systems based on their own NOS, such as Arrcus and Israel-based DriveNets, which already makes a hyperscale routing solution for the telecommunications market.
There are yet more vendors to watch in this explosive space. For example, startup Enfabrica offers a compute-to-compute interconnect switch for AI servers that acts as a high-bandwidth “crossbar of NICs,” augmenting compute, network, and memory connections within a cluster. And multicloud networking and network-as-a-service (NaaS) vendors such as Alkira, Aryaka, Aviatrix, Itential, and Prosimo are making it easier for organizations to build secure network connections to shuttle data to and from AI sources.
The AI networking boom will also fuel the optical market, in which high-speed optics are needed to support the boom in bandwidth. Here, optical equipment market leader Ciena’s position in coherent optics provides an opportunity to speed up interconnections in datacenters. Thailand-based Fabrinet has become a darling of AI investors, seeing strong growth in optical components for AI applications, as do rivals Coherent and Lumentum. Shares of optical fiber manufacturer Corning recently popped 10% after an earnings pre-announcement in which it increased its second-quarter sales expectations by around $200 million due in large part to greater-than-expected demand for fiber connections inside of datacenters running AI applications. This is also one of the areas where Cisco is well-positioned, with its own optical components which can be packaged with its Silicon One chip platform.
Put all this together and what you get is a huge and interesting scrum for AI infrastructure networking leadership, which is expected to provide plenty of twists and turns. Networking is cool again. Grab the popcorn!

title: The Rise Of Data-Centric Incident Response
text:
In many organizations, there is a divide between IT and security teams that can significantly hamper effective incident response.
Traditionally, IT and security teams have operated in silos, each focusing on different aspects of organizational protection. IT teams concentrate on maintaining system availability and recovering from user errors, application corruption, and disasters, while security teams focus on perimeter and production security.
During a cyber incident, this lack of coordination can lead to a chaotic race to understand what happened, prolonging the incident and exacerbating its impact.
The Need for a Unified Approach
A unified approach to incident response can streamline efforts, minimize damage, and enhance overall security posture. By fostering collaboration and integrating data insights across teams, organizations can bridge this operational gap. Effective incident response requires a common terminology and shared understanding of the data environment, enabling IT and security teams to work together seamlessly.
Druva recently announced a new Threat Hunting function that enhances its data security capabilities to accelerate incident response.
Stephen Manley, CTO of Druva, agreed that more effective collaboration between IT and security teams is crucial, but also emphasized the importance of data-centric strategies, stating, "We're seeing signals that would help you identify attacks better and troubleshoot them faster. By doing that, recovery gets easier because there's less to recover."
Data-Centric Security Strategies
The traditional perimeter faded into obscurity years ago, but many of the core defenses organizations rely on were designed with this “castle-and-moat” philosophy. Those solutions are increasingly insufficient in today's threat landscape.
According to Manley, organizations must prioritize data-centric security strategies that protect and govern data across its entire lifecycle. This shift allows for enhanced visibility into data movements, improved threat detection, and more effective incident response.
Data offers a unique perspective as a sort of “canary in the coal mine” early warning system. "Our unique view on the data allows us to feed valuable information back into security tools and Incident Response teams,” declared Manely. “This helps them understand the spread of attacks and map them accurately, ultimately leading to more effective remediation."
Leveraging Automation and AI in Cyber Defense
The future of threat hunting and incident response lies in the integration of automation and artificial intelligence. These technologies can revolutionize how organizations detect and respond to cyber threats by uncovering hidden threats and enabling rapid responses.
The role of AI in IT and cybersecurity is quickly evolving. Generative AI is being used by bad guys for social engineering and to understand environments better. Organizations need to embrace AI to respond in real-time.
While humans play a significant role, AI will increasingly drive detection and initial response.
Practical Implementation and Benefits
Implementing a unified, data-centric approach requires practical steps and strategic investments. Organizations should focus on continuous monitoring, integrating AI for rapid response, and fostering collaboration between IT and security teams.
Manley highlights the practical benefits of this approach: "We see this as a way for customers to start using generative AI without having to invest heavily in infrastructure. Trust us with your data and security monitoring, and we can help you respond faster and more effectively to incidents."
Future of Incident Response
Bridging the divide between IT and security teams is essential for effective incident response.
This proactive strategy not only streamlines incident response but also ensures robust data governance and protection in an increasingly complex threat landscape.
As Manley succinctly puts it, "It's not enough to generate alerts; we need to provide the right information and immediate action to stop threats in their tracks."
